cases.title: Tata Consultancy Services Limited v. Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
The genesis of this monumental corporate dispute lies in the intricate
relationship between Tata Sons Limited (the principal investment holding
company and promoter of Tata companies) and the Shapoorji Pallonji (SP)
Group. The SP Group, through Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. and Sterling
Investment Corporation Pvt. Ltd., held approximately 18.37% of the equity
share capital in Tata Sons. Tata Trusts, a group of philanthropic
entities, held the majority 66% stake.

In 2012, Ratan Tata retired as Chairman of Tata Sons, and Cyrus Mistry
(representing the SP Group) was appointed as the Executive Deputy
Chairman, subsequently elevated to Executive Chairman. The transition was
initially smooth, but over the next four years, fundamental differences
arose regarding corporate governance, capital allocation, and the
handling of legacy "hotspot" companies (such as Tata Steel Europe, Tata
Motors' Nano project, and the dispute with NTT Docomo).

The underlying friction centered on the interpretation of the Articles of
Association (AoA) of Tata Sons, specifically Article 121, which required
the affirmative vote of the directors nominated by Tata Trusts for any
board resolution to pass. Mistry alleged that this article was being used
by Ratan Tata and the Trusts as a "super-board" to interfere with his
fiduciary duties to the operating companies.

On October 24, 2016, in a sudden board meeting, a resolution was passed
replacing Cyrus Mistry as the Executive Chairman of Tata Sons. Ratan Tata
was appointed as Interim Chairman. Shortly thereafter, Mistry was removed
from the directorships of various Tata operating companies, often through
extraordinary general meetings (EGMs) called specifically for that
purpose.

Following his ouster, Cyrus Investments and Sterling Investment (the
respondents in the Supreme Court, hereafter "SP Group") filed a petition
before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) under Sections 241, 242,
and 244 of the Companies Act, 2013, alleging oppression and
mismanagement. They also challenged the conversion of Tata Sons from a
public company to a private company. The NCLT dismissed the SP Group's
petition. However, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT)
spectacularly reversed this decision, reinstating Mistry as Executive
Chairman and declaring the conversion of Tata Sons to a private company
illegal. Tata Sons appealed to the Supreme Court of India.
cases.issues:
Did the removal of Cyrus Mistry as Executive Chairman of Tata Sons, and
subsequently as a director, amount to "oppressive and prejudicial"
conduct under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013?

Did the affirmative voting rights of the Tata Trusts' nominee directors
under Article 121 of the Articles of Association constitute a tool for
oppression and a breach of corporate governance norms?

Was the conversion of Tata Sons from a public limited company to a
private limited company legally valid, or was it a surreptitious act of
oppression against the minority shareholders (SP Group)?

Did the NCLAT possess the jurisdiction to grant relief (reinstating
Mistry) that was not explicitly prayed for by the respondents in their
original pleadings?

Is the concept of a "quasi-partnership" applicable to Tata Sons, thereby
granting the SP Group a legitimate expectation of management
participation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Tata Sons Limited)
Tata Sons argued that the NCLAT's decision was fundamentally flawed and
legally untenable. They contended that Section 241 of the Companies Act,
2013, requires a continuous course of oppressive conduct that is "harsh,
burdensome, and wrongful." The removal of an Executive Chairman, a
position devoid of inherent legal tenure and subject to the pleasure of
the Board, is a matter of corporate democracy and loss of confidence, not
oppression.

Counsel for Tata argued that the Board of Directors had objectively lost
faith in Mistry's leadership due to his handling of sensitive corporate
matters and his leakage of internal documents to the media, which harmed
the Tata brand. Regarding Article 121, Tata Sons submitted that the
Articles of Association constitute a binding contract. The SP Group had
willingly bought shares and participated in the company fully aware of
these Articles. The affirmative rights were designed to protect the
philanthropic objectives of the Trusts, not to oppress minority
shareholders.

Furthermore, Tata Sons argued that the NCLAT committed a gross
jurisdictional error by reinstating Mistry. Mistry's original tenure had
already expired by the time of the NCLAT judgment, and the SP Group had
not even explicitly prayed for his reinstatement as Executive Chairman in
their final pleadings. Lastly, Tata Sons emphasized that it is not a
"quasi-partnership." It is a massive corporate conglomerate, and the SP
Group's shares were acquired through ordinary commercial transactions,
not as part of an underlying partnership agreement.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Cyrus Investments / SP Group)
The SP Group argued that Mistry's removal was a meticulously orchestrated
"coup," executed in blatant violation of the principles of natural
justice and corporate governance. They argued that the removal was the
culmination of continuous interference by Ratan Tata and the nominee
directors of Tata Trusts, who acted as a "shadow board."

Counsel for the SP Group relied on the "just and equitable" clause under
Section 242, arguing that the affairs of the company were being conducted
in a manner prejudicial to public interest and the interests of the
company. They cited the continued funding of loss-making enterprises
(like the Nano project) out of emotional attachment rather than sound
business logic, which constituted mismanagement.

The respondents further argued that the structural relationship between
the majority shareholders (Trusts) and the company essentially functioned
as a quasi-partnership, given the long-standing historical relationship
between the Tata and Shapoorji Pallonji families. Therefore, Mistry had a
"legitimate expectation" of continued participation in management, and
his abrupt removal was an oppressive exclusion. They also vehemently
attacked the conversion of Tata Sons to a private company, arguing it was
a deliberate mechanism to restrict the SP Group's ability to freely
transfer their shares, thereby locking in their capital and diluting
their rights.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India, in a comprehensive judgment delivered by a
bench headed by Chief Justice S.A. Bobde, ruled decisively in favor of
Tata Sons Limited. The Court set aside the NCLAT's judgment in its
entirety, dismissing the allegations of oppression and mismanagement
raised by the SP Group. The Court upheld Mistry's removal and validated
the conversion of Tata Sons into a private company.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court meticulously dismantled the NCLAT's reasoning. The
Court began by clarifying the strict threshold required to trigger
Sections 241 and 242. It held that the mere removal of a director or an
executive officer does not, ipso facto, constitute oppression. For
conduct to be oppressive, it must involve a persistent and continuing
course of action that is visibly burdensome and wrongful to the minority
shareholder in their capacity as a shareholder, not merely as a director.
The Court found that the Tata Sons board was well within its rights to
remove an Executive Chairman in whom it had lost confidence.

Addressing the "quasi-partnership" argument, the Court categorically
rejected its application to Tata Sons. The Court noted that the SP
Group's holding was acquired over decades through various transactions,
and there was no foundational agreement of equal participation in
management. The mere historical association of two business families does
not legally transform a massive corporate entity into a quasi-
partnership. Therefore, Mistry had no legally enforceable "legitimate
expectation" to a board seat or the chairmanship.

On the issue of the Articles of Association (specifically Article 121),
the Court ruled that the NCLAT erred in rewriting the corporate contract.
The SP Group had been a shareholder for decades under the same Articles
without complaint. The affirmative voting rights were a valid mechanism
incorporated by the majority shareholders to protect their interests,
which is a standard corporate practice and does not inherently constitute
oppression.

Furthermore, the Court severely criticized the NCLAT for granting reliefs
that were never prayed for. Reinstating Mistry to a tenure that had
already legally expired, and doing so for operating companies that were
not even parties to the suit, was deemed a massive overreach of judicial
authority. Finally, regarding the conversion of Tata Sons to a private
company, the Court held that the procedures laid down in the Companies
Act were duly followed, and the structural change was a legitimate
corporate action, not an oppressive tactic.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Separation of Shareholder Rights and Directorial Tenure: The Court
definitively established that disputes regarding directorial tenure,
removal, or employment terms do not fall within the ambit of "oppression"
under Section 241 of the Companies Act unless they directly and
prejudicially impact the proprietary rights of the person as a
shareholder.

Threshold for Oppression: To succeed in an oppression claim, the minority
must prove a continuous, deliberate, and wrongful course of conduct.
Isolated acts, even if procedurally flawed, do not meet the threshold for
winding up a company on "just and equitable" grounds.

Rejection of Broad Quasi-Partnership Applications: The judgment
significantly narrowed the scope of the "quasi-partnership" doctrine in
India. It clarified that this equitable principle cannot be loosely
applied to large corporate entities merely based on historical family
ties; there must be clear evidence of a foundational agreement for joint
management.

Sanctity of Articles of Association: The ruling reinforced the principle
that the AoA is a binding commercial contract. Courts and tribunals
cannot rewrite these articles or strike down affirmative voting rights of
majority shareholders unless they are demonstrably illegal or actively
used to commit fraud.

Judicial Restraint in NCLT/NCLAT Rulings: The Supreme Court set a stern
precedent regarding the jurisdictional limits of company tribunals,
emphasizing that they cannot grant sweeping reliefs beyond what is
explicitly pleaded, nor can they interfere in the internal commercial
wisdom of the Board of Directors without compelling evidence of statutory
breach.

cases.title: Balwant Rai Saluja v. Air India Ltd.
cases.facts:
The dispute arose concerning the employment status of workmen engaged in
the canteens established at the premises of Air India Limited. Air India,
a statutory body (at the time), had incorporated a wholly-owned
subsidiary named Hotel Corporation of India (HCI) in 1971. HCI was tasked
with managing flight kitchens and providing catering services. To fulfill
its operational requirements, HCI employed various workmen.

The core of the conflict began when the workmen employed by HCI to run
the canteens at Air India's establishments raised an industrial dispute.
They contended that since the canteens were being run on Air India's
premises, for the benefit of Air India's employees, and because Air India
had a statutory obligation under the Factories Act, 1948, to maintain a
canteen, they should be legally recognized as the direct employees of Air
India, not HCI.

The workmen argued that HCI was merely a corporate facade-a camouflage
created by Air India to evade its statutory responsibilities towards the
canteen workers and to deny them the pay scales and benefits enjoyed by
regular Air India employees. They sought regularization of their services
directly under the principal employer, Air India.

The matter went through the Central Government Industrial Tribunal (CGIT)
and the Delhi High Court. The High Court ruled against the workmen,
stating that they were employees of HCI, a separate legal entity, and
could not be deemed employees of Air India. The workmen subsequently
appealed to the Supreme Court of India.
cases.issues:
Whether the workmen employed by Hotel Corporation of India (HCI) in the
canteens situated on Air India's premises could be treated as the direct
employees of Air India?

Under what specific circumstances can the courts pierce the "corporate
veil" to hold a parent company (Air India) liable for the employment
obligations of its wholly-owned subsidiary (HCI)?

Does the statutory obligation of an employer to provide a canteen under
Section 46 of the Factories Act automatically make the workers of that
canteen the direct employees of the principal employer?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Balwant Rai Saluja / Workmen)
The appellants argued forcefully that the corporate veil of HCI should be
lifted. They contended that HCI was completely controlled and managed by
Air India, with Air India providing the infrastructure, premises, and
capital. Since HCI was a wholly-owned subsidiary, its distinct legal
personality was merely an illusion meant to deprive the workers of their
rightful status and benefits.

Furthermore, the appellants relied heavily on the statutory obligations
mandated by the Factories Act. They argued that because Air India was
legally mandated to run a canteen, anyone employed to fulfill this
statutory duty must automatically be considered an employee of the
principal establishment. They asserted that Air India exercised pervasive
control over the canteen's functioning, determining the prices, the menu,
and the subsidies, thereby passing the "control test" for an employer-
employee relationship.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Air India Ltd.)
Air India defended its position by relying on the fundamental principle
of separate corporate personality established in Salomon v. Salomon & Co.
They argued that HCI was an independent corporate entity registered under
the Companies Act, with its own Memorandum and Articles of Association,
its own board of directors, and its own distinct business operations
(which extended beyond just Air India canteens to managing hotels and
flight kitchens for other airlines).

Air India contended that there was no "sham" or "camouflage" intended to
defraud workers. The subsidiary was created for valid commercial and
administrative reasons. Regarding the Factories Act, the respondents
argued that a statutory obligation to provide a canteen does not
translate into a statutory mandate to directly employ the staff running
it. An employer is free to engage an independent contractor or a
subsidiary to fulfill this obligation. Crucially, Air India pointed out
that it had no disciplinary control over the HCI workmen; HCI handled
their hiring, firing, and salaries.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India dismissed the appeals filed by the workmen.
The Court held that the workmen were employees of HCI and could not be
declared the direct employees of Air India. The Court refused to pierce
the corporate veil, reinforcing the separate legal entity of the
subsidiary company.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court undertook a meticulous examination of the employer-
employee relationship and the doctrine of piercing the corporate veil.

First, the Court addressed the "control test." It clarified that to
establish an employer-employee relationship, the principal employer must
exercise absolute and effective control over the workers. This means
having the power to appoint, dismiss, take disciplinary action, and
dictate not just what work is to be done, but how it is to be done. In
this case, while Air India controlled the quality and pricing of the food
(the end product), HCI exercised absolute administrative and disciplinary
control over the workmen. Therefore, no direct employment relationship
existed.

Second, the Court analyzed the Factories Act argument. The Court held
that while the Act requires the establishment of a canteen, it does not
dictate the mode of its operation. Fulfilling a statutory duty through an
independent entity or a subsidiary is perfectly legal and does not
automatically make the principal company the employer of the canteen
staff.

Finally, the Court delivered a seminal ruling on piercing the corporate
veil. The Court held that the separate legal personality of a company is
a foundational rule of corporate law. The veil can only be pierced in
highly restrictive circumstances: specifically, when the subsidiary is a
mere "sham" or "facade" created with the deliberate and specific intent
to commit fraud, evade legal obligations, or avoid taxation. The mere
fact that a parent company holds 100% of the shares, or exercises general
operational oversight, is entirely insufficient to lift the veil. Because
HCI was a legitimate business entity engaged in broader commercial
activities beyond just Air India's canteens, there was no evidence of
fraudulent intent to justify disregarding its corporate personality.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Strict Application of Piercing the Veil: The Supreme Court severely
restricted the grounds for lifting the corporate veil in India, moving
away from a loose application based on "justice and equity" to a strict
requirement of proving a "sham" or deliberate "fraud" designed to evade
existing obligations.

The "Effective Control" Test: The judgment clarified the parameters of
the control test in labor jurisprudence. It established that supervisory
control over the final product or service does not constitute an
employer-employee relationship; the principal must have disciplinary and
administrative control over the worker.

Statutory Duty vs. Employment Liability: The case firmly established that
a statutory obligation to provide a facility (like a canteen) does not
legally bind the principal employer to absorb the workers providing that
facility as direct employees, preserving the legality of outsourcing and
subsidiary management.

cases.title: Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement
cases.facts:
Standard Chartered Bank (SCB), a multinational banking corporation, was
issued notices by the Directorate of Enforcement (DoE) in India for
alleged contraventions of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973
(FERA). The DoE initiated adjudicatory proceedings against the bank for
various violations related to foreign exchange transactions.

Under Section 56 of FERA, certain offenses carried a mandatory statutory
punishment of imprisonment for a term that could extend to six months, in
addition to a fine. As the proceedings progressed, Standard Chartered
Bank filed a writ petition challenging the prosecution.

The bank's primary contention was rooted in the physical impossibility of
the punishment. They argued that a corporation is an artificial, juristic
person. It does not have a physical body and therefore cannot be
subjected to custodial imprisonment. Since the statute explicitly
mandated imprisonment and fine ("shall be punishable with imprisonment...
and with fine") for the alleged offenses, the bank argued that a
corporate body simply could not be prosecuted for such offenses. The
legal maxim relied upon was Lex non cogit ad impossibilia (the law does
not compel the doing of impossibilities).

The Bombay High Court rejected the bank's plea, holding that the company
could be prosecuted and subjected to a fine, even if imprisonment was
impossible. Standard Chartered Bank subsequently appealed to the Supreme
Court of India.
cases.issues:
Can a company or a corporate entity be prosecuted for a criminal offense
where the statute mandates a mandatory minimum sentence of imprisonment
coupled with a fine?

Does the physical impossibility of imprisoning a juristic entity grant it
blanket immunity from prosecution under statutes that prescribe mandatory
custodial sentences?

How should courts interpret penal statutes involving corporate offenders
when a strict literal interpretation leads to the complete exemption of
the corporation from liability?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Standard Chartered Bank)
SCB's legal team presented a heavily formalistic and literal
interpretation of criminal jurisprudence. They argued that penal statutes
must be construed strictly. Section 56 of FERA explicitly used the
conjunctive "and" (imprisonment and fine).

The bank argued that when a statute provides for a mandatory sentence of
imprisonment, the court has no judicial discretion to sever the
punishment and impose only the fine. Because a company cannot be
imprisoned, prosecuting it for an offense requiring mandatory
imprisonment is legally absurd. If the legislature had intended for
corporations to be prosecuted under this specific section, it would have
drafted the statute differently, perhaps allowing for imprisonment or
fine, or providing a separate fine-only provision for corporate bodies.
Therefore, SCB argued that the legislative intent implicitly excluded
corporate entities from the purview of offenses carrying mandatory
imprisonment.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Directorate of Enforcement)
The DoE, representing the State, argued that granting corporations
immunity from severe economic offenses simply because they lack a
physical body would lead to disastrous consequences for corporate
regulation and public policy.

The DoE urged the Court to adopt a purposive approach to statutory
interpretation. The intention of FERA was to strictly regulate foreign
exchange and penalize severe economic violations. Large corporations are
the primary actors capable of committing massive foreign exchange frauds.
To say they cannot be prosecuted for the most serious offenses under the
Act would defeat the entire purpose of the legislation. The State argued
that while the court cannot physically imprison the company, it can
enforce the monetary penalty (the fine). The maxim Lex non cogit ad
impossibilia should be applied to mean that the court is excused from
imposing the impossible part of the sentence (imprisonment) but must
still impose the possible part (fine).
cases.judgment:
In a landmark 3:2 majority decision, the Supreme Court of India ruled in
favor of the Directorate of Enforcement. The Court held that a company
can indeed be prosecuted for offenses that carry a mandatory sentence of
imprisonment and fine. In such cases, the Court ruled, the judicial
magistrate has the authority to impose only the fine on the corporate
entity.
cases.reasoning:
The majority opinion, delivered by Justice K.G. Balakrishnan, marked a
significant evolution in Indian corporate criminal liability. The Court
rejected the strict literal interpretation advanced by the bank, noting
that it would result in a gross miscarriage of justice by giving large
corporations a "blanket immunity" for serious economic crimes, while
prosecuting poor individuals for minor infractions.

The Court held that the legislative intent behind severe economic
statutes is to deter corporate crimes, not to immunize the corporations
committing them. The Court applied the principle that if a statute
intends to penalize an act, the procedural or physical impossibility of
enforcing one part of the punishment on a specific class of offenders
(corporations) does not invalidate the prosecution itself.

The Court observed that there is no immunity for companies from
prosecution merely because the prosecution relates to offenses for which
the punishment of imprisonment is mandatory. The judicial discretion lies
in the sentencing phase. When the offender is a corporate body, the court
cannot impose the custodial sentence, but it must enforce the fine. The
dissenting judges, however, maintained a strict constructionist view,
arguing that courts cannot rewrite statutes to split mandatory
punishments, and it was up to Parliament to amend the law (which
Parliament eventually did in several subsequent economic statutes).
cases.legalPrinciples:
Corporate Criminal Liability for Mandatory Imprisonment: This case
definitively established that juristic persons are not immune from
prosecution for offenses carrying mandatory imprisonment. It shattered
the traditional defense that corporations cannot commit serious crimes
requiring custodial sentences.

Purposive Interpretation of Penal Statutes: The Supreme Court
demonstrated a willingness to depart from strict literal interpretation
of penal statutes when such an interpretation leads to an absurd result
or defeats the core objective of the legislation (e.g., granting immunity
to major economic offenders).

Severability of Punishment: The Court created a jurisprudential mechanism
allowing judges to sever a conjunctive mandatory punishment (imprisonment
and fine), applying only the monetary penalty to corporate entities,
thereby bridging the gap between corporate reality and traditional
criminal law drafting.

cases.title: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts:
Mafatlal Industries Ltd. (MIL) and Mafatlal Fine Spinning and
Manufacturing Co. Ltd. (MFL) proposed a scheme of amalgamation. The
scheme was approved by the requisite statutory majority of shareholders
and creditors. However, Miheer H. Mafatlal, a minority shareholder and
member of the promoter family engaged in a separate family feud, objected
to the amalgamation. He argued that the share exchange ratio was unfair
to minority shareholders and that the scheme was a ploy to dilute his
holding.
cases.issues:
What is the scope of the Court's jurisdiction when sanctioning a scheme
of amalgamation under Sections 391 and 394 of the Companies Act, 1956
(now Sections 230-232 of the 2013 Act)?

Can the Court substitute its own commercial wisdom for the commercial
wisdom of the shareholders who approved the scheme?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Miheer H. Mafatlal)
The appellant argued that the Court must act as an appellate authority
and scrutinize the intrinsic fairness of the valuation and share exchange
ratio. He contended that the majority shareholders acted oppressively and
that the scheme was a facade to marginalize him, thereby violating the
"just and equitable" standard required for court sanction.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Mafatlal Industries)
The respondent argued that the valuation was conducted by recognized
experts and approved by an overwhelming majority of shareholders who
understood their commercial interests. They contended that the Court's
role is strictly supervisory-to ensure statutory compliance and lack of
fraud-not to second-guess the commercial prudence of the deal.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court upheld the scheme of amalgamation, dismissing Miheer
Mafatlal's objections, and ruled in favor of the respondent company.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the "Broad Contours" of its jurisdiction in
amalgamation cases. It reasoned that a scheme is fundamentally a
commercial document. The Court acts as an umpire, not an appellate
authority. As long as statutory procedures were followed, the meetings
were fairly conducted, there was no coercion or fraud, and the scheme was
not blatantly contrary to public policy, the Court must respect the
commercial wisdom of the statutory majority. Minor deviations in
valuation do not render a scheme unfair.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Commercial Wisdom of the Majority: The Court will not interfere with the
commercial merits of an amalgamation if approved by the statutory
majority.

Supervisory Role of Courts: The judiciary's role is restricted to
ensuring procedural fairness, statutory compliance, and ensuring the
scheme is not unconscionable or contrary to public interest.

cases.title: SEBI v. Rakesh Agrawal
cases.facts:
Rakesh Agrawal, the Managing Director of ABS Industries Ltd., was
negotiating a corporate tie-up with Bayer AG. Prior to the public
announcement of this tie-up, Agrawal orchestrated the purchase of ABS
shares through his brother-in-law to consolidate promoter holdings. SEBI
initiated action against him for insider trading, arguing he traded while
in possession of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI).
cases.issues:
Is mens rea (the intention to make an unfair profit or cause loss) an
essential ingredient to establish the offense of insider trading under
SEBI regulations?

Does trading to consolidate promoter holdings for corporate benefit,
rather than personal gain, constitute a defense against insider trading?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (SEBI)
SEBI argued that the Insider Trading Regulations are absolute. Trading
while possessing UPSI is a strict liability offense. Motive, intent, or
mens rea are irrelevant. The very act of the Managing Director buying
shares before a major announcement undermines market integrity.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Rakesh Agrawal)
Agrawal argued that he did not trade for personal profiteering. The
shares were bought to ensure the Bayer AG deal went through smoothly by
stabilizing promoter holdings. He argued that without the intent to cheat
the market or make a personal windfall (mens rea), the charge of insider
trading cannot stand.
cases.judgment:
The Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) ruled in favor of Rakesh Agrawal,
holding that mens rea is an essential ingredient for insider trading.
(Note: SEBI later amended regulations to make insider trading a strict
liability offense, overturning the practical application of this ruling).
cases.reasoning:
SAT reasoned that the core objective of insider trading laws is to
prevent corporate insiders from abusing their position for personal
enrichment at the expense of ordinary investors. Since Agrawal's actions
were driven by corporate necessity (securing a joint venture) rather than
a desire for personal, illicit profit, the foundational requirement of
fraudulent intent was missing.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Fiduciary Intent: Highlighted the early jurisprudential debate in India
regarding whether regulatory offenses require criminal intent (mens rea).

Evolution of Strict Liability: While SAT favored the mens rea approach,
this case is legally significant because it forced SEBI to amend its
regulations, unequivocally shifting insider trading in India to a strict
liability regime where motive is largely irrelevant.

cases.title: Dale & Carrington Invt. P. Ltd. v. P.K. Prathapan
cases.facts:
Ramanujam, the Managing Director of Dale & Carrington (a private
company), allotted additional equity shares to himself without informing
the other major shareholder, P.K. Prathapan. This allotment reduced
Prathapan from a majority shareholder to a minority shareholder.
Ramanujam claimed the company needed funds and the board was authorized
to issue shares. Prathapan sued for oppression and mismanagement.
cases.issues:
Can the Board of Directors use their power to issue additional shares
solely to alter the balance of power within the company?

What is the standard of fiduciary duty owed by a Managing Director when
allotting shares?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (P.K. Prathapan)
Prathapan argued that the allotment was a mala fide exercise of power.
The sole purpose was not to raise genuine capital for the company, but to
clandestinely dilute his shareholding and seize absolute control,
constituting severe oppression.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Ramanujam)
Ramanujam argued that the company was facing a financial crunch, and he
infused his own capital to save it. He claimed the Articles of
Association gave the Board absolute discretion in the allotment of
unissued shares.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of P.K. Prathapan, declaring the
allotment of shares to the Managing Director illegal and setting it
aside.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that directors act as fiduciaries. Their power to issue
shares is a fiduciary power that must be exercised bona fide and in the
paramount interest of the company, not for personal aggrandizement. The
Court found no evidence of a genuine financial emergency that required
such a clandestine allotment. The true motive was to convert a majority
shareholder into a minority, which is a blatant breach of fiduciary duty
and an act of oppression.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Fiduciary Duty in Share Allotment: Directors cannot issue shares to
themselves or their allies merely to maintain or seize corporate control.

Bona Fide Corporate Purpose: Any exercise of directorial power that
structurally alters the company's ownership must be justified by a
genuine, overarching corporate need.

cases.title: Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Following the enactment of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC),
2016, several corporate debtors and operational creditors filed writ
petitions challenging the constitutional validity of various provisions
of the Code. A primary contention was the differential treatment given to
Financial Creditors (e.g., banks) versus Operational Creditors (e.g.,
suppliers). Financial creditors were given seats on the Committee of
Creditors (CoC) and voting rights to decide the company's fate, while
operational creditors were largely excluded.
cases.issues:
Is the classification between "Financial Creditors" and "Operational
Creditors" under the IBC violative of Article 14 (Right to Equality) of
the Constitution?

Does the IBC arbitrarily strip promoters of their rights by ousting them
from management during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
(CIRP)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Petitioners (Swiss Ribbons / Corporate Debtors /
Operational Creditors)
The petitioners argued that treating operational and financial creditors
differently for the purpose of CoC representation was discriminatory.
They also argued that Section 29A, which bars promoters from bidding for
their own company during insolvency, was draconian and retrospectively
penalized even innocent promoters.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Union of India)
The government argued that the IBC was vital economic legislation
designed to resolve India's massive Non-Performing Asset (NPA) crisis.
They justified the distinction by arguing that financial creditors
(banks) have the expertise to assess the viability of a corporate debtor,
whereas operational creditors only care about recovering their specific
dues. Section 29A was defended as necessary to prevent defaulting
promoters from buying back their assets at a steep discount.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the IBC in its
entirety, ruling in favor of the Union of India.
cases.reasoning:
The Court deferred to legislative wisdom on economic matters. It held
there is an "intelligible differentia" between financial and operational
creditors. Financial creditors deal in large-scale capital and have the
capability to restructure a failing entity. Operational creditors merely
supply goods and services. Therefore, prioritizing financial creditors in
the CoC is rationally linked to the IBC's goal of corporate revival. The
Court also upheld the ouster of promoters, noting that a company in
default belongs to its creditors, validating the shift to a "creditor-in-
control" regime.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Creditor-in-Control Regime Validated: Cemented the fundamental shift in
Indian insolvency law from debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control.

Intelligible Differentia in Commercial Law: Reaffirmed that the
legislature has broad latitude to classify entities (like types of
creditors) based on commercial realities without violating the right to
equality.

cases.title: Re: Apex Industries Ltd.
cases.facts:
Apex Industries Ltd., a highly profitable manufacturing firm, posted a
net profit of INR 500 Crores. Under Section 135 of the Companies Act,
2013, it was mandated to spend 2% of its average net profits on Corporate
Social Responsibility (CSR). The CSR Committee approved a project to
build rural schools. However, by the end of the financial year, the funds
remained unspent. To avoid transferring the unspent amount to a
government fund, the Board created a shell trust and transferred the
money there, claiming the CSR obligation was "fulfilled," though no
schools were built.
cases.issues:
Does transferring mandated CSR funds to an unapproved trust without
executing the actual project constitute compliance under Section 135?

What are the penal consequences for the Board of Directors for
obfuscating the unspent CSR amount in the Director's Report?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Prosecution (Registrar of Companies)
The RoC argued that CSR is not a mere accounting entry. Section 135
requires actual, measurable deployment of capital toward approved social
projects. Transferring funds to a shell trust is a fraudulent
circumvention of the law, making the directors liable for penal action
and fines.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Apex Industries Board)
The Board argued that the funds were irrevocably earmarked and moved out
of the company's operational accounts, thus satisfying the requirement of
"spending" from the company's perspective.
cases.judgment:
(As a composite problem) The Tribunal found the Board of Directors guilty
of non-compliance and misreporting under the Companies Act.
cases.reasoning:
The Tribunal noted that the 2019 and 2020 amendments to Section 135
shifted CSR from a "comply or explain" model to a mandatory obligation
with strict penal consequences. Funds not spent on an ongoing project
must be transferred to a Schedule VII fund (like the Prime Minister's
National Relief Fund). Creating a private trust as a holding pen violates
both the letter and spirit of the law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Mandatory Nature of CSR: CSR in India is a hard legal obligation, not
voluntary philanthropy.

Director Accountability: Directors face direct financial penalties for
failing to oversee the actual execution of CSR projects and for
falsifying the Board's report regarding these expenditures.

cases.title: Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. Mindtree Ltd.
cases.facts:
Engineering giant Larsen & Toubro (L&T) launched a hostile takeover bid
for Mindtree Ltd., a mid-sized IT services company. L&T purchased a
20.32% stake from Mindtree's largest investor (V.G. Siddhartha) and
simultaneously made an open offer under the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition
of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011, to acquire a controlling
stake. Mindtree's promoters vehemently opposed the takeover, attempting
to institute defensive measures (like a share buyback) to thwart L&T.
cases.issues:
Under the SEBI Takeover Code, what defensive mechanisms are legally
permissible for a target company's promoters facing a hostile bid?

What is the fiduciary duty of the Independent Directors of a target
company during a hostile takeover?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Acquirer (L&T)
L&T argued that its bid was purely a commercial, value-creating
proposition. It strictly followed SEBI Takeover Code procedures. L&T
contended that Mindtree's promoters, who held a relatively small
percentage of shares, had no legal right to block shareholders from
accepting a premium offer, and that defensive tactics like sudden
buybacks breached corporate governance norms.

B. Arguments for the Target Promoters (Mindtree)
Mindtree promoters argued that a hostile takeover by a non-IT engineering
conglomerate would destroy Mindtree's unique corporate culture and client
trust. They attempted to rally institutional investors to reject the open
offer.
cases.judgment:
The takeover was successful. L&T acquired a controlling stake (over 60%),
and the Mindtree promoters eventually capitulated and resigned from the
board.
cases.reasoning:
While not heavily litigated in court, this case defined modern Indian M&A
law. SEBI regulations severely restrict "poison pills" and defensive
tactics once an open offer is triggered. The target board cannot
undertake material restructuring or buybacks without shareholder approval
once a bid is live. The Committee of Independent Directors was forced to
remain neutral, ultimately advising shareholders to evaluate the open
offer on its financial merits alone.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Shareholder Primacy in Takeovers: The SEBI Takeover Code prioritizes the
right of shareholders to exit at a premium over the promoters' desire to
retain control.

Strict Limitations on Defenses: Indian corporate law provides very little
room for target boards to deploy structural defenses against a hostile
acquirer who complies with SEBI pricing and procedural norms.

cases.title: Sandvik Asia Ltd. v. Bharat Kumar Padamsi
cases.facts:
Sandvik Asia Ltd. was predominantly owned by its foreign parent company.
The promoters decided to take the company fully private. To do so, they
utilized Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Reduction of Share
Capital), proposing to extinguish the shares held by the minority public
shareholders. In return, the minority shareholders were offered a
substantial premium over the market price of the shares. A minority
shareholder objected, arguing this was a forcible "squeeze-out" and
deprived them of their property rights.
cases.issues:
Can a company use capital reduction mechanisms to selectively cancel the
shares of minority shareholders, effectively forcing them out of the
company?

Does a "squeeze-out" of minority shareholders constitute oppression if
they are compensated with a fair valuation premium?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Minority Shareholders)
The minority argued that capital reduction should be applied pro-rata to
all shareholders. Singling out the minority to extinguish their holding
is inherently discriminatory and oppressive. They argued they had a right
to remain invested in a profitable company.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Sandvik Asia)
The company argued that Section 100 allows for selective reduction of
capital if approved by the special majority of shareholders and confirmed
by the Court. They emphasized that the valuation was done by an
independent valuer and offered a massive premium, meaning the minority
was not being prejudiced financially.
cases.judgment:
The Bombay High Court (and subsequently upheld in principle by higher
courts in similar matters) sanctioned the capital reduction, allowing the
squeeze-out.
cases.reasoning:
The Court noted that corporate democracy relies on the rule of the
majority. If the majority decides that taking the company private is in
its best commercial interest, they can use Section 100 to reduce capital
by paying off the minority. The critical safeguard is valuation. Because
the minority was being paid a fair and substantial premium, and the
special resolution was passed validly, the Court held there was no
oppression. The right to hold shares is subject to the statutory
provisions of the Companies Act, which includes the power of the majority
to reduce capital.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Legality of Squeeze-Outs: Established that selective capital reduction is
a legally valid mechanism for promoters to buy out minority shareholders
and delist/privatize a company.

Valuation as the Ultimate Safeguard: In minority squeeze-out scenarios,
courts will not block the transaction based on emotional or proprietary
arguments, provided the financial valuation is demonstrably fair and
independent.

cases.title: Salomon v. A Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Aron Salomon operated a successful leather business as a sole trader. He
incorporated a limited liability company, A Salomon & Co. Ltd., selling
his business to it. In return, he received 20,000 shares and a secured
debenture of £10,000. His wife and five children held one share each to
meet the statutory requirement of seven members. When the company
subsequently failed and went into liquidation, its assets were
insufficient to pay both Salomon (the secured creditor) and the unsecured
trade creditors.
cases.issues:
Is a company legally distinct from its members, even if one person holds
almost all the shares and absolute control?

Could Salomon, as a majority shareholder and director, also be a secured
creditor ranking ahead of unsecured creditors?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Liquidator/Unsecured Creditors)
The liquidator argued that the company was a mere sham or an "alias" for
Salomon. Because he essentially traded with himself, the company was his
agent, and Salomon should personally indemnify the company's debts.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Aron Salomon)
Salomon argued that the company was duly incorporated under the Companies
Act. Upon incorporation, it became a separate legal entity. Therefore,
his secured debentures were valid and took priority over unsecured
creditors.
cases.judgment: The House of Lords unanimously ruled in favor of Aron Salomon.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that once a company is legally incorporated, it must be
treated like any other independent person with its rights and liabilities
appropriate to itself. The motives of those who took part in the
promotion of the company are irrelevant to its legal existence. The
company is not the agent of the subscribers or members.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Separate Corporate Personality: The bedrock principle that a corporation
is a distinct legal entity separate from its shareholders and directors.

Corporate Veil: Established the foundational concept of the corporate
veil, protecting shareholders from personal liability for the company's
debts.

cases.title: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts:
Richard Foss and Edward Turton, two minority shareholders in the Victoria
Park Company, brought a lawsuit against the company's directors
(including Harbottle). They alleged that the directors had misapplied and
wasted company property and had improperly mortgaged the company's assets
to themselves, effectively defrauding the company.
cases.issues:
Can individual minority shareholders initiate a lawsuit on behalf of the
company for wrongs committed against the company by its directors?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Foss & Turton)
The plaintiffs argued that because the directors controlled the company,
the company itself could not realistically initiate a lawsuit against
them. Therefore, minority shareholders must be allowed to sue to protect
the company's assets.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Harbottle/Directors)
The defendants argued that the injury was allegedly done to the company,
not to the individual shareholders. Therefore, only the company, acting
through an ordinary resolution of the majority of shareholders, had the
standing to sue.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Chancery dismissed the plaintiffs' claim, ruling in favor of
the defendants.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reasoned that the company and its members are separate
entities. If a wrong is done to the company, the company is the proper
plaintiff. Furthermore, if the alleged wrong is something that the
majority of shareholders could lawfully ratify or approve in a general
meeting, courts should not interfere at the behest of a minority.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Proper Plaintiff Rule: If a wrong is done to a company, the company
itself is the only proper plaintiff to sue.

Majority Rule Doctrine: Courts will not intervene in the internal
management of a company at the request of a minority if the act
complained of can be ratified by the majority. (Note: This established
the general rule, to which modern oppression and mismanagement laws act
as exceptions).

cases.title: Royal British Bank v. Turquand
cases.facts:
The registered deed of settlement (Articles of Association) of the Royal
British Bank allowed its directors to borrow money on bonds, provided
they were authorized by a resolution passed at a general meeting of the
company. The directors borrowed money from Turquand and issued a bond
bearing the company seal. However, no such resolution had actually been
passed by the shareholders. When the company defaulted, Turquand sued.
cases.issues:
Is an outsider dealing with a company obligated to verify if the internal
administrative procedures required by the company's articles have been
strictly followed?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Turquand)
Turquand argued that he read the public documents (the deed) and saw the
directors had the power to borrow. As an outsider, he had no way of
checking the internal minute books to verify if the specific resolution
was passed. He acted in good faith.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Royal British Bank)
The Bank argued that since the condition precedent (the shareholder
resolution) was not met, the directors acted beyond their authority, and
the bond was invalid and not binding on the company.
cases.judgment:
The Court ruled in favor of Turquand, holding the company liable for the
debt.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established that people dealing with a company are presumed to
have read its public documents (Memorandum and Articles) and understand
them (Constructive Notice). However, they are not bound to inquire into
the regularity of internal proceedings. If a transaction appears valid
based on the public documents, the outsider can assume the internal
procedures were properly executed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Doctrine of Indoor Management (The Turquand Rule): Outsiders dealing with
a company in good faith are entitled to assume that acts within its
constitution and powers have been properly and duly performed, protecting
them from internal irregularities.

cases.title: Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche
cases.facts:
The company's Memorandum of Association stated its objects were "to make
and sell, or lend on hire, railway carriages and wagons, and all kinds of
railway plant, fittings, machinery, and rolling stock." The directors
entered into a contract with Riche to finance the construction of a
railway line in Belgium. Later, the company repudiated the contract, and
Riche sued for breach. The shareholders attempted to ratify the contract
retrospectively.
cases.issues:
Is a contract that falls entirely outside the stated objects in the
Memorandum of Association legally valid?

Can the shareholders of a company unanimously ratify an act that is
beyond the company's constitutional objects?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Riche)
Riche argued that the contract was generally related to railways and
that, even if it was initially beyond the directors' powers, the
shareholders' attempt to ratify it made it binding.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Ashbury Railway)
The company argued that financing a railway line is fundamentally
different from manufacturing railway carriages. Therefore, the contract
was beyond the legal capacity of the company as defined by its
Memorandum.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Ashbury Railway, declaring the
contract void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the Memorandum is the foundational charter of the
company. A company only exists for the purposes stated within it. Any
contract made beyond these objects is strictly void at its inception.
Because it is void from the beginning, not even the unanimous consent of
all shareholders can ratify it, as the company lacks the legal capacity
to engage in that business.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Doctrine of Ultra Vires: Any act or contract undertaken by a company that
falls outside the objects clause of its Memorandum of Association is
completely void and legally unenforceable.

cases.title: Lee v. Lee's Air Farming Ltd.
cases.facts:
Geoffrey Lee formed a company for the purpose of aerial top-dressing. He
held 2999 of the 3000 shares and was appointed the governing director for
life. He was also employed by the company as its chief pilot. While
piloting an aircraft for the company, he was killed in a crash. His widow
claimed worker's compensation under the relevant statute, arguing he was
an employee of the company.
cases.issues:
Can the majority shareholder and governing director of a company
simultaneously hold the status of a legally recognized "worker" or
"employee" of that same company?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mrs. Lee)
The appellant argued, relying on Salomon v. Salomon, that the company and
Mr. Lee were distinct legal entities. Therefore, the company (as a legal
person) could enter into a valid contract of employment with Mr. Lee (as
a natural person).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Insurance Company)
The insurer argued that one cannot be both the master and the servant.
Since Lee had absolute control over the company, he was essentially
employing himself, and no true master-servant relationship existed for
the purposes of worker's compensation.
cases.judgment: The Privy Council ruled in favor of Mrs. Lee.
cases.reasoning:
Applying the strict logic of Salomon, the Privy Council held that the
company is a separate legal entity. The capacity of the company to make a
contract is not negated by the fact that the person directing the company
is also the other party to the contract. The company, as a separate
person, could legally employ Mr. Lee as a pilot, making him a "worker"
entitled to compensation.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Dual Capacity: An individual can simultaneously hold the positions of
majority shareholder, sole director, and employee within the same
corporate entity, reinforcing the absolute nature of separate corporate
personality.

cases.title: Percival v. Wright
cases.facts:
The directors of a company were approached by a third party interested in
buying the entire undertaking of the company at a high price per share.
Before this was made public, the directors bought shares from individual
shareholders (the plaintiffs) at the current, lower market price. The
plaintiffs later discovered the impending buyout and sued the directors,
seeking to have the sale set aside on the grounds that the directors
breached a fiduciary duty by not disclosing the ongoing negotiations.
cases.issues:
Do directors owe a direct fiduciary duty to individual shareholders of
the company to disclose price-sensitive information before purchasing
their shares?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Percival)
The plaintiffs argued that directors are trustees not only for the
company but also for the individual shareholders, and therefore must
disclose any secret information that affects the value of the shares
before transacting with them.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Wright/Directors)
The directors argued that their fiduciary duties are owed strictly to the
corporate entity as a whole, not to individual members. In the open
market, they are entitled to buy shares just like any other individual.
cases.judgment:
The High Court of Justice (Chancery Division) ruled in favor of the
directors.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that directors owe their fiduciary duties to the company
as a whole, not to individual shareholders. To hold otherwise would
paralyze the stock market, as directors would be unable to trade in their
own company's shares without making premature disclosures of confidential
corporate negotiations.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Locus of Fiduciary Duty: Establishes the traditional rule that a
director's fiduciary duties are owed to the company (the separate legal
entity) and not directly to individual shareholders. (Note: This is
subject to modern insider trading regulations which now penalize such
conduct).

cases.title: Shanti Prasad Jain v. Kalinga Tubes Ltd.
cases.facts:
Two groups of original promoters of Kalinga Tubes brought in a third
party (S.P. Jain) to provide financing. An agreement was reached giving
Jain equal representation on the board and a specific shareholding.
Later, the original promoters issued new shares to their friends and
relatives, deliberately excluding Jain from the new allotment, thereby
diluting his voting power and violating the prior agreement. Jain sued
for oppression.
cases.issues:
Does the breach of a private agreement between shareholders regarding
board representation and shareholding amount to "oppression" under the
Companies Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (S.P. Jain)
Jain argued that the secret issuance of shares was a deliberate, mala
fide act designed to reduce him to a minority, contrary to the
foundational agreement under which he invested, constituting oppressive
conduct.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Kalinga Tubes/Promoters)
The promoters argued that the company was not a party to the private
agreement between the shareholders. The shares were issued in accordance
with the Articles of Association and the Companies Act to raise necessary
capital.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled against S.P. Jain, dismissing the claim
of oppression.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that for conduct to be "oppressive," it must be
burdensome, harsh, and wrongful, involving a lack of probity or fair
dealing in the affairs of the company. A breach of a private contract
between shareholders, to which the company is not a party and which is
not incorporated into the Articles of Association, does not bind the
company. Therefore, actions taken contrary to that private agreement but
within the company's legal powers do not legally constitute oppression.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Privity of Corporate Constitution: Private agreements between
shareholders are not enforceable against the company unless they are
incorporated into the Articles of Association.

Standard for Oppression: Established a high threshold for oppression,
requiring a continuous course of oppressive conduct affecting the
shareholder in their capacity as a member, not merely as a contracting
party.

cases.title: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts:
Needle Industries (India) was a subsidiary of an English company (Holding
Ltd). Due to Indian regulatory changes (FERA), the foreign holding had to
be reduced to 40%. The Indian directors resolved to issue rights shares
to achieve this. The English holding company failed to subscribe to its
rights shares in time. The Indian directors then allotted those
unsubscribed shares exclusively to themselves and their allies,
effectively wresting control of the company from the foreign majority.
cases.issues:
Does the issuance of shares by directors to themselves, resulting in the
transfer of corporate control, constitute oppression and mismanagement if
the company genuinely needed funds?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Holding Ltd / English Parent)
The parent company argued that the Indian directors abused their
fiduciary power. The allotment of unsubscribed shares was not done to
raise capital, but as a deliberate mechanism to oust the majority
shareholder, constituting blatant oppression.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Indian Directors)
The Indian directors argued that they strictly followed the law. They
offered the rights shares, the parent company failed to take them, and
the directors were authorized by the Articles to dispose of unsubscribed
shares. They claimed it was necessary to comply with FERA regulations.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India held that while the directors breached their
fiduciary duties, the strict test for "oppression" under the Companies
Act was not met.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a nuanced distinction. The directors did act
improperly by issuing shares to themselves to gain control; the power to
issue shares is a fiduciary power that must be used for the company's
benefit, not for personal power struggles. However, because the company
did need to comply with FERA regulations, and the foreign parent's
conduct was also obstructive, the Court found that winding up the company
on "just and equitable" grounds would unfairly prejudice the thriving
company.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Incidental Alteration of Control: If directors issue shares for a
genuinely required corporate purpose (like statutory compliance), the
fact that it incidentally alters the balance of power does not
automatically make it oppressive.

Breach of Duty vs. Oppression: A solitary act of a breach of fiduciary
duty by directors does not automatically fulfill the continuous
"burdensome and harsh" requirement for an oppression claim.

cases.title: Jones v. Lipman
cases.facts:
Mr. Lipman entered into a contract to sell a piece of land to Mr. Jones.
Before the completion of the sale, Lipman changed his mind. To avoid the
legal obligation to transfer the land, Lipman formed a company (of which
he and a clerk were the sole shareholders and directors) and transferred
the land to this newly formed company. When Jones sued for specific
performance, Lipman argued that he no longer owned the land, and the
company was a separate legal entity not bound by his personal contract.
cases.issues:
Can the corporate veil be pierced when a company is formed specifically
to evade an existing legal obligation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Jones)
Jones argued that the company was a mere facade, created solely to
defraud him and defeat his equitable right to specific performance of the
land contract.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Lipman)
Lipman relied on Salomon v. Salomon, arguing that the company was a
separate legal entity, properly incorporated, and as the legal owner of
the land, it could not be compelled to honor a contract to which it was
not a party.
cases.judgment:
The English High Court ruled in favor of Jones, ordering specific
performance against both Lipman and his company.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the company was a "device and a sham, a mask which he
holds before his face in an attempt to avoid recognition by the eye of
equity." The Court pierced the corporate veil because the company was
incorporated and used strictly for the fraudulent purpose of evading a
pre-existing legal obligation.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Piercing the Veil (Evasion of Liabilities): Courts will disregard the
separate legal personality of a company if it is used as a mere facade or
sham to evade an existing legal or contractual obligation.

cases.title: Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta
cases.facts:
During the insolvency resolution of Essar Steel under the IBC, the
Committee of Creditors (CoC) approved a resolution plan submitted by
ArcelorMittal. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT)
subsequently modified the plan, ruling that the CoC could not treat
distinct classes of creditors (secured and unsecured/operational)
differently regarding the distribution of funds, mandating equal pro-rata
distribution.
cases.issues:
Does the NCLT or NCLAT have the jurisdiction to modify the commercial
wisdom of the CoC regarding the distribution of funds in an insolvency
resolution plan?

Must secured and operational creditors be treated absolutely equally in a
resolution plan?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (CoC / Financial Creditors)
The CoC argued that the IBC grants absolute supremacy to the commercial
wisdom of the financial creditors regarding how funds are distributed,
provided the minimum liquidation value is paid to dissenting/operational
creditors. Equating secured and unsecured creditors destroys the
fundamentals of banking and credit.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Operational Creditors)
Operational creditors argued that the IBC demands "fair and equitable"
treatment. Paying secured creditors nearly 90% of their dues while paying
operational creditors practically nothing is discriminatory and violates
the spirit of the law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court overturned the NCLAT order, ruling decisively in favor
of the Committee of Creditors.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the "commercial wisdom" of the CoC is paramount and
non-justiciable. The NCLT/NCLAT cannot act as courts of equity to alter
the financial distribution approved by the CoC. Furthermore, the Court
ruled that the principle of equality cannot be stretched to treat
unequals as equals. Secured creditors take risks based on collateral;
operational creditors do not. Prioritizing secured creditors is a valid
commercial principle essential for the functioning of the credit market.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Supremacy of Commercial Wisdom: Solidified the absolute authority of the
CoC in Indian insolvency proceedings, restricting judicial tribunals from
rewriting the commercial terms of a resolution plan.

Equitable vs. Equal Treatment: Clarified that under the IBC, fair and
equitable treatment does not mandate mathematically equal distribution
among fundamentally different classes of creditors.

cases.title: Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Escorts Ltd.
cases.facts:
The Swraj Paul group (Caparo Group), non-resident Indians, began
aggressively purchasing shares in Escorts Ltd., an Indian company managed
by the Nanda family. The Nanda management refused to register the
transfer of these shares, citing violations of the Foreign Exchange
Regulation Act (FERA). Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), a
financial institution holding a majority 52% stake in Escorts, issued a
requisition to call an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) to remove the
existing Nanda-aligned directors and appoint their own. The Nanda
management filed a writ petition against LIC, arguing that LIC, as an
instrumentality of the State, was acting arbitrarily and maliciously to
facilitate a hostile takeover.
cases.issues:
Can a majority shareholder (even if it is a State entity) be injuncted
from exercising its statutory right to call an EGM and remove directors?

Under what circumstances can the court pierce the corporate veil to
examine the underlying motives of foreign investors?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Escorts / Nanda Management)
The Nanda management argued that LIC, being a State entity under Article
12 of the Constitution, must act reasonably and not arbitrarily. They
argued LIC's move to oust the board was a mala fide attempt to aid an
illegal foreign takeover by the Caparo Group. They urged the court to
pierce the corporate veil of the Caparo Group's shell companies to expose
the FERA violations.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (LIC)
LIC argued that as a shareholder, it has absolute statutory rights under
the Companies Act to requisition an EGM and vote out directors without
assigning any reasons. When a State entity acts as a shareholder in a
commercial corporation, its actions are governed by corporate law, not
public law, and it is not required to justify its commercial voting
decisions to the courts.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of LIC, upholding its absolute
right to call the EGM and exercise its voting rights as a majority
shareholder.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a massive victory for shareholder democracy. It held
that every shareholder has a statutory right to requisition a meeting and
vote out directors. A shareholder is not required to disclose the reasons
for their vote, nor can the courts inquire into their commercial motives,
even if the shareholder is a State entity. On the issue of piercing the
corporate veil, the Court held that the veil can only be lifted if a
statute specifically allows it or if there is blatant fraud. Since the
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had the statutory authority to investigate
FERA violations, it was not the Court's place to pierce the veil at the
behest of the target company's management.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Absolute Shareholder Rights: A majority shareholder has an unfettered
statutory right to call an EGM and remove directors; courts will not
injunct this right based on alleged "mala fide" motives.

State as a Shareholder: When the State acts as a shareholder in a
company, its rights and obligations are determined by the Companies Act,
not by constitutional administrative law principles.

cases.title: V.B. Rangaraj v. V.B. Gopalakrishnan
cases.facts:
Two branches of a family held 50% shares each in a private limited
company. The family members entered into a private Shareholders'
Agreement (SHA) which stipulated that if any member wished to sell their
shares, they must first offer them to the other branch of the family (a
Right of First Refusal). However, this restriction was never incorporated
into the company's Articles of Association (AoA). Later, one member sold
his shares to an outsider in violation of the SHA. The other family
branch sued to invalidate the transfer.
cases.issues:
Is a restriction on the transfer of shares contained in a private
Shareholders' Agreement legally binding on a private company if it is not
incorporated into its Articles of Association?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (V.B. Gopalakrishnan)
The plaintiff argued that the SHA was a valid, binding contract between
the shareholders. Since a private company restricts the free
transferability of shares by its very nature, the family agreement should
be enforced to maintain the agreed-upon balance of power.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (V.B. Rangaraj)
The defendant argued that the Companies Act mandates that any restriction
on the transfer of shares must be explicitly stated in the AoA. Since the
AoA of this company contained no such restriction, the shares were freely
transferable, and a private contract cannot override the company's
constitutional document.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of V.B. Rangaraj, declaring the transfer
valid and the private SHA restriction unenforceable against the company.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the Articles of Association are the paramount
regulations of a company. Section 82 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now
Section 44 of the 2013 Act) states that shares are movable property
transferable in the manner provided by the articles. Therefore, any
restriction on transferability that is not codified in the AoA is
entirely void and unenforceable against the company. A private agreement
between shareholders cannot bind the company or restrict a shareholder's
statutory right to transfer shares.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Supremacy of the Articles: In Indian corporate law, Shareholders'
Agreements are subordinate to the Articles of Association. For any share
transfer restriction (like ROFR or tag-along rights) to be binding, it
must be expressly embedded in the AoA.

cases.title: Re Yenidje Tobacco Co Ltd.
cases.facts:
Weinberg and Rothman, two rival tobacco manufacturers, merged their
businesses into a single private company. They were the only two
shareholders and the only two directors, holding equal voting rights. The
Articles of Association provided for arbitration in case of a dispute.
The relationship between the two completely broke down; they despised
each other, refused to speak, and communicated only through the company
secretary. Despite the company being highly profitable, Weinberg
petitioned the court to wind it up.
cases.issues:
Can a highly profitable and solvent company be ordered to wind up on
"just and equitable" grounds solely due to an irreconcilable deadlock
between its only directors/shareholders?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Weinberg)
Weinberg argued that the absolute deadlock made it impossible to manage
the company. The underlying trust required to run the business had
vanished, making it just and equitable to dissolve the entity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Rothman)
Rothman argued that the company was making massive profits. He contended
that winding up a solvent, thriving business merely because the directors
disliked each other was against commercial logic, especially when the
Articles provided for an arbitration mechanism.
cases.judgment:
The English Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Weinberg and ordered the
winding up of the company.
cases.reasoning:
The Court recognized that while this was legally a company, it was
practically a partnership in the guise of a private corporation. The
Court applied the principles of partnership law, which state that a
partnership can be dissolved if there is a complete destruction of mutual
trust and confidence. Since there was an absolute deadlock with no
dominant majority to break it, and the parties could not even speak to
each other, the corporate machinery had completely failed. The
profitability of the company did not negate the fact that the underlying
foundation of the "quasi-partnership" had collapsed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Deadlock Doctrine: A company can be wound up on just and equitable
grounds if there is a complete and irreconcilable deadlock in its
management.

Quasi-Partnership Concept: The genesis of treating closely held,
intimately managed private companies as partnerships for the purpose of
equitable remedies.

cases.title: Ebrahimi v. Westbourne Galleries Ltd.
cases.facts:
Ebrahimi and Nazar had been partners in a rug business for years. They
incorporated the business into a company, becoming equal shareholders and
directors. Later, Nazar's son was brought in, receiving shares from both,
making Ebrahimi a minority shareholder. Following a dispute, Nazar and
his son used their majority voting power to pass an ordinary resolution
removing Ebrahimi as a director, legally excluding him from the
management and the profits (which were paid out as directors'
remuneration, not dividends). Ebrahimi petitioned for winding up.
cases.issues:
Can the strict legal exercise of majority voting rights to remove a
director constitute grounds for a "just and equitable" winding up if it
breaches an underlying understanding between the founders?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Ebrahimi)
Ebrahimi argued that the company was formed on the basis of a personal
relationship involving mutual confidence and an understanding that he
would participate in the management. Removing him breached this equitable
"legitimate expectation."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Nazar)
Nazar argued that they simply followed the statutory procedure under the
Companies Act to remove a director. The company is a separate legal
entity, and Ebrahimi had no legal right to remain a director
indefinitely.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Ebrahimi, ordering the winding up of
the company on just and equitable grounds.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Wilberforce delivered a landmark judgment, stating that while
company law relies on statutory rules (like majority voting), there is
room for equitable considerations. A company might be subjected to
equitable principles (a "quasi-partnership") if it features: (1) a
business formed on a personal relationship of mutual confidence, (2) an
agreement that all or some shareholders will participate in management,
and (3) restrictions on the transfer of shares. Because Ebrahimi was
locked in (he couldn't sell his shares) and locked out (removed from
management and profits), the strict application of legal rights by the
majority was unjust.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Legitimate Expectation: In quasi-partnerships, minority shareholders have
an equitable right or "legitimate expectation" to participate in
management.

Equitable Limitations on Statutory Rights: The courts will prevent
majority shareholders from using their strict statutory rights (like the
power to remove directors) in a manner that breaches the underlying
equitable understanding of the company's founders. (Note: This was the
very case Cyrus Mistry unsuccessfully tried to apply to Tata Sons).

cases.title: Bajaj Auto Ltd. v. N.K. Firodia
cases.facts:
The Firodia group began aggressively purchasing shares in Bajaj Auto Ltd.
on the open market, threatening the control of the Bajaj family
management. The Articles of Association of Bajaj Auto gave the Board of
Directors the absolute discretion to refuse the registration of any
transfer of shares without assigning any reason. Using this power, the
Board refused to register the transfer of shares bought by the Firodia
group. The Firodias challenged this refusal before the Company Law Board
(CLB), and subsequently, the Supreme Court.
cases.issues:
Is the discretionary power of the Board of Directors to refuse share
transfers absolute and immune from judicial review?

What is the legal standard required for directors to validly exercise
their power to refuse a share transfer?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (N.K. Firodia)
The Firodias argued that the directors were acting with a corrupt,
personal motive: to protect their own management control at the expense
of the company's best interests. They argued the refusal was arbitrary
and a violation of the free transferability of shares in a public
company.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Bajaj Auto Board)
The Board argued that their power under the AoA was absolute. They
contended that they genuinely believed the Firodia group was acquiring
shares with a hostile intent that would destabilize the company, and thus
the refusal was in the paramount interest of the company.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of N.K. Firodia, ordering Bajaj Auto to
register the shares.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the directors' power to refuse registration, even if
stated as "absolute" in the Articles, is a fiduciary power. It must be
exercised bona fide (in good faith), in the interest of the company, and
with due regard to the rights of the shareholders. The Court established
that directors cannot refuse a transfer merely because they dislike the
purchaser or want to retain their own control. Since the Firodia group
was not legally disqualified and the Board failed to prove how the
transfer would actually harm the company's business (as opposed to
harming the directors' control), the refusal was an abuse of fiduciary
power.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Fiduciary Limits on Discretion: Discretionary powers granted to directors
by the Articles are not dictatorial; they are fiduciary and subject to
judicial review for bad faith or collateral motives.

Bona Fide Test: Directors must justify the refusal of share transfers by
proving it is genuinely necessary to protect the company from real harm,
not just to protect the incumbent management.

cases.title: Ruben v. Great Fingall Consolidated
cases.facts:
Rowe, the company secretary of Great Fingall Consolidated, forged the
signatures of two directors on a share certificate. He affixed the
company seal without authorization and issued the forged certificate to
Ruben to secure a personal loan. When Ruben attempted to register the
shares, the company discovered the forgery and refused. Ruben sued the
company, arguing that as an outsider, he had relied on an official
document bearing the company seal and secretary's signature.
cases.issues:
Does the doctrine of "Indoor Management" protect an outsider who relies
on a corporate document that has been forged by an officer of the
company?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Ruben)
Ruben argued, relying on Royal British Bank v. Turquand, that an outsider
cannot be expected to know if the directors actually signed the
certificate or authorized the seal. Since the secretary, who typically
handles such documents, issued it, the company should be bound by the
certificate.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Great Fingall Consolidated)
The company argued that a forged document is a nullity-it is completely
void in the eyes of the law. The rule of indoor management applies to
irregularities in procedure, not to outright criminal forgery to which
