the company never consented.
cases.judgment: The House of Lords ruled in favor of the company, denying Ruben's claim.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a hard limit on the Turquand rule. The Court
reasoned that a forged document is not merely an "irregularly" issued
document; it is not a document of the company at all. The doctrine of
indoor management is designed to protect outsiders from administrative
oversights, but it cannot be used to validate a pure nullity. The company
cannot be held liable for an act it never authorized and a signature its
directors never made.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Forgery Exception: The Rule of Indoor Management does NOT apply to
forged documents. A forged corporate document is void ab initio (void
from the beginning), and no legal rights can be derived from it,
regardless of the good faith of the third party.

cases.title: Rajahmundry Electric Supply Corpn. v. A. Nageshwara Rao
cases.facts:
The Chairman of Rajahmundry Electric Supply Corporation was highly
autocratic, misappropriated company funds, and managed the affairs to his
personal advantage, bringing the company to the brink of ruin. A group of
shareholders filed a petition before the court, seeking to wind up the
company on "just and equitable" grounds due to severe mismanagement and
oppression. The management contested the maintainability of the petition.
cases.issues:
Does the mere misconduct or misappropriation of funds by directors
justify a winding-up order on "just and equitable" grounds?

How does the availability of an alternative remedy affect the court's
discretion to wind up a company?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (A. Nageshwara Rao/Shareholders)
The shareholders argued that the Chairman's dictatorial conduct and
financial fraud had destroyed the substratum of the company and
completely eroded shareholder trust, making it just and equitable to kill
the company and salvage whatever assets remained.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Rajahmundry Electric /
Chairman)
The Chairman argued that winding up is an extreme measure.
Misappropriation of funds is a wrong done to the company, for which the
directors can be sued (Foss v. Harbottle). He argued that winding up a
public utility company would harm the public and the shareholders.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the shareholders, holding that a case
for winding up had been made out, but opted to appoint administrators to
save the company instead of liquidating it.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that mere mismanagement or isolated acts of fraud do not
automatically warrant winding up. However, when the mismanagement is so
pervasive that it amounts to a lack of probity and fair dealing, creating
a continuous state of oppression against the minority, the "just and
equitable" clause is triggered. Crucially, the Court noted that a
winding-up order is the remedy of last resort. Under the Companies Act,
if the court finds the facts justify a winding up, but doing so would
unfairly prejudice the members, the court can issue alternative orders to
regulate the company's future conduct (like removing the board and
appointing an administrator).
cases.legalPrinciples:
Winding Up as a Last Resort: Established the jurisprudence that while
severe oppression justifies winding up, courts will actively seek
alternative remedies (like replacing management) to preserve the
corporate entity and protect employment/public interest.

cases.title: Macaura v. Northern Assurance Co Ltd.
cases.facts:
Macaura owned an estate with significant timber. He sold all the timber
to a company he incorporated, in exchange for all of its shares. He was
the sole shareholder and the primary creditor. Crucially, Macaura insured
the timber against fire in his own name, rather than in the name of the
company. Later, a massive fire destroyed the timber. Macaura claimed the
insurance money.
cases.issues:
Does a sole shareholder and creditor of a company have an "insurable
interest" in the specific physical assets owned by the company?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Macaura)
Macaura argued that since he owned all the shares and the company owed
him money, he was the only person who practically suffered a financial
loss when the timber burned. Therefore, he had an insurable interest.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Northern Assurance)
The insurance company argued that a contract of insurance requires the
insured to have a legal or equitable interest in the property. Applying
Salomon v. Salomon, the timber belonged to the company, not Macaura.
Since he did not own the timber, his insurance policy was void.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of the insurance company. Macaura
received nothing.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly applied the doctrine of separate corporate
personality. The Court held that a shareholder has no legal or equitable
interest in the property of the company. A shareholder merely has a right
to a share of the profits while the company is ongoing, and a share of
the surplus assets in a winding up. The company owned the timber. Because
Macaura insured property he did not legally own, the insurance contract
was invalid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
No Proprietary Interest of Shareholders: Reaffirms that shareholders do
not own the company's assets. The separate legal entity principle applies
strictly, even resulting in severe financial loss to a sole owner who
fails to distinguish between personal and corporate property.

cases.title: Shree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax
cases.facts:
Shree Meenakshi Mills, a textile manufacturing company, was subject to
price controls on cotton in India. To evade taxes and maximize profits,
the company created a complex web of "dummy" or "sham" companies (some
located outside British India in princely states to avoid tax
jurisdiction). The company sold its yarn at artificially low, controlled
prices to these dummy companies, which then sold the yarn on the open
market at massive premiums. The Income Tax authorities sought to assess
the entire profit (including the premium) in the hands of Shree Meenakshi
Mills.
cases.issues:
Can the tax authorities pierce the corporate veil of the subsidiary
companies to tax the parent company on profits technically earned by the
subsidiaries?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Shree Meenakshi Mills)
The company relied on Salomon v. Salomon, arguing that the purchasing
companies were distinct legal entities. The sales were legally valid, and
the parent company cannot be taxed on the profits earned by separate
corporations.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Commissioner of Income Tax)
The tax authorities argued that the dummy companies had no independent
business, capital, or staff. They were created for the sole, fraudulent
purpose of evading price controls and income tax. They urged the court to
look at the economic reality, not the legal fiction.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of the Commissioner of Income
Tax, piercing the corporate veil.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a major exception to the separate entity rule.
While acknowledging the Salomon principle, the Court held that it is not
absolute. When a corporate entity is used as a cloak or sham to evade
taxes, circumvent statutory obligations, or commit fraud, the courts have
the power and the duty to look behind the corporate facade. The Court
found that the dummy companies were mere agents or instruments of the
parent company, created purely for tax evasion, and therefore, their
separate existence must be disregarded.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Piercing the Veil for Tax Evasion: Indian courts will aggressively pierce
the corporate veil when the corporate structure is a deliberate
contrivance specifically designed to evade taxes or statutory
regulations.

cases.title: Allen v. Gold Reefs of West Africa Ltd.
cases.facts:
Zuccani held two classes of shares in Gold Reefs: fully paid-up shares
and partly paid-up shares. The company's original Articles of Association
gave the company a lien for all debts and liabilities only on the partly
paid-up shares. Zuccani failed to pay calls on his partly paid shares,
accumulating a massive debt to the company. Realizing they couldn't
recover the money, the company passed a special resolution altering its
Articles to extend the lien to fully paid-up shares as well. Zuccani's
executors (Allen) sued, claiming the alteration was a retrospective fraud
designed solely to seize Zuccani's specific assets.
cases.issues:
What is the legal standard and limitation on a company's statutory power
to alter its Articles of Association by a special resolution?

Can a company alter its Articles if the alteration disproportionately
prejudices one specific shareholder?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Allen/Executors)
Allen argued that the alteration was mala fide (in bad faith). It was not
done for the general benefit of the company, but as a targeted attack to
seize Zuccani's fully paid shares to cover debts on his other shares,
retrospectively changing his contract with the company.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Gold Reefs)
The company argued that Section 50 of the Companies Act gives them an
absolute statutory right to alter the Articles via special resolution.
The alteration was necessary to recover a massive debt owed to the
company, which benefits all other shareholders.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Gold Reefs, upholding the validity
of the alteration.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down the fundamental test for altering Articles. The power
to alter Articles is subject to one overarching equitable limitation: it
must be exercised bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole.
The Court found that it is the duty of the directors to recover debts
owed to the company. Extending the lien to fully paid shares was a
rational commercial decision to protect the company's financial
interests. The fact that this alteration primarily and harshly affected
one shareholder (Zuccani) did not make it mala fide, as long as the
primary intent was the company's benefit.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Bona Fide for the Benefit of the Company: The bedrock test for the
validity of any alteration of the Articles of Association. Alterations
cannot be used to maliciously oppress a minority, but if they are
genuinely for the commercial benefit of the corporate entity as a whole,
they will be upheld even if they disadvantage specific members.

cases.title: Trevor v. Whitworth
cases.facts:
James Whitworth was a shareholder in a flannel manufacturing company. The
company's Articles of Association authorized it to purchase its own
shares. The company bought Whitworth's shares, paying him partially, with
the balance remaining as a debt. Later, the company went into
liquidation. Whitworth's executors sued the company (represented by the
liquidator, Trevor) for the unpaid balance of the share purchase price.
cases.issues:
Is it legally valid for a limited liability company to purchase its own
shares, even if authorized by its Articles of Association?

Does a share buyback violate the foundational rule of the maintenance of
capital?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Trevor / Liquidator)
The liquidator argued that a company cannot buy its own shares because it
essentially returns capital to the shareholders before creditors are
paid. The statutory capital of a company is a sacred fund meant for
creditor protection. The Articles cannot override the foundational
principles of the Companies Act.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Whitworth's Executors)
The executors argued that the transaction was a straightforward contract
explicitly authorized by the company's internal constitution (the
Articles). Since the company agreed to the purchase, it must honor the
debt.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of the liquidator (Trevor), declaring
the company's purchase of its own shares completely void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the strict doctrine of capital maintenance. Lord
Herschell reasoned that creditors extend credit to a limited liability
company based entirely on its stated capital. If a company could buy its
own shares, it would be secretly shrinking this capital pool, leaving
creditors exposed to unexpected risk. The paid-up capital must only be
spent on the legitimate objects of the business, not returned to
shareholders (except via strict statutory capital reduction procedures).
Therefore, even if the Articles authorize it, a company cannot be its own
shareholder.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Capital Maintenance Doctrine: A limited liability company cannot purchase
its own shares. The capital fund must be preserved for the protection of
creditors. (Note: Modern statutes, like the Indian Companies Act 2013,
now permit buybacks, but only under highly restrictive, heavily regulated
conditions that ensure creditors are not prejudiced).

cases.title: Bushell v. Faith
cases.facts:
A private company had three siblings as its only shareholders and
directors, each holding 100 shares. The Companies Act (Section 184 at the
time) stated that a director could be removed by an ordinary resolution
(simple majority) of shareholders. However, the company's Articles
contained a special provision (Article 9): if a resolution was proposed
at a general meeting to remove a director, the shares held by that
specific director would carry three votes per share. Two siblings banded
together to vote the third (Faith) off the board. Due to Article 9,
Faith's 100 shares became 300 votes, defeating the 200 votes of the other
siblings.
cases.issues:
Can a company's Articles of Association grant weighted voting rights to a
director to effectively render them immune from statutory removal by an
ordinary majority?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Bushell / Sibling)
Bushell argued that the Companies Act explicitly guarantees the
shareholders' right to remove a director by a simple majority. Article 9
was a blatant, artificial device designed to bypass and defeat this
mandatory statutory provision. Therefore, the Article should be struck
down as illegal.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Faith)
Faith argued that the Companies Act regulates how a resolution is passed
(by a majority of votes), but it does not prohibit companies from
attaching different voting weights to different shares in specific
circumstances. The shares were property, and the founders legally agreed
to this weighted voting mechanism to prevent any one sibling from being
ousted.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords (by a 4:1 majority) ruled in favor of Faith, upholding
the validity of the weighted voting rights.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly separated the statutory power to remove a director
from the contractual right to attach voting weights to shares. The
Parliament mandated that an ordinary resolution is required, but it did
not mandate the principle of "one share, one vote" for all occasions.
Since the Act allowed companies to issue shares with special or
disproportionate voting rights, an Article granting weighted votes in a
specific scenario (self-defense against removal) was perfectly legal,
even if its practical effect made the director unremovable.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Weighted Voting Rights / Poison Pills: Established that Articles can
validly confer enhanced voting rights on specific shares under specific
conditions to protect directors from removal, prioritizing freedom of
corporate contract over the absolute power of the statutory majority.

cases.title: Rayfield v. Hands
cases.facts:
The Articles of Association of a private company stated: "Every member
who intends to transfer shares shall inform the directors who will take
the said shares equally between them at a fair value." Rayfield, a
member, informed the directors (Hands and others) of his intention to
sell his shares. The directors refused to buy them. Rayfield sued the
directors directly to enforce the Article.
cases.issues:
Do the Articles of Association constitute a binding contract between
individual members of the company (members inter se), or only between the
company and its members?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Rayfield)
Rayfield argued that Section 20 of the Companies Act makes the Memorandum
and Articles a binding covenant on the members. In a closely held private
company, this provision was a specific agreement between the members
themselves (who happened to be the directors) regarding the transfer of
shares.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Hands/Directors)
The directors argued that the Articles only create a contract between the
company and its members. Therefore, an individual member cannot sue
another individual member (or director) directly for a breach of the
Articles without involving the company as a party to the suit.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of Rayfield, ordering the directors
to purchase the shares.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the Articles do indeed constitute a binding contract
between the members inter se (amongst themselves), particularly in quasi-
partnership-style private companies. The Court noted that the directors
in this specific context were acting in their capacity as members. Since
the Article imposed a specific, personal obligation on the members-who-
are-directors to buy the shares, Rayfield had a personal right to enforce
this contract directly against them without joining the company to the
suit.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Articles as a Contract: The Articles of Association can create legally
enforceable contractual obligations directly between shareholders,
bypassing the need to treat the company as the necessary intermediary in
disputes regarding share transfers.

cases.title: Re City Equitable Fire Insurance Co Ltd
cases.facts:
The company suffered massive financial losses due to the fraudulent
actions of its managing director, Bevan, who misappropriated funds for
personal speculations. The other directors, who were honest but highly
negligent, signed cheques and approved loans without any real scrutiny or
understanding of the company's financial position, blindly trusting
Bevan. When the company collapsed, the liquidator sued the honest "dummy"
directors for breach of their duty of care and diligence.
cases.issues:
What is the standard of care, skill, and diligence expected of a
corporate director under common law?

Can a director be held liable for mere negligence if they relied entirely
on the management of others?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Liquidator)
The liquidator argued that directors are not merely ornamental. They owe
a duty to the company to actively monitor its affairs. By rubber-stamping
Bevan's fraudulent transactions without asking questions, they breached
their duty of care and caused the company's ruin.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (The Directors)
The directors argued they acted honestly. They were not finance experts
and reasonably trusted the managing director and the auditors.
Furthermore, the company's Articles contained an exemption clause
protecting them from liability for anything other than "willful neglect
or default."
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal found that while the directors were negligent, they
were protected from liability by the exemption clause in the company's
Articles.
cases.reasoning:
Despite the ultimate ruling relying on the exemption clause, Justice
Romer laid down the foundational common law tests for a director's duty
of care (which remains highly relevant). He stated three principles:

A director need not exhibit a greater degree of skill than may reasonably
be expected from a person of their knowledge and experience (a subjective
standard).

A director is not bound to give continuous attention to the company's
affairs (they are not full-time employees unless appointed as such).

Directors may properly leave the day-to-day management to appointed
officials, provided there are no grounds for suspicion. Because the
directors honestly believed Bevan was acting properly, and they were
protected by the "willful default" clause, they escaped financial ruin.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Subjective Standard of Care: Historically established a surprisingly low,
subjective standard of care for directors. (Note: Modern corporate law
has drastically shifted from this case, imposing a dual
objective/subjective standard, and modern statutes explicitly outlaw
clauses that exempt directors from negligence).

cases.title: Ooregum Gold Mining Co of India v. Roper
cases.facts:
The company was in severe financial distress and its £1 shares were
trading on the market at just 2 shillings and 6 pence. To raise emergency
capital, the company issued new £1 preference shares but offered them to
buyers for only 5 shillings, crediting the remaining 15 shillings as
"fully paid up" (issuing shares at a massive discount). The company later
became profitable. Roper, a shareholder, sued the company and the new
shareholders, arguing that the discounted shares were issued illegally
and the new shareholders still owed the company the unpaid 15 shillings
per share.
cases.issues:
Can a limited liability company issue its shares at a discount to their
nominal (par) value?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Roper)
Roper argued that the nominal value of a share dictates the liability of
the shareholder. A £1 share means the shareholder must contribute £1 of
capital to the company. Issuing it for 5 shillings and calling it fully
paid is a fraud on the capital maintenance rule, falsely representing the
company's financial backing.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Ooregum Gold Mining)
The company argued it was a commercial necessity. Nobody would pay £1 for
a share in a failing company when they were trading at 2 shillings on the
market. Issuing at a discount was the only way to save the business, and
it was done openly via a valid contract.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Roper, declaring the issuance of
shares at a discount completely void. The new shareholders were ordered
to pay the balance.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the dominant feature of a limited liability company
is that the shareholder's liability is limited to the nominal amount of
their shares. The capital of the company must be paid up in money or
money's worth. A contract by the company to accept less than the nominal
value is contrary to the fundamental principles of the Companies Act.
Creditors rely on the stated nominal capital; therefore, an agreement to
release a shareholder from paying the full nominal value is ultra vires
(beyond the power of) the company.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Prohibition of Discounted Shares: Firmly established the rule that shares
cannot be issued at a discount to their par value, protecting the
integrity of the corporate capital pool.

cases.title: Gaiman v. National Association for Mental Health
cases.facts:
The National Association for Mental Health was a company limited by
guarantee. A group of individuals affiliated with the Church of
Scientology, who held fundamentally opposed views on psychiatry compared
to the Association, orchestrated a mass enrollment campaign to join the
Association. Their goal was to use their voting numbers to take over the
board of directors. Realizing the threat, the existing council of the
Association invoked a power in their Articles of Association to expel
members and terminated the memberships of the Scientologists just before
the annual general meeting.
cases.issues:
Do the directors of a company have the power to expel members if
authorized by the Articles?

What is the legal standard for exercising the power of expulsion?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Gaiman / Scientologists)
The plaintiffs argued that the expulsion was a mala fide exercise of
power. They contended the directors acted purely to protect their own
board seats from a democratic vote, depriving the members of their
property rights (membership) without natural justice or a fair hearing.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (National Association)
The Association argued that the Articles explicitly granted the council
the power to terminate memberships. They acted to protect the very
existence and core philosophy of the company from a hostile takeover by a
group whose beliefs were fundamentally antithetical to the company's
stated objects.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of the Association, upholding the
expulsions.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the power to expel members, if clearly written into
the Articles, is a valid fiduciary power. The standard for exercising
this power is the "bona fide" test-the directors must act in what they
genuinely believe to be the best interests of the company as a whole. The
Court found that the Scientologists' goals were totally hostile to the
Association's work. The directors were not merely protecting their seats;
they were protecting the company from being destroyed from within.
Furthermore, the Court held that strict rules of natural justice (like
the right to a hearing) do not necessarily apply to corporate expulsions
unless the Articles require them.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Power of Expulsion: Validated the use of expulsion clauses in Articles of
Association (common in non-profits/guarantee companies) to defend the
corporate entity from hostile infiltration, provided the directors act
strictly bona fide in the company's interest.

cases.title: Gilford Motor Co Ltd v. Horne
cases.facts:
Horne was the managing director of Gilford Motor Co. His employment
contract contained a restrictive covenant preventing him from soliciting
the company's customers if he left his job. Horne resigned and shortly
thereafter wanted to start a competing business. Knowing he was
personally bound by the non-compete clause, he directed his wife and an
employee to incorporate a new limited company (J.M. Horne & Co Ltd).
Horne was not a shareholder or director on paper, but he completely
controlled it. The new company then began soliciting Gilford's customers.
Gilford Motor Co sued for an injunction.
cases.issues:
Can the corporate veil be pierced to enforce a personal restrictive
covenant against a company that is not a party to the contract?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Gilford Motor Co)
Gilford argued that the new company was a mere sham, a "cloak" created by
Horne specifically to evade his legal obligations. Horne was the puppet
master, and allowing the company to solicit customers was identical to
Horne doing it himself.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Horne / New Company)
Horne, relying on Salomon v. Salomon, argued that the new company was a
distinct and separate legal entity. The new company never signed a non-
compete agreement with Gilford Motor Co and therefore had every legal
right to solicit any customer it chose.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Gilford Motor Co, piercing the
corporate veil and issuing an injunction against both Horne AND his new
company.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that while the separate legal personality of a company is
the general rule, equity will not allow a person to use the corporate
form to commit a fraud or evade a pre-existing legal duty. The Court
found that the new company was formed "as a device, a stratagem" for the
express purpose of masking Horne's breach of his non-compete covenant.
Because the company was merely Horne's alter ego used for an illicit
purpose, the court treated the company's actions as Horne's actions and
restrained the company.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Piercing the Veil (Evasion of Legal Obligations): A classic exception to
the Salomon principle. The corporate veil will be aggressively pierced if
a company is incorporated primarily as a facade to help an individual
evade an existing contractual or legal duty.

cases.title: Hutton v. West Cork Railway Co
cases.facts:
The West Cork Railway Company was being wound up and its business
transferred to another railway company. The company had a surplus of
funds left over. At a general meeting, a majority of the shareholders
passed a resolution to take a portion of this surplus to pay remuneration
to the directors for their past unpaid services, and to provide severance
compensation to the company's employees who were losing their jobs.
Hutton, a dissenting minority shareholder, sued to stop these payments.
cases.issues:
Does a company have the legal capacity to make gratuitous (ex gratia)
payments to directors and employees when it is no longer a going concern?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Hutton)
Hutton argued that the funds belonged to the shareholders. Because the
company was being wound up, paying severance to employees or back-pay to
directors produced no future benefit for the company. It was purely an
act of charity with the shareholders' money, which was ultra vires
(beyond the powers) of the company.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (West Cork Railway)
The company argued that the shareholders, by majority vote, had the right
to decide how to dispose of surplus funds. Providing severance was a
decent and honorable corporate action.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Hutton, declaring the payments
invalid.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Justice Bowen delivered one of the most famous judgments in
corporate law, stating: "The law does not say that there are to be no
cakes and ale, but there are to be no cakes and ale except such as are
required for the benefit of the company." He reasoned that a company can
be generous to its employees because happy employees work harder, which
ultimately generates profit for the company. However, because West Cork
Railway was being wound up, it had no future business. Therefore,
severance payments could not possibly generate future commercial benefit.
As such, the charity was ultra vires.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Corporate Benefit Rule: Gratuitous payments (charity, severance) are only
legally valid if they are reasonably incidental to the carrying on of the
company's business and are done for the ultimate benefit of the company.
Charity for charity's sake, especially in insolvency, is illegal. (Note:
Modern statutes have largely overridden this to allow companies to
provide for employees upon cessation of business).

cases.title: Pender v. Lushington
cases.facts:
The Articles of Association of a company stated that no shareholder could
cast more than 100 votes at a general meeting, regardless of how many
shares they owned. Pender, a wealthy shareholder, owned far more than 100
shares. To circumvent the voting restriction, Pender temporarily
transferred chunks of his shares to several nominees (his friends),
intending for them to vote as he directed at an upcoming meeting. The
chairman of the meeting (Lushington) realized the scheme and refused to
count the votes of Pender's nominees. Pender sued the chairman.
cases.issues:
Does a shareholder have an absolute property right to vote their
registered shares, even if those shares were transferred to them solely
to evade a corporate voting restriction?

Can a shareholder sue the company in their own name to enforce their
right to vote?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Pender)
Pender argued that the nominees were the legally registered owners of the
shares on the company's books. A share is a piece of property, and the
right to vote is intrinsically attached to that property. The chairman
had no legal right to look behind the register to investigate the
"motives" of the shareholders.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Lushington)
Lushington argued that Pender was committing a blatant fraud on the
company's constitution. The voting limit was designed to prevent a single
individual from dominating the company, and allowing this "vote
splitting" scheme would render the restriction entirely meaningless.
cases.judgment:
The Court ruled in favor of Pender, ordering the chairman to accept the
nominees' votes.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the right to vote is a proprietary right attached to
the share. The company's register is absolute; whoever is registered is
legally entitled to vote. The motives of a shareholder in voting, or how
they acquired the shares, are irrelevant to the company. Master of the
Rolls George Jessel established that a shareholder's vote is a right of
property, and they may exercise it exactly as they please, even out of
malice or personal interest. The chairman cannot act as a judge of
morals. Furthermore, depriving a member of their vote is a wrong done to
the individual, giving them a personal right to sue.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Voting as a Proprietary Right: Established the absolute nature of voting
rights. A company cannot look behind the register to deny a vote based on
the shareholder's motives or beneficial ownership.

Individual Right of Action: A shareholder has a personal right to sue if
their vote is unlawfully rejected, distinct from the rule in Foss v.
Harbottle.

cases.title: Rolled Steel Products (Holdings) Ltd v. British Steel Corp
cases.facts:
Rolled Steel Products (RSP) owed a debt to British Steel. A sister
company of RSP (owned by the same individual) also owed a massive debt to
British Steel. To secure the sister company's debt, the directors of RSP
caused RSP to guarantee the sister company's debt to British Steel. RSP's
Memorandum of Association allowed it to give guarantees. However, the
directors of RSP executed the guarantee for their own personal reasons,
not for the benefit of RSP. When RSP went bankrupt, the liquidator argued
the guarantee was invalid.
cases.issues:
What is the distinction between an act that is ultra vires (beyond the
legal capacity of the company) and an act that is an abuse of authority
by the directors?

Can a third party enforce a contract that was within the company's
capacity, but executed by directors abusing their powers?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Liquidator of RSP)
The liquidator argued that giving away the company's assets to guarantee
a sister company's debt provided zero commercial benefit to RSP.
Therefore, it was an abuse of corporate power, making the guarantee void
and unenforceable.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (British Steel Corp)
British Steel argued that RSP's Memorandum explicitly stated it had the
power to give guarantees. Therefore, the act was not ultra vires. Even if
the directors acted improperly, as an outsider, British Steel is
protected by the rule of indoor management and can enforce the guarantee.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the liquidator, invalidating the
guarantee, but for nuanced reasons regarding "notice."
cases.reasoning:
The Court provided a masterclass in separating capacity from authority.
First, the Court held that the guarantee was NOT ultra vires. The
Memorandum gave the company the legal capacity to issue guarantees.
Second, the Court held that the directors executed the guarantee in
breach of their fiduciary duty, as it provided no benefit to RSP. This
was an abuse of authority.
Third, the critical factor: British Steel knew that the guarantee was
being given to secure a sister company's debt and that it provided no
benefit to RSP. Because British Steel had "constructive notice" of the
directors' breach of fiduciary duty, they could not rely on the rule of
indoor management. Had British Steel been an innocent third party unaware
of the internal dynamics, the guarantee would have been enforceable.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Capacity vs. Authority: Clarified the massive legal difference between a
company lacking the constitutional power to do an act (ultra vires =
completely void) and directors misusing a power the company does possess
(abuse of authority = voidable depending on the third party's knowledge).

cases.title: Automatic Self-Cleansing Filter Syndicate Co Ltd v. Cuninghame
cases.facts:
The company's Articles of Association vested the general management and
control of the company entirely in the Board of Directors. A majority of
the shareholders, led by a Mr. McDiarmid, wished to sell the company's
assets to a new entity. The directors, believing the sale was not in the
company's best commercial interest, refused to execute it. The
shareholders subsequently passed an ordinary resolution at a general
meeting expressly commanding the directors to proceed with the sale. The
directors (Cuninghame and others) ignored the resolution. The
shareholders sued to compel the board to obey.
cases.issues:
Can the shareholders of a company, by a simple majority vote at a general
meeting, override the commercial decisions of the Board of Directors when
the Articles vest management power in the Board?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (McDiarmid/Shareholders)
The shareholders argued the foundational principle of agency. The
directors are merely the agents and servants of the company. The
shareholders, assembled in a general meeting, represent the ultimate will
of the corporate principal. Therefore, the principal has the absolute
right to direct its agents on how to act.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Cuninghame/Directors)
The directors argued that the Articles of Association represent a binding
contract among all members. By agreeing to the Articles, the shareholders
contracted away their right to manage the company on a day-to-day basis,
entrusting it exclusively to the directors. Until the Articles are
formally altered by a special resolution, the board cannot be dictated to
by an ordinary majority.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the directors, dismissing the
shareholders' claim.
cases.reasoning:
The Court fundamentally reshaped the understanding of the board-
shareholder relationship. It rejected the simple principal-agent analogy.
The Court held that the division of powers in the Articles creates
distinct, mutually exclusive zones of authority. If the Articles delegate
management exclusively to the directors, the general meeting cannot
interfere with those management decisions via an ordinary resolution. The
shareholders' remedies, if they dislike the board's decisions, are
limited: they can either alter the Articles (requiring a supermajority),
or they can vote to remove the directors at the next election. They
cannot, however, usurp the board's management function from the floor of
the general meeting.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Division of Powers: Establishes the absolute independence of the Board of
Directors in exercising management powers vested in them by the Articles,
protecting them from micro-management by a simple majority of
shareholders.

cases.title: Regal (Hastings) Ltd v. Gulliver
cases.facts:
Regal (Hastings) Ltd owned a cinema and wanted to acquire two more. They
formed a subsidiary company to lease the new cinemas. The landlord
demanded a personal guarantee from the directors unless the subsidiary's
paid-up capital was £5,000. Regal only had £2,000 available to invest. To
save the deal, four directors and the company solicitor personally
subscribed for the remaining £3,000 of shares in the subsidiary. The
cinemas were acquired, and later, all shares in Regal and the subsidiary
were sold at a massive profit. The new owners of Regal sued the former
directors, demanding they hand over the personal profits they made from
the subsidiary's shares.
cases.issues:
Are directors liable to account to the company for personal profits made
from an opportunity that came to them by virtue of their directorial
positions, even if the company itself lacked the funds to take the
opportunity?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Regal [New Management])
The company argued that the directors stand in a strict fiduciary
relationship to the company. They only learned of the cinema leases and
the share investment because of their roles on the board. Therefore, any
profit made from this "corporate opportunity" rightfully belongs to the
company.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Gulliver/Former Directors)
The directors argued they acted completely bona fide (in good faith).
They only stepped in with their own money because Regal was financially
incapable of funding the subsidiary. Without their personal investment,
Regal would have lost the deal entirely. They took the financial risk;
therefore, they should keep the reward.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Regal, ordering the former directors
to disgorge their personal profits to the company.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the strict, uncompromising rule of equity regarding
fiduciaries. The liability to account for secret profits does not depend
on fraud, bad faith, or whether the company itself suffered a loss or
could have taken the opportunity. The sole test is whether the directors
obtained the shares and the profit by reason of and in the course of
their execution of their office. Because they used their directorial
positions to acquire the shares, the profit belonged in equity to the
company. The directors could have protected themselves by fully
disclosing their investment to the shareholders and obtaining a
ratification vote in a general meeting, which they failed to do.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Corporate Opportunity Doctrine / Strict Fiduciary Duty: Directors are
absolutely barred from making undisclosed personal profits from
opportunities that arise out of their corporate positions, regardless of
their good faith or the company's inability to exploit the opportunity
itself.

cases.title: Howard Smith Ltd v. Ampol Petroleum Ltd
cases.facts:
Ampol Petroleum and another company controlled 55% of the shares in
Millers Ltd, and they intended to launch a joint takeover bid for the
remaining shares. Howard Smith Ltd made a competing, higher takeover bid.
The directors of Millers favored Howard Smith's bid. Knowing that Ampol's
55% majority would block Howard Smith, the Millers directors used their
power under the Articles to issue new shares to Howard Smith. This
massive share allotment diluted Ampol's holding to a minority,
effectively destroying their takeover block and allowing Howard Smith's
bid to succeed. Ampol sued to invalidate the share allotment.
cases.issues:
Can directors legally exercise their fiduciary power to issue new shares
if their primary motive is to destroy an existing majority shareholder's
voting block to facilitate a favored takeover?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Ampol Petroleum)
Ampol argued that the directors abused their fiduciary power. The power
to issue shares exists solely to raise capital for the company's
legitimate business needs. The directors used this power for an improper,
collateral purpose: to manipulate the voting power within the company and
dictate who buys the majority of shares.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Howard Smith / Millers
Directors)
The directors argued that they honestly believed Howard Smith's higher
bid was better for the company's future. Furthermore, Millers actually
did need capital to finance some tankers. Therefore, the allotment served
a dual purpose, and since they acted without personal corruption, the
court should respect their commercial judgment.
cases.judgment:
The Privy Council ruled in favor of Ampol, declaring the share allotment
void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the "Proper Purpose" doctrine. Even if directors
act honestly and without personal financial gain, their actions can still
be invalidated if they exercise a corporate power for a purpose other
than what it was granted for. The power to issue shares is primarily for
raising capital. While creating a new majority is sometimes an incidental
side-effect of a genuine capital raising, it cannot be the primary
purpose. The Court examined the objective facts and concluded that the
directors' dominant motive was to destroy Ampol's majority. Manipulating
corporate control and shareholder democracy is an improper use of the
board's power.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Proper Purpose Doctrine: Directors must not only act in good faith
but must also use their delegated corporate powers strictly for the
specific purposes for which those powers were conferred, particularly
prohibiting the issuance of shares merely to manipulate voting control.

cases.title: Adams v. Cape Industries plc
cases.facts:
Cape Industries was a UK-based multinational parent company that mined
asbestos in South Africa and marketed it globally. It operated a wholly-
owned subsidiary in the United States (NAAC) to sell the asbestos.
Hundreds of US factory workers contracted severe illnesses from asbestos
dust and won massive default judgments against Cape and its subsidiaries
in a Texas court. Cape had no assets in the US. The plaintiffs sought to
enforce the Texas judgments in the UK against the parent company, Cape
Industries, arguing that the US subsidiary was merely a branch or facade
of the UK parent.
cases.issues:
Under what circumstances will a court pierce the corporate veil within a
multinational corporate group to hold a parent company liable for the
torts of its foreign subsidiary?

Does the "single economic unit" theory legally collapse the distinction
between parent and subsidiary?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Adams / US Claimants)
The plaintiffs argued that Cape Industries and its US subsidiaries
functioned as a "single economic entity." The parent company completely
controlled the subsidiary, directed its operations, and reaped all its
profits. To treat them as separate legal entities would allow
multinational corporations to shield themselves from horrific tort
liabilities by simply placing a shell subsidiary in the high-risk
jurisdiction.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Cape Industries)
Cape relied on Salomon v. Salomon. They argued that NAAC was a
legitimately incorporated US company with its own premises, staff, and
operations. Cape deliberately structured its business this way
specifically to limit its liability to the capital invested in the
subsidiary. This is a lawful use of corporate architecture, not a fraud.
cases.judgment:
The English Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Cape Industries, refusing
to pierce the corporate veil and denying the enforcement of the US
judgments against the UK parent.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a highly orthodox and restrictive judgment regarding
corporate groups. The Court expressly rejected the "single economic unit"
argument, stating there is no general principle that allows courts to
ignore separate legal personalities just because companies operate as one
business enterprise. The Court held that a parent company is legally
entitled to organize its group structure to minimize future liabilities.
The corporate veil will only be pierced if the subsidiary was set up as a
"mere facade" concealing the true facts to evade an existing legal
obligation. Because Cape created the US subsidiary to avoid future tort
liabilities, it was a legitimate use of the corporate form, not a sham.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Corporate Group Immunity: Solidified the principle that parent and
subsidiary companies are entirely distinct legal entities. Courts will
not pierce the veil merely in the interests of "justice" or because they
operate as a single economic unit, severely limiting the ability of tort
victims to reach the deep pockets of multinational parent companies.

cases.title: Bacha F. Guzdar v. Commissioner of Income Tax
cases.facts:
Mrs. Bacha F. Guzdar was a shareholder in two tea companies. The
companies were engaged in the business of growing, manufacturing, and
selling tea. Under the Indian Income Tax Act, 60% of the income earned by
these tea companies was classified as "agricultural income" and was
therefore entirely exempt from taxation. When Mrs. Guzdar received
dividends on her shares, she claimed that 60% of her dividend income
should also be exempt from tax, arguing that the dividend was simply her
share of the company's agricultural profits.
cases.issues:
Does a shareholder have a legal or equitable interest in the property and
specific income streams of the company?

Does the character of the income (e.g., agricultural) in the hands of the
company retain its character when distributed as a dividend to the
shareholders?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Bacha Guzdar)
The appellant argued that a company is essentially an association of
persons. Since 60% of the company's revenue was generated from
agriculture, the dividend paid out of that revenue is merely the
distribution of agricultural income. Taxing it as ordinary income would
defeat the purpose of the agricultural exemption.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Commissioner of Income Tax)
The Revenue Department argued that a dividend is not a direct share of
the company's assets or its specific revenue streams. It is a distinct
return on the capital invested by the shareholder in the shares.
Therefore, the source of the dividend is the share itself, not the land
the company owns.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of the Commissioner of Income
Tax, holding that the entire dividend was fully taxable.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court emphatically reinforced the separate corporate
personality doctrine in Indian law. The Court held that a shareholder
acquires no interest in the property of the company. A company is a
juristic entity distinct from its shareholders. The company earns
agricultural income because it owns the land and farms it. However, when
the company declares a dividend, the shareholder receives it solely by
virtue of their ownership of the shares, not ownership of the land.
Therefore, the dividend income loses its "agricultural" character the
moment it leaves the company and enters the hands of the shareholder,
becoming ordinary taxable income from investments.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Nature of a Share: A share represents a bundle of statutory and
contractual rights (right to vote, right to receive dividends if
declared, right to surplus in winding up), but it unequivocally does NOT
grant the shareholder any proprietary interest in the physical assets or
specific revenues of the corporate entity.

cases.title: Hickman v. Kent or Romney Marsh Sheep-Breeders' Association
cases.facts:
The Association was incorporated to encourage the breeding of a specific
type of sheep. Article 49 of its Articles of Association contained a
strict arbitration clause: any dispute arising between the Association
and any of its members regarding the affairs of the company must be
referred to arbitration. Hickman, a member, became involved in a bitter
dispute with the Association over his expulsion and initiated a lawsuit
in the High Court. The Association applied to stay the court proceedings,
arguing that Hickman was contractually bound by the Articles to go to
arbitration.
cases.issues:
Do the Articles of Association constitute a binding statutory contract
between the company and its individual members?

Can a member be forced to comply with a dispute resolution mechanism
embedded in the Articles?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Hickman)
Hickman argued that the Articles are merely internal regulations, not a
formal, signed contract between him and the company. He argued he never
signed a specific agreement waiving his fundamental right to access the
civil courts.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (The Association)
The Association pointed to the Companies Act (equivalent to modern
Section 10 in India), which states that the Memorandum and Articles, when
registered, bind the company and the members to the same extent as if
they had been signed by each member. Therefore, the arbitration clause is
a legally enforceable contract.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of the Association, staying the
court proceedings and forcing Hickman into arbitration.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive interpretation of the statutory contract
created by the Articles. The Court laid out three foundational
propositions:

The Articles do not constitute a contract between the company and
outsiders.

The Articles do not grant enforceable rights to a member in a capacity
other than as a member (e.g., a member acting as a solicitor cannot
enforce a clause in the Articles guaranteeing his employment).

The Articles do constitute a binding contract between the company and its
members concerning their ordinary rights and obligations as members.
Since the dispute over expulsion was a dispute regarding Hickman's
fundamental rights as a member, the arbitration clause in the Articles
functioned as a valid, binding written agreement between him and the
company.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Statutory Contract (Insider Rights): Established that the Articles of
Association legally bind the members to the company (and the company to
the members) regarding matters intrinsic to their membership status,
functioning as a mutually enforceable contract.

cases.title: Re Smith & Fawcett Ltd
cases.facts:
Smith and Fawcett were the only two directors and equal shareholders of a
private company. The Articles of Association contained a clause stating:
"The directors may at any time in their absolute and uncontrolled
discretion refuse to register any transfer of shares." Fawcett died. His
executor (his son) sought to be registered as a member for all of
Fawcett's shares. Smith, the surviving director, used his "uncontrolled
discretion" to refuse registration. Instead, Smith offered to register
half the shares if the son sold the other half to Smith at a specific
price. The son sued, claiming Smith was abusing his directorial power.
cases.issues:
When Articles grant directors "absolute and uncontrolled discretion," is
there any legal limit on how they exercise that power?

What is the standard by which courts evaluate a director's exercise of
discretion?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Fawcett's Executor)
The executor argued that Smith was acting oppressively and using his veto
power not for the benefit of the company, but to extort a personal
advantage (buying the shares cheaply to seize majority control).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Smith)
Smith argued that the Articles specifically used the words "absolute and
uncontrolled discretion." In a tightly knit two-person private company,
it is essential that surviving members have the right to veto new
partners they do not wish to work with. He argued the court cannot
rewrite the corporate constitution.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Smith, upholding his refusal to
register the transfer.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Greene MR delivered one of the most cited maxims regarding
directorial duties. He held that directors must exercise their discretion
"bona fide in what they consider - not what a court may consider - is in
the interests of the company, and not for any collateral purpose." The
Court established a highly subjective test. The phrase "absolute
discretion" means exactly what it says. As long as Smith honestly
believed that bringing the son into the company would be disruptive to
its operations, he was legally entitled to refuse the transfer. The Court
will not substitute its own commercial judgment for the honest judgment
of the directors, unless there is concrete evidence of mala fides or
fraud.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Subjective Test of Good Faith: Directors are judged by what they
subjectively and honestly believed was best for the company. Wide
discretionary powers granted by the Articles are valid, and courts are
deeply reluctant to interfere with them absent clear proof of corrupt
intent.

cases.title: Caparo Industries plc v. Dickman
cases.facts:
Caparo Industries purchased shares in Fidelity plc. Caparo then launched
a successful takeover bid for the rest of the company. After the
takeover, Caparo discovered that Fidelity's accounts were disastrously
inaccurate; a reported pre-tax profit of £1.3 million was actually a loss
of £400,000. Caparo sued Dickman (the auditors of Fidelity), alleging
they were negligent in carrying out their statutory audit. Caparo argued
that as an investor, they relied on the audited accounts to make their
investment decision, and therefore the auditors owed them a duty of care.
cases.issues:
Do statutory auditors of a company owe a duty of care to individual
shareholders or to members of the investing public who rely on the audit
report to buy shares?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Caparo Industries)
Caparo argued that the entire purpose of publishing audited accounts is
to provide the public and shareholders with accurate financial
information. It was highly foreseeable that investors would rely on these
accounts to make financial decisions. Therefore, the auditors owed a duty
of care to anyone foreseeably relying on their negligent report.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Dickman / Auditors)
The auditors argued that they were appointed by the company pursuant to
the Companies Act to report to the shareholders as a collective body for
the purpose of exercising corporate governance (e.g., voting on
management). They did not prepare the report for individual investors to
use as investment advice. Imposing liability to the general public would
create indeterminate liability for an indeterminate time to an
indeterminate class.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of the auditors (Dickman), finding they
owed no duty of care to Caparo as individual investors.
cases.reasoning:
The Court radically redefined the law of negligence regarding economic
loss. To establish a duty of care, there must be foreseeability,
proximity, and it must be "fair, just and reasonable." The Court held
that the statutory purpose of an audit is exclusively to allow the
existing shareholders, as a body, to scrutinize management and exercise
their voting rights at the general meeting. The audit is NOT designed to
provide investment advice to individual shareholders looking to buy more
shares, nor to outsiders looking to launch takeovers. Because Caparo used
the audit report for a purpose it was not legally intended for, there was
no sufficient "proximity" between the auditors and Caparo.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Auditors' Limited Liability: Statutory auditors owe a duty of care to the
company itself and to the shareholders collectively (for governance
purposes), but they owe NO duty of care to individual shareholders or the
public relying on the accounts for making investment or takeover
decisions.

cases.title: Cotman v. Brougham
cases.facts:
The Essequibo Rubber and Tobacco Estates Ltd had an extraordinarily
lengthy Memorandum of Association. The "Objects Clause" contained 30 sub-
clauses authorizing the company to do almost every conceivable type of
business globally. Crucially, it concluded with an "Independent Objects
Clause" which stated that every single sub-clause should be read as a
distinct, independent, and primary object of the company, and none should
be deemed subsidiary to the first clause (which was rubber and tobacco).
The company engaged in financing other businesses, lost money, and went
into liquidation. The liquidator (Brougham) challenged the financing
transactions as ultra vires, arguing the company was just a rubber
company.
cases.issues:
Is an "Independent Objects Clause" legally valid, allowing a company to
engage in entirely unrelated businesses without violating the doctrine of
ultra vires?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Cotman / Creditor)
The creditor who facilitated the financing argued that the Memorandum was
clear. The independent objects clause specifically stated that the
company was authorized to finance businesses as a primary object.
Therefore, the transaction was perfectly intra vires (within its powers).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Brougham / Liquidator)
The liquidator argued that the Companies Act requires a company to state
its specific objects. Listing every business in the world makes a mockery
of the requirement. The court should read the first clause (rubber) as
the main object, and treat the rest as ancillary powers. Since financing
had nothing to do with rubber, it was ultra vires.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords reluctantly ruled in favor of Cotman, upholding the
validity of the transactions.
cases.reasoning:
The House of Lords severely criticized the practice of drafting hyper-
inflated Memorandums, noting it defeated the legislative intent of
informing creditors what business the company actually did. However, the
Court held that the Registrar of Companies had accepted and registered
the Memorandum. Once registered, the certificate of incorporation is
conclusive evidence that the statutory requirements were met. Because the
Memorandum explicitly contained an "Independent Objects Clause," the
Court was legally bound to interpret the financing clause not as an
ancillary power to rubber farming, but as a standalone, valid object.
Therefore, the transaction was not ultra vires.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Erosion of Ultra Vires: This case demonstrated how clever corporate
drafting (the Independent Objects Clause) effectively neutralized the
strict doctrine of ultra vires, allowing companies to legally engage in
practically any business they chose.

cases.title: Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India
cases.facts:
The Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Company Ltd suffered severe
mismanagement, leading to a complete halt in production and the
unemployment of thousands of workers. Due to the national economic
importance of the textile mill, the Government of India passed a specific
ordinance (later an Act) dismissing the company's directors, terminating
the managing agents, and transferring the entire management of the
company to directors appointed by the Government. Chiranjit Lal, an
ordinary shareholder holding one fully paid share, filed a writ petition
directly in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. He
claimed the legislation violated his fundamental rights to property and
equality.
cases.issues:
Can an individual shareholder maintain a writ petition claiming that the
fundamental rights of the company have been violated by state action?

Did the government takeover of management deprive the shareholder of his
"property" (his share)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri)
The petitioner argued that by stripping the elected directors of their
power and taking over the management, the government essentially acquired
the company's property without compensation. Furthermore, passing
legislation targeting only one specific company violated the right to
equality (Article 14). He argued that an injury to the company is an
injury to his proprietary rights as a shareholder.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that the company is a distinct legal entity. Any
alleged violation of property rights was suffered by the corporate
entity, not the individual shareholder. The shareholder still owned his
share and could still receive dividends. Therefore, he had no legal
standing (locus standi) to challenge the Act on behalf of the company.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India dismissed the writ petition by a majority,
ruling that the shareholder could not challenge the legislation on these
grounds.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court deeply analyzed the nature of corporate property vis-à-
vis shareholder property. The Court held that the fundamental rights
guaranteed by the Constitution (particularly property rights under the
old Article 31) apply to the specific property owned by the citizen. A
shareholder's property is the share. The company's property is the mill.
The Government took over the management of the mill, but it did not
confiscate Chiranjit Lal's share. He still held the right to receive
dividends and the right to dispose of his share. Because his specific
property was not acquired, his fundamental right to property was not
violated. The Court reinforced that an individual shareholder cannot don
the mantle of the company to fight its constitutional battles.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Locus Standi & Corporate Veil: An individual shareholder has no standing
to seek enforcement of the fundamental rights of the company. The
distinction between the property of the company and the property of the
shareholder is absolute in constitutional law, mirroring its absolute
nature in corporate law.

cases.title: Aberdeen Railway Co v. Blaikie Bros
cases.facts:
Aberdeen Railway Company contracted to purchase iron chairs from Blaikie
Brothers, a partnership firm. Crucially, the Chairman of the Board of
Directors of Aberdeen Railway, Mr. Thomas Blaikie, was simultaneously the
managing partner of Blaikie Brothers. After accepting partial delivery,
the railway company attempted to repudiate the contract, refusing to
accept the remaining iron chairs. Blaikie Bros sued for specific
performance of the contract. The railway company argued that the contract
was unenforceable because their Chairman was acting on both sides of the
transaction, creating an illegal conflict of interest.
cases.issues:
Is a contract entered into by a company valid if one of its directors has
a personal financial interest in the other party to the contract?

Does the fairness of the contract terms or the actual lack of fraud
excuse a director's conflict of interest?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Blaikie Bros)
Blaikie Bros argued that the contract was struck at standard, fair market
prices. They contended that there was no actual fraud, no money was
stolen, and the railway company genuinely needed the iron chairs.
Therefore, a mere technical conflict of interest should not invalidate a
commercially fair transaction.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Aberdeen Railway)
The company argued that directors are fiduciaries and agents of the
company. A fundamental rule of agency is that an agent cannot enter into
engagements where their personal interest conflicts with the interests of
their principal. Blaikie's duty to the railway was to buy at the lowest
price, while his personal interest as a partner was to sell at the
highest price.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Aberdeen Railway, declaring the
contract voidable at the option of the company.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Cranworth delivered an uncompromising judgment establishing the
strict "No Conflict" rule. He held that a corporate director is a
fiduciary whose duties strictly prohibit them from entering into any
engagement in which they have, or can have, a personal interest
conflicting with the interests of the company. This rule is absolute and
inflexible. The Court will not even allow an inquiry into whether the
contract was "fair" or whether the director actually exploited the
company. The mere existence of the conflict of interest is sufficient to
render the contract voidable in equity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Strict No-Conflict Rule: Directors must absolutely avoid situations
where their personal interests conflict with their duties to the company.
The fairness of the resulting transaction is entirely irrelevant as a
defense. (Note: Modern statutes allow such contracts ONLY IF the director
makes full and prior disclosure of their interest to the
board/shareholders).

cases.title: DHN Food Distributors Ltd v. Tower Hamlets London Borough Council
cases.facts:
DHN was the parent company of a grocery business. The business operated
on a piece of land owned entirely by Bronze Ltd, a wholly-owned
subsidiary of DHN. Another wholly-owned subsidiary owned the delivery
vehicles. Tower Hamlets Council compulsorily acquired the land. Under the
law, compensation for "disturbance of business" is only payable if the
entity that runs the business also possesses a legal interest in the
land. Because Bronze Ltd owned the land (but ran no business) and DHN ran
the business (but owned no land, being a mere licensee), the Council
refused to pay disturbance compensation, treating them as separate legal
entities under Salomon.
cases.issues:
Can the courts pierce the corporate veil of a wholly-owned corporate
group to treat parent and subsidiary companies as a "single economic
entity" for the purpose of claiming statutory compensation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (DHN Food Distributors)
DHN argued that the strict application of Salomon would lead to a gross
injustice. The three companies functioned as a single commercial
enterprise. The directors were identical, and DHN completely controlled
the subsidiaries. Therefore, they should be treated as one economic unit,
entitling DHN to compensation for the destruction of its business.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Tower Hamlets Council)
The Council relied on strict corporate orthodoxy. They argued that DHN
chose to structure its business across three separate legal entities for
tax and liability benefits. Having chosen the benefits of the corporate
veil, DHN must accept its burdens. Since DHN did not legally own the
land, it had no statutory right to compensation.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of DHN, treating the group as a single
economic entity and awarding compensation.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Denning MR, known for prioritizing equitable outcomes over strict
formalism, pierced the corporate veil. He held that this group of
companies was virtually the same as a partnership. They should not be
treated separately merely because of technical legal formalities. He
established the "Single Economic Unit" doctrine, ruling that when a
parent company exerts absolute control over its subsidiaries, and they
share a singular commercial purpose, courts can look past the corporate
veil to reflect the commercial reality.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Single Economic Entity Doctrine: A rare, high-water mark for piercing the
corporate veil based on enterprise reality. (Note: This doctrine was
later severely restricted and largely overturned by the House of Lords in
Adams v. Cape Industries, but remains vital for understanding the tension
between legal fiction and commercial reality).

cases.title: Guinness plc v. Saunders
cases.facts:
During Guinness plc's massive and highly controversial takeover of
Distillers, a committee of Guinness directors was formed to manage the
bid. Ward, one of the directors on this committee, was paid a massive
£5.2 million fee for his strategic services in securing the takeover.
However, this payment was authorized only by the special committee, not
by the full Board of Directors. Guinness's Articles of Association
explicitly stated that the remuneration of directors must be determined
by the whole Board. When new management took over Guinness, they sued
Ward to recover the £5.2 million.
cases.issues:
Can a director retain remuneration for special services if the payment
was not authorized in strict compliance with the procedures laid down in
the company's Articles of Association?

Can a director claim payment on a quantum meruit basis (equitable payment
for services rendered) if the contract is void?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Guinness plc)
Guinness argued that directors are not automatically entitled to pay; any
remuneration must be strictly authorized by the Articles. Since the full
board did not approve the payment, the committee had no authority to
grant it. Therefore, Ward received corporate funds in breach of trust and
must return them.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Ward/Saunders)
Ward argued that he provided incredibly valuable services that resulted
in a wildly successful takeover for Guinness. He claimed that even if
there was a technical procedural flaw, he was entitled to keep the money
under the equitable doctrine of quantum meruit because the company
benefited immensely from his work.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Guinness plc, ordering Ward to repay
the entire £5.2 million.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly enforced fiduciary principles. A director is
fundamentally a trustee of company funds and cannot contract with the
company for personal remuneration except as expressly permitted by the
Articles. Because the Articles required full board approval, the
committee's payout was ultra vires its delegated powers. Furthermore, the
Court utterly rejected the quantum meruit claim. Equity will not step in
to award a director pay that the company's own constitution forbade.
Allowing an equitable claim would completely undermine the strict
fiduciary rules designed to prevent directors from secretly enriching
themselves.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Strict Compliance for Remuneration: Directors have no inherent right to
be paid. Any remuneration must be authorized strictly in accordance with
the Articles of Association; procedural bypasses render the payments
recoverable by the company.

Rejection of Equitable Relief for Fiduciaries: Directors cannot use
quantum meruit to circumvent the strict disclosure and authorization
rules regarding their pay.

cases.title: Re D'Jan of London Ltd
cases.facts:
Mr. D'Jan was the director and 99% shareholder of a company. He signed an
insurance proposal form for the company's premises. The form was filled
out by his insurance broker. Without reading it, D'Jan signed it. The
form contained a critical factual error regarding D'Jan's past history as
a director of insolvent companies. When a fire subsequently destroyed the
company's premises, the insurance company refused to pay out, citing the
misrepresentation on the form. The company went into liquidation, and the
liquidator sued D'Jan for negligence and breach of his duty of care to
the company.
cases.issues:
What is the modern standard for the duty of care and skill owed by a
director to their company?

Can a director be held liable in negligence for failing to read a
standard commercial document before signing it?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Liquidator)
The liquidator argued that a competent director would read an insurance
proposal before signing it, especially since a mistake could (and did)
ruin the company. D'Jan's failure to do so was a breach of his duty of
care, making him personally liable for the lost insurance money.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Mr. D'Jan)
D'Jan argued, relying on older cases like Re City Equitable Fire
Insurance, that he trusted his professional broker. He argued the
standard of care was subjective, and as a busy businessman, it was normal
practice to sign documents prepared by professionals without reading
every line.
cases.judgment:
The High Court (Hoffmann LJ) ruled in favor of the liquidator, finding
D'Jan negligent, but granted him partial relief from liability.
cases.reasoning:
This case fundamentally updated the director's duty of care. Hoffmann LJ
discarded the purely subjective historical test. He applied the new
standard found in the Insolvency Act (and later codified in the Companies
Act): a director must exercise the care, skill, and diligence that would
be exercised by a reasonably diligent person with (a) the general
knowledge, skill, and experience that may reasonably be expected of a
person carrying out the same functions (the Objective Test), AND (b) the
general knowledge, skill, and experience that that director actually has
(the Subjective Test). Failing to read a simple, one-page insurance form
failed the objective test of a reasonable director. However, because
D'Jan owned 99% of the shares, the economic loss primarily hit his own
pocket, so the court exercised its statutory discretion to partially
relieve him of the financial penalty.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Modern Dual Objective/Subjective Test: Established the modern
standard for directorial negligence: a baseline objective standard of a
reasonable director, which can be elevated (but never lowered) if the
specific director possesses special skills or experience.

cases.title: Williams v. Natural Life Health Foods Ltd
cases.facts:
Mr. Mistlin was the managing director and principal shareholder of
Natural Life Health Foods Ltd, a company that sold health food shop
franchises. Williams was interested in buying a franchise. The company
provided Williams with a brochure containing detailed financial
projections, which turned out to be wildly inaccurate and negligently
prepared. Williams relied on these projections, bought the franchise, and
suffered heavy financial losses. Because the company went into
liquidation, Williams sued Mistlin personally in tort for negligent
misstatement.
cases.issues:
Can a director be held personally liable to a third party in tort for
negligent advice given by their company?

Under what circumstances does a director "assume personal responsibility"
towards a third party?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Williams)
Williams argued that Mistlin's personal expertise dictated the brochure's
content. Because Mistlin was the driving force behind the company and
effectively authored the negligent projections, he should be personally
liable for the resulting economic loss, regardless of the corporate veil.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Mistlin)
Mistlin argued that all dealings were strictly between Williams and the
limited liability company. He signed the documents in his capacity as a
director, not in his personal capacity. To hold him personally liable
would destroy the foundation of limited liability.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of the director (Mistlin), dismissing
the personal liability claim.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that a director acting on behalf of a company is not
personally liable in tort merely because they are the managing director
or the one who dictated the company's actions. To pierce the veil in tort
(specifically negligent misstatement), the plaintiff must prove that the
director "assumed personal responsibility" for the statement, and that
the plaintiff reasonably relied on that personal assumption. There must
be some specific conduct-like a personal guarantee, or personal
correspondence bypassing the corporate letterhead-that indicates the
director was stepping outside their corporate role to vouch for the
advice personally. Since Mistlin never communicated directly with
Williams and all documents were on company letterhead, there was no
assumption of personal responsibility.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Protection from Corporate Torts: Directors are shielded from personal
liability for negligent acts committed in the course of the company's
business, unless they explicitly "assume personal responsibility" toward
the third party, preserving the utility of limited liability.

cases.title: Eclairs Group Ltd v. JKX Oil & Gas plc
cases.facts:
JKX Oil & Gas suspected a hostile takeover attempt by two minority
shareholders (Eclairs Group). Under the company's Articles (and the
Companies Act), a company can issue a "disclosure notice" to shareholders
asking for information about the beneficial ownership of their shares. If
the shareholder fails to provide accurate information, the Board has the
