power to suspend their voting rights. Believing Eclairs' disclosure
responses were evasive, the JKX Board suspended their voting rights just
days before a crucial AGM, effectively preventing Eclairs from voting
against management's resolutions.
cases.issues:
Does the "Proper Purpose" rule apply to the board's power to restrict
shareholder voting rights?

Can directors use the power of disenfranchisement as a defensive
mechanism to defeat a hostile shareholder block at a general meeting?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Eclairs Group)
Eclairs argued that the Board abused its fiduciary power. The statutory
power to suspend votes is strictly designed to compel the disclosure of
information. The JKX Board, however, used it for an improper, collateral
purpose: to manipulate the outcome of the impending AGM and protect their
own management positions by disenfranchising a hostile voting block.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (JKX Oil & Gas)
The Board argued that Eclairs was actively trying to destabilize the
company. They argued that because Eclairs breached the disclosure rules,
the Board had a strict right under the Articles to suspend the votes, and
their underlying motive regarding the AGM was secondary and irrelevant.
cases.judgment:
The UK Supreme Court ruled in favor of Eclairs Group, declaring the
suspension of voting rights invalid.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court emphatically reinforced the Proper Purpose doctrine
(from Howard Smith). The Court held that the power to suspend voting
rights is a draconian power designed only as a sanction to induce
compliance with disclosure requests. It is unconstitutional for directors
to use this power for the ulterior motive of influencing the outcome of a
shareholder vote. Even if the directors genuinely believed that
disenfranchising Eclairs was in the best commercial interest of the
company, manipulating the constitutional balance of power between
shareholders and the board is an improper use of fiduciary power.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Fiduciary Limits on Disenfranchisement: Directors cannot use
administrative or sanctioning powers (like suspending votes) for the
improper purpose of manipulating shareholder democracy or surviving
corporate battles, establishing a strict check on management's defensive
tactics.

cases.title: Prest v. Petrodel Resources Ltd
cases.facts:
In a high-stakes divorce proceeding, Mrs. Prest sought a financial
settlement from her wealthy husband, Mr. Prest. Mr. Prest owned several
multi-million-pound residential properties in London. However, these
properties were not held in his personal name; they were legally owned by
Petrodel Resources Ltd and other offshore companies over which Mr. Prest
had absolute control. Mr. Prest refused to pay the divorce settlement,
claiming he had no personal assets. Mrs. Prest asked the Family Court to
pierce the corporate veil of the Petrodel companies to seize the
properties to satisfy the divorce judgment.
cases.issues:
Under what precise legal circumstances can the corporate veil be pierced
to reach the assets of a company controlled by an individual?

Does the Family Court have a broader equitable jurisdiction to pierce the
veil compared to commercial courts?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mrs. Prest)
Mrs. Prest argued that the companies were merely the alter ego of her
husband. He treated the corporate properties as his own personal piggy
bank. Allowing him to hide behind the corporate veil to evade his legal
obligations to his wife would be a gross abuse of corporate law.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Petrodel Companies / Mr.
Prest)
The companies (controlled by the husband) argued that under Salomon, they
were distinct legal entities. The properties belonged to the company, not
the husband. The veil cannot be pierced merely because it is "necessary
to achieve justice" in a divorce case.
cases.judgment:
The UK Supreme Court ruled in favor of Mrs. Prest, awarding her the
properties, but refused to pierce the corporate veil to do so. (They used
trust law instead).
cases.reasoning:
This is the definitive modern case on piercing the veil. Lord Sumption
strictly narrowed the doctrine, creating two classifications:

The Concealment Principle: The company is used to hide the true actors.
The court doesn't pierce the veil; it just looks behind it to see what
the company is actually doing.

The Evasion Principle: The only time the veil can be pierced. This
applies strictly when a person is under an existing legal obligation or
liability, and they deliberately interpose a company to defeat or evade
that pre-existing obligation.
Because Mr. Prest transferred the properties to the companies long before
the marriage broke down, he was not "evading" an existing divorce
liability. Therefore, the veil could not be pierced. However, the Court
found that because the companies paid nothing for the properties, they
held them on a "Resulting Trust" for Mr. Prest personally. Thus, Mrs.
Prest got the houses through trust law, while the strict sanctity of
corporate law was preserved.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Evasion vs. Concealment Test: The ultimate restriction on piercing
the corporate veil. It can only be pierced to prevent the deliberate
evasion of an already existing legal liability, definitively ending the
era of courts piercing the veil simply for "justice" or "fairness."

cases.title: Re Barings plc (No 5)
cases.facts:
Barings Bank, one of the oldest merchant banks in the UK, spectacularly
collapsed due to massive, unauthorized speculative trading by a single
rogue trader, Nick Leeson, based in the Singapore office. The UK
regulatory authorities sought disqualification orders under the Company
Directors Disqualification Act against three senior directors based in
London. The directors had not participated in the fraud, but they were
the managers responsible for overseeing Leeson's department.
cases.issues:
To what extent can senior directors delegate responsibility to lower-
level management?

Can directors be disqualified for "unfitness" based purely on a
catastrophic failure to supervise an employee, even if they were unaware
of the fraud?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Secretary of State /
Regulators)
The regulators argued that the directors were grossly incompetent. They
ignored massive warning signs (like astronomical funding requests from
Singapore) and failed to establish basic internal controls. Their failure
to supervise directly enabled the collapse of the bank, making them unfit
to manage companies.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (The Senior Directors)
The directors argued they were based in London and reasonably delegated
the Singapore operations to local management. Leeson actively deceived
them, falsifying records. They argued that holding them liable for a
sophisticated fraud committed thousands of miles away would impose an
impossible burden on the directors of multinational corporations.
cases.judgment:
The Court ruled in favor of the regulators, disqualifying the directors
for periods ranging from 4 to 6 years.
cases.reasoning:
The Court issued a landmark ruling on the duty to supervise. The Court
held that while directors are absolutely entitled to delegate functions
to management, delegation does not equal abdication. Directors have a
proactive, continuing duty to supervise the discharge of the delegated
functions. The London directors failed to understand the nature of
Leeson's trading, failed to act on audit warnings, and allowed Leeson to
control both the trading desk and the back-office settlements (a fatal
lack of segregation of duties). Their passive reliance on a rogue
employee, without putting control mechanisms in place, amounted to
serious incompetence rendering them unfit for corporate office.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Duty to Supervise: Directors cannot use delegation as a complete
shield against liability. They have a proactive, non-delegable fiduciary
duty to maintain oversight, establish risk management systems, and
monitor the executives to whom they have delegated power.

cases.title: O'Neill v. Phillips
cases.facts:
Phillips owned 100% of a company. He brought in O'Neill as an employee,
eventually giving him 25% of the shares and making him managing director.
Phillips unofficially promised O'Neill that he would eventually get 50%
of the profits and more shares if the company hit certain targets. When
an economic downturn hit, Phillips took back control of the management,
stopped paying O'Neill the 50% profit share, and refused to give him the
promised shares. O'Neill sued for "unfair prejudice" (the UK equivalent
of oppression), claiming his legitimate expectations were breached.
cases.issues:
What constitutes "unfair prejudice" in a quasi-partnership company?

Can a vague, unwritten promise form the basis of a legally enforceable
"legitimate expectation" in corporate law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (O'Neill)
O'Neill argued that the company was a quasi-partnership. He worked for
years based on the mutual understanding that he would be an equal
partner. Phillips' actions in stripping his management role and cutting
his profits were unfair and breached this equitable understanding.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Phillips)
Phillips argued that the promises were never formalized into a contract
or the Articles of Association. As the majority shareholder, he had the
strict legal right under the Companies Act to manage his company and
declare dividends as he saw fit.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Phillips, dismissing O'Neill's claim
of unfair prejudice.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Hoffmann clarified the limits of the "unfair prejudice" remedy. He
held that "unfairness" in company law is not judged by personal morality
or vague notions of fairness, but must be based on established equitable
principles. A minority shareholder cannot complain of unfair prejudice
unless there is a breach of the agreed terms of the corporate
constitution (the Articles), OR a breach of a clear, underlying equitable
agreement between the founders. The Court found that Phillips' promises
regarding the 50% share were merely negotiations and informal
aspirations, never a binding equitable contract. Therefore, Phillips
merely exercised his strict legal rights, which does not amount to unfair
prejudice.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Limits of Unfair Prejudice: "Legitimate expectations" must be grounded in
clear, provable equitable agreements, not just vague promises. The courts
will not use oppression remedies to enforce informal business
negotiations that were never finalized.

cases.title: Allen v. Hyatt
cases.facts:
The directors of a company were negotiating an amalgamation with another
larger company. To secure the deal, the directors needed the consent of
the other shareholders. The directors approached the shareholders and
actively induced them to give the directors the "options" to buy their
shares at par value, claiming this was necessary to facilitate the
amalgamation on behalf of everyone. The directors then used these options
to buy the shares themselves, and immediately sold them to the
amalgamating company at a massive premium, pocketing the profit.
cases.issues:
Does the rule in Percival v. Wright (that directors owe no direct
fiduciary duty to individual shareholders) apply when directors actively
solicit shareholders to act as their agents?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Hyatt / Shareholders)
The shareholders argued that the directors deliberately deceived them. By
asking the shareholders to entrust them with the share options to
"facilitate" the deal, the directors had stepped out of their purely
corporate role and made themselves the personal agents of the
shareholders. Therefore, they owed them a direct fiduciary duty to
account for the secret profit.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Allen / Directors)
The directors relied strictly on Percival v. Wright. They argued their
fiduciary duty was exclusively to the corporate entity. When buying
shares from individual members, it was an arm's-length commercial
transaction, and they were under no obligation to disclose the higher
price negotiated with the acquiring company.
cases.judgment:
The Privy Council ruled in favor of the shareholders, ordering the
directors to disgorge the profits made on the shares.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a vital exception to the Percival v. Wright rule.
While the general rule holds that directors do not owe duties to
individual shareholders, the facts of this case created an explicit
agency relationship. The directors did not just quietly buy shares on the
open market; they actively approached the shareholders, represented that
they were acting on their behalf to secure the amalgamation, and used
that trust to extract the options. By actively placing themselves in an
agency relationship with the individual shareholders, the directors
assumed a direct fiduciary duty to them, prohibiting them from making a
secret personal profit at the shareholders' expense.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Agency Exception (Duty to Shareholders): Directors can owe direct
fiduciary duties to individual shareholders if the directors place
themselves in a position of agency or specific trust regarding the
shareholders' personal property (shares), particularly in the context of
takeovers or buyouts.

cases.title: State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer
cases.facts:
The State Trading Corporation (STC), a company incorporated under the
Companies Act and entirely owned by the Government of India, was assessed
for commercial taxes. STC filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court
under Article 32 of the Constitution, arguing that the tax assessment
violated its fundamental right to carry on trade and business under
Article 19(1)(g). The Commercial Tax Officer contested the
maintainability of the petition.
cases.issues:
Can a corporation, which is a juristic person, be considered a "citizen"
of India under Part III of the Constitution to claim fundamental rights
guaranteed exclusively to citizens?

Does the fact that a corporation is 100% owned by Indian citizens (or the
Government) make the corporate entity a citizen?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (STC)
STC argued that since all its shareholders (the President of India and
two joint secretaries) were citizens, the corporate veil should be lifted
to grant the entity the fundamental rights of its constituent members.
Depriving a state-owned company of Article 19 rights would severely
hamper its ability to conduct business.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Commercial Tax Officer)
The State argued that Part II of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act
explicitly restrict citizenship to natural persons. A company is a
separate legal entity distinct from its shareholders (Salomon principle).
Therefore, a non-citizen juristic person cannot claim rights under
Article 19.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled against STC, holding that a company is not a
citizen and cannot claim fundamental rights under Article 19.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly applied the separate corporate personality doctrine to
constitutional law. It held that "nationality" and "citizenship" are not
synonymous. A company has a nationality (Indian, by virtue of
incorporation in India), which gives it certain rights and subjects it to
Indian laws. However, it cannot be a "citizen" because citizenship
involves political rights and duties applicable only to natural persons.
The Court refused to pierce the veil to confer citizenship based on the
shareholders' status.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Corporate Citizenship: A company incorporated in India is an Indian
domicile and possesses Indian nationality, but it is definitively not a
"citizen" under the Indian Constitution and cannot claim rights
exclusively reserved for citizens (like Article 19).

cases.title: Dr. A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar v. Life Insurance Corporation of India
cases.facts:
The Directors of a life insurance company passed a resolution donating ₹2
lakhs from the company's funds to a charitable trust established to
promote technical and business education. Subsequently, the life
insurance sector was nationalized, and the Life Insurance Corporation of
India (LIC) took over the company's assets. LIC sued the former directors
to recover the ₹2 lakhs, arguing the donation was illegal.
cases.issues:
Was the donation of corporate funds to a charitable trust ultra vires the
company's Memorandum of Association?

Are directors personally liable to refund money spent on ultra vires
charitable acts?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (LIC)
LIC argued that the company's primary object was life insurance. The
Memorandum did not explicitly authorize massive charitable donations.
Spending shareholders' money on a trust that provided no direct
commercial benefit to the insurance business was ultra vires and void.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Directors)
The directors relied on a general, sweeping clause in the Memorandum that
allowed the company to do "all such other things as are incidental or
conducive to the attainment of the above objects." They argued that
promoting business education was broadly conducive to the corporate
environment.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of LIC, declaring the donation ultra
vires and ordering the directors to personally refund the money.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly construed the Objects Clause. It held that an act is
only "incidental or conducive" if it has a direct, proximate connection
to the company's main business. A charitable donation to an educational
trust had no direct nexus to selling life insurance. Generosity with
corporate funds is only legally valid if it serves a corporate purpose
(the Hutton rule). Because the payment was completely outside the legal
capacity of the company, the directors breached their fiduciary duty by
misapplying corporate funds and were held personally liable to restore
the wealth.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Strict Ultra Vires & Charity: Corporate philanthropy is not a general
right. Unless explicitly authorized by the Memorandum, or directly
beneficial to the company's commercial operations, charitable donations
are ultra vires, triggering the personal liability of the directors.
(Note: Modern Section 135 CSR obligations now explicitly mandate such
spending).

cases.title: Twycross v. Grant
cases.facts:
Grant and another individual devised a scheme to build a tramway. They
purchased the necessary concessions, drafted the company's prospectus,
found individuals to act as the first directors, and paid for the initial
advertising. However, Grant's name did not appear anywhere on the
official documents as a director or shareholder; he operated entirely
behind the scenes. When the company failed due to undisclosed financial
arrangements, shareholders sued Grant, claiming he was a promoter and had
breached his duties.
cases.issues:
What constitutes the legal definition of a "promoter" in corporate law?

Can an individual be held liable as a promoter even if they hold no
official position within the newly formed company?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Twycross / Shareholders)
The plaintiffs argued that Grant was the mastermind. He did all the
foundational work to bring the company into existence. His lack of a
formal title was merely a facade to avoid the legal liabilities
associated with company formation.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Grant)
Grant argued that he was merely an independent contractor or an agent
executing specific tasks for a fee. Since he was not a director or an
incorporating member, he owed no fiduciary duty to the company as a
promoter.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled against Grant, holding that he was indeed a
promoter and liable as such.
cases.reasoning:
Chief Justice Cockburn delivered the classic, universally accepted
definition of a promoter: "A promoter is one who undertakes to form a
company with reference to a given project and to set it going, and who
takes the necessary steps to accomplish that purpose." The Court
emphasized that "promoter" is not a legal term of art, but a term of
business. It is a question of fact, not title. Because Grant orchestrated
the formation, drafted the prospectus, and appointed the board, he was
factually a promoter and therefore owed strict fiduciary duties to the
company he created.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Factual Definition of Promoter: Promotion is determined by an
individual's actual actions in bringing a company into existence, not by
their official designation. Anyone who plays a substantial role in
setting up the company is bound by fiduciary duties.

cases.title: Erlanger v. New Sombrero Phosphate Co.
cases.facts:
Erlanger, acting as a promoter, purchased a lease for a phosphate mine on
Sombrero Island for £55,000. He then formed a company (New Sombrero
Phosphate Co.) and appointed a board of directors who were entirely his
puppets (one was his agent, others were unaware of the true facts).
Erlanger then sold the lease to his newly formed company for £110,000,
pocketing a massive secret profit without disclosing his original
purchase price to the shareholders. When the independent shareholders
discovered this, the company sued to rescind the contract.
cases.issues:
What is the nature of the fiduciary duty owed by a promoter to the newly
formed company?

Is a promoter required to disclose their profits to an independent board
of directors, or is disclosure to a puppet board sufficient?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (New Sombrero Co.)
The company argued that Erlanger stood in a fiduciary position. By
appointing a puppet board that did not scrutinize the sale, he
essentially negotiated a contract with himself, stealing from the
incoming shareholders.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Erlanger)
Erlanger argued caveat emptor (let the buyer beware). He claimed he
legally owned the lease and had the right to sell it at whatever price
the company agreed to. He argued that the board, as the legal
representative of the company, approved the purchase.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of the company, ordering the rescission
of the contract and the return of the purchase money.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down the absolute foundation of promoter liability.
Promoters stand in a fiduciary relationship to the company they create.
While promoters are allowed to sell their own property to the new company
and make a profit, they have an absolute duty to make full and fair
disclosure of all material facts, including the profit they are making.
Crucially, this disclosure must be made to an independent and competent
Board of Directors who can objectively evaluate the transaction.
Disclosing the profit to a board of "dummies" controlled by the promoter
is no disclosure at all and constitutes a breach of trust.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Promoter's Fiduciary Duty: Promoters cannot make secret profits at the
expense of the company.

Requirement of Independent Scrutiny: Any transaction between a promoter
and the company requires full disclosure to an independent executive
board; lacking this, the company has the right to rescind the contract.

cases.title: Kelner v. Baxter
cases.facts:
Baxter and others were acting as promoters for a proposed hotel company
that had not yet been incorporated. On behalf of the unformed company,
they signed a contract to purchase wine from Kelner. The contract was
explicitly signed "on behalf of the proposed Gravesend Royal Alexandra
Hotel Co." The company was later incorporated, received the wine, but
went bankrupt before paying for it. Kelner sued the promoters (Baxter)
personally for the debt.
cases.issues:
Can a person be held personally liable for a contract they sign
explicitly on behalf of a company that does not yet legally exist?

Can a company, once incorporated, legally ratify a pre-incorporation
contract made by its promoters?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Kelner)
Kelner argued that since the company did not exist at the time of
signing, it could not be the principal. Therefore, the people who
actually signed the paper must be held personally liable, otherwise, the
contract would be a legal nullity and he would have no remedy.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Baxter/Promoters)
The promoters argued they explicitly signed as agents, not as principals.
Since the company took the wine and used it, the company implicitly
ratified the contract, transferring the liability to the corporate entity
and discharging the agents.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Common Pleas ruled in favor of Kelner, holding the promoters
personally liable for the debt.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the strict common law rule regarding pre-
incorporation contracts. A fundamental rule of agency is that an agent
cannot act for a principal that does not exist. Since the company was not
yet incorporated, it had no legal capacity to contract. Furthermore, a
principal cannot ratify a contract retroactively if it did not possess
the legal capacity to make the contract at the time it was signed.
Therefore, the company could never legally adopt the contract. To prevent
the contract from being completely void, the law presumes that the
individuals who signed it intended to bind themselves personally.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Personal Liability of Promoters: Promoters are strictly, personally
liable for pre-incorporation contracts, even if they sign "on behalf of"
the proposed company.

No Retroactive Ratification: A company cannot ratify pre-incorporation
contracts. (Note: In India, Section 15 & 19 of the Specific Relief Act
provide a narrow statutory exception allowing companies to adopt such
contracts if explicitly warranted by their incorporating documents).

cases.title: Bell Houses Ltd v. City Wall Properties Ltd
cases.facts:
Bell Houses Ltd was incorporated with the primary object of developing
housing estates. Its Memorandum of Association contained a highly
subjective ancillary objects clause: "To carry on any other trade or
business whatsoever which can, in the opinion of the board of directors,
be advantageously carried on by the company in connection with or as
ancillary to any of the above businesses." The directors used their
business contacts to act as mortgage brokers, introducing a financier to
City Wall Properties for a massive fee. City Wall refused to pay, arguing
that mortgage brokering was ultra vires a housing developer.
cases.issues:
Is a "subjective objects clause" (one that relies on the opinion of the
directors rather than an objective list of activities) legally valid?

Was the act of mortgage brokering intra vires based on the directors'
subjective assessment?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Bell Houses)
Bell Houses argued that the Memorandum explicitly delegated the power to
determine ancillary businesses to the Board. Since the Board honestly
believed that brokering this financing deal was advantageous and
connected to their general knowledge of real estate finance, the contract
was intra vires.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (City Wall)
City Wall argued that such a clause destroys the purpose of the ultra
vires doctrine. If directors can subjectively decide what is intra vires,
there are no limits on the company's capacity, leaving creditors
completely uninformed.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Bell Houses, holding that the
contract was intra vires and City Wall must pay the fee.
cases.reasoning:
The Court upheld the validity of the subjective objects clause. The Court
reasoned that business requires flexibility. If the shareholders agreed
in the Memorandum to trust the honest business judgment of the directors
to identify advantageous ancillary businesses, the courts should not
interfere. The test is not an objective judicial assessment of whether
the new business is connected to the old one, but a subjective test: Did
the directors bona fide (genuinely and honestly) form the opinion that it
could be advantageously carried on? Since there was no evidence of bad
faith, the directors' opinion legitimized the transaction.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Subjective Objects Clause Validity: Confirmed the legality of drafting
Memorandums that empower the board to subjectively expand the company's
activities, further weakening the traditional ultra vires doctrine in
favor of commercial agility.

cases.title: T.R. Pratt (Bombay) Ltd. v. E.D. Sassoon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts:
T.R. Pratt Ltd needed funds. Its directors borrowed a massive sum from
E.D. Sassoon & Co. However, under Pratt's Articles of Association, the
directors had no authority to borrow such a large amount without the
prior consent of the shareholders in a general meeting, which was never
obtained. Crucially, several directors of Pratt Ltd were simultaneously
directors of E.D. Sassoon & Co. When Pratt went into liquidation, the
liquidator sought to void the loan, claiming it was unauthorized. Sassoon
relied on the rule of indoor management.
cases.issues:
Can a third party rely on the Doctrine of Indoor Management (Turquand's
Rule) if they have actual or constructive knowledge of the internal
irregularity?

Does the common directorship of both companies impute the knowledge of
one company to the other?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Liquidator of Pratt)
The liquidator argued that the borrowing was beyond the directors'
authority and therefore void. They argued Sassoon could not claim
innocent reliance on indoor management because the very same people who
authorized the illegal borrowing for Pratt were managing Sassoon.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (E.D. Sassoon & Co)
Sassoon argued that as an external lender, they were only required to
read Pratt's Memorandum and Articles. Finding that borrowing was
permitted (subject to a resolution), they were entitled to assume the
internal resolution had been properly passed (Turquand).
cases.judgment:
The Bombay High Court ruled in favor of the liquidator, invalidating the
loan.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a major exception to the Turquand rule. The rule of
indoor management is designed exclusively to protect innocent outsiders
who have no way of knowing about internal corporate failures. It cannot
be used as a shield by someone who actually knew the proper procedures
were not followed. Because the two companies shared common directors who
orchestrated the transaction, the knowledge of the directors (that no
shareholder resolution was passed) was legally imputed to the lending
company (Sassoon). Therefore, Sassoon had actual notice of the
irregularity and could not claim the protection of indoor management.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Actual Notice Exception: The Doctrine of Indoor Management does not
protect a third party who has actual or constructive notice that the
company's internal procedures have not been complied with, especially in
cases of interlocking directorates.

cases.title: Sri Gopal Jalan & Co. v. Calcutta Stock Exchange Association Ltd.
cases.facts:
The Calcutta Stock Exchange (CSE) expelled a defaulting member and, under
the provisions of its Articles of Association, forfeited his shares.
Subsequently, the CSE re-allotted these forfeited shares to another
member. Under Section 75 of the Companies Act (1956), a company is
strictly required to file a "Return of Allotment" with the Registrar of
Companies (RoC) whenever it makes an allotment of shares. The CSE did not
file this return. The RoC initiated penal action, arguing the re-issuance
of forfeited shares constituted an "allotment."
cases.issues:
What is the precise legal definition of an "allotment" of shares in
corporate law?

Does the re-issue or sale of shares that have been previously forfeited
by the company amount to a fresh "allotment" requiring statutory
compliance?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Registrar of Companies)
The RoC argued that handing out shares to a new person, generating new
share certificates, and adding a new name to the register constitutes an
allotment, regardless of whether the shares were new or previously
forfeited.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Calcutta Stock Exchange)
The CSE argued that an allotment refers exclusively to the creation and
first issuance of shares from the unissued, authorized capital. Forfeited
shares have already been issued and created. Therefore, re-issuing them
is just a sale of existing corporate property, not a new allotment.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of the Calcutta Stock Exchange,
holding that the re-issue of forfeited shares is not an allotment.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court analyzed the jurisprudence of share capital. The Court
held that "allotment" means the appropriation out of the previously
unappropriated capital of a company to a specific number of shares to a
person. It is the very act of creating the share and giving it life. When
a share is validly issued and later forfeited due to non-payment of
calls, the share does not cease to exist; it becomes the property of the
company. Therefore, when the company re-issues that forfeited share, it
is merely selling or transferring an asset it already owns. Since no new
capital is being created or appropriated, it is not an "allotment" within
the meaning of the Companies Act.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Legal Definition of Allotment: Allotment is strictly the initial
appropriation of unissued share capital.

Status of Forfeited Shares: The re-issuance of a forfeited share is
legally a sale, not an allotment, exempting the company from the strict
procedural and filing requirements associated with fresh capital
issuance.

cases.title: Hely-Hutchinson v. Brayhead Ltd
cases.facts:
Mr. Richards was the Chairman of the Board of Directors of Brayhead Ltd.
Although he was never formally appointed by a board resolution to the
position of Managing Director, the rest of the board essentially allowed
him to run the company, making executive decisions and committing the
company to contracts without prior board approval. In this capacity,
Richards issued a financial guarantee on behalf of Brayhead Ltd to Mr.
Hely-Hutchinson to secure a business deal. When the deal went bad, Hely-
Hutchinson sued Brayhead on the guarantee. Brayhead argued that Richards
was just the Chairman, had no authority to issue guarantees without a
board resolution, and therefore the company was not bound.
cases.issues:
Can a director bind the company if they have not been formally granted
authority, but have been allowed by the board to act as the de facto
chief executive?

What is the difference between "actual" authority and "implied" actual
authority?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Hely-Hutchinson)
The plaintiff argued that he dealt with the man running the company. By
sitting back and allowing Richards to act as the undisputed boss for
months, the Board of Directors implicitly gave him the authority to make
such contracts.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Brayhead Ltd)
The company relied on strict corporate procedure. The Articles stated
that only the Board could issue guarantees. Since no resolution delegated
this power to Richards, he acted outside his authority, making the
guarantee void.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Hely-Hutchinson, holding Brayhead
Ltd liable on the guarantee.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Denning articulated the concept of "implied actual authority."
Actual authority does not only come from express written resolutions; it
can be implied from the conduct of the parties and the circumstances of
the case. Because the Board of Directors of Brayhead knew that Richards
had been acting as the de facto Managing Director and committing the
company to contracts for months, and they had acquiesced to this
behavior, they had implicitly delegated actual authority to him. Because
he possessed implied actual authority to run the business, the guarantee
he signed was binding on the company.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Implied Actual Authority: Formal board resolutions are not the only
source of executive power. A company is bound by the acts of a director
if the board, through a course of continuous acquiescence, permits that
director to act as the de facto executive.

cases.title: Freeman & Lockyer v. Buckhurst Park Properties (Mangal) Ltd
cases.facts:
Kapoor and Hoon formed a company to buy and resell an estate. The
Articles required four directors to form a quorum, but effectively only
Kapoor ran the business. Kapoor, acting entirely on his own but behaving
as if he were the Managing Director, engaged a firm of architects
(Freeman & Lockyer) to draw up plans for the estate. The Board never
appointed Kapoor as MD and never formally authorized the hiring of the
architects. When the company refused to pay the architects' fees, they
sued.
cases.issues:
When is a company bound by the acts of a director who has no actual
authority (express or implied) but merely appears to have authority?

What are the legal requirements to establish "ostensible" (or apparent)
authority?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Freeman & Lockyer)
The architects argued they dealt with Kapoor in good faith. He was
working from the company office, directing the project, and the other
directors clearly knew what he was doing and did not stop him. He had the
apparent authority of an MD, and the company must pay for the work it
requested.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Buckhurst Park Properties)
The company argued that under its Articles, only the full Board could
make such a contract. Kapoor had no actual authority, and therefore the
contract was a nullity.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the architects, holding the company
liable to pay the fees based on ostensible authority.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Diplock delivered the definitive judgment on "ostensible" (apparent)
authority in corporate law. He established that a company is bound by an
agent who lacks actual authority if four conditions are met:

Representation: A representation was made to the contractor that the
agent had authority (Kapoor acting as MD).

By Authorized Person: The representation was made by a person who had
actual authority to manage the business (The Board, by their silent
acquiescence, made the representation).

Reliance: The contractor relied on this representation.

Capacity: The company's Memorandum actually allowed it to enter into such
a contract.
Because the Board, which had actual authority, stood by and let Kapoor
hold himself out as the Managing Director, they "represented" to the
architects that he had the power to hire them. The company was therefore
legally estopped from denying his authority.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Doctrine of Ostensible Authority: A company is estopped from denying the
authority of an unappointed officer if the Board of Directors permits
that person to act outwardly as if they hold that position, protecting
innocent third parties who rely on that appearance.

cases.title: Scottish Co-operative Wholesale Society Ltd v. Meyer
cases.facts:
The Scottish Co-operative Wholesale Society (the parent company) formed a
subsidiary company to manufacture rayon. Meyer and another individual
were the minority shareholders and managing directors of the subsidiary.
The parent company appointed three nominee directors to the subsidiary's
board. Over time, the parent company decided to manufacture rayon itself,
setting up a competing department. The nominee directors deliberately
starved the subsidiary of raw materials and business, causing its value
to plummet. Meyer sued the parent company for oppression.
cases.issues:
Can the conduct of a parent company be considered "oppressive" to the
minority shareholders of its subsidiary if the parent simply starves the
subsidiary of business?

What are the fiduciary duties of nominee directors appointed by a parent
company to a subsidiary's board?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Meyer)
Meyer argued that the parent company, through its nominee directors,
actively destroyed the subsidiary's business to steal its market share.
This deliberate destruction of the minority's investment constituted
severe and continuous oppression.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Scottish Co-operative)
The parent company argued that it was a separate legal entity and had
every right to compete in the open market. They claimed the nominee
directors simply did nothing (omission), and mere inaction does not
amount to the active "wrongful conduct" required for an oppression claim.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Meyer, holding the parent company
guilty of oppression and ordering it to buy out Meyer's shares at a fair
value.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established strict rules regarding nominee directors. Lord
Denning held that when a parent company appoints directors to a
subsidiary, those directors owe a fiduciary duty to the subsidiary, not
to the parent. By actively advancing the parent's competing business and
remaining silent while the subsidiary was destroyed, the nominee
directors breached their duties. Furthermore, the parent company used its
majority control not to manage the subsidiary, but to crush it. This
blatant conflict of interest and deliberate destruction of minority value
is the textbook definition of oppressive conduct.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Duties of Nominee Directors: A director nominated by a majority
shareholder owes their fiduciary duty to the company on whose board they
sit, not to the shareholder who appointed them.

Oppression via Competition: A parent company cannot use its control to
deliberately starve and destroy a subsidiary to appropriate its business;
doing so is oppressive to the subsidiary's minority shareholders.

cases.title: Re Bugle Press Ltd
cases.facts:
Bugle Press had three shareholders. Two majority shareholders (Shaw and
Jackson) held 4,500 shares each, and a minority shareholder (Trevlis)
held 1,000 shares. Shaw and Jackson wanted to buy Trevlis out, but he
refused. To force a squeeze-out, Shaw and Jackson formed a new shell
company (Jackson & Shaw Ltd) which they wholly owned. This new company
made a takeover bid for Bugle Press. Shaw and Jackson (as the 90%
majority of Bugle Press) accepted the bid. They then invoked the
statutory "drag-along" provision of the Companies Act to compulsorily
acquire Trevlis's 10% minority shares. Trevlis challenged the compulsory
acquisition in court.
cases.issues:
Can majority shareholders use a shell company and statutory takeover
provisions specifically to expropriate the shares of a dissenting
minority shareholder?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Trevlis / Minority)
Trevlis argued that the takeover bid was a sham. The acquiring company
was just the majority shareholders wearing a different corporate hat. The
statutory power of compulsory acquisition was meant for genuine external
takeovers, not for internal expropriation of a minority.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Bugle Press / Majority)
The majority argued that they strictly followed the letter of the
Companies Act. A 90% majority accepted the bid, triggering the statutory
mechanism to buy out the remaining 10%. They argued the court should not
look behind the corporate veil of the acquiring company.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Trevlis, blocking the compulsory
acquisition of his shares.
cases.reasoning:
The Court struck down the scheme, ruling that the statutory provision for
compulsory acquisition was designed to prevent a small, stubborn minority
from blocking a genuine, independent commercial takeover. It was never
intended to be used as a weapon by the majority to expropriate a
minority. The Court effectively pierced the corporate veil of the
acquiring shell company, recognizing that the "buyer" and the "90%
accepting majority" were the exact same people. Using the Companies Act
to execute a bad-faith squeeze-out was an abuse of statutory power.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Abuse of Statutory Squeeze-Out: Courts will not permit majority
shareholders to use shell companies and statutory takeover mechanisms
purely as a device to forcibly expropriate the shares of a minority
member.

cases.title: Re Duomatic Ltd
cases.facts:
Duomatic Ltd had two directors who were also the only two voting
shareholders. They routinely drew remuneration from the company without
ever holding a formal general meeting or passing formal resolutions to
authorize the payments, as strictly required by the company's Articles of
Association. When the company went into liquidation, the liquidator sued
the directors to recover the remuneration, arguing that the payments were
unauthorized and ultra vires the directors' powers since no formal
meeting ever took place.
cases.issues:
Are corporate actions legally valid if all voting shareholders consent to
them informally, without holding a statutorily required general meeting?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Liquidator)
The liquidator argued strict compliance. The Companies Act and the
Articles require formal meetings, notice periods, and recorded minutes.
Bypassing these procedures makes the authorization void, rendering the
directors liable for misapplying company funds.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Directors/Shareholders)
The directors argued that since they owned 100% of the voting shares,
holding a formal meeting to vote on something they already agreed upon
was an empty, absurd formality. Their unanimous, albeit informal, consent
should be legally equivalent to a formal resolution.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of the directors, validating the
payments.
cases.reasoning:
Buckley J established the famous "Duomatic Principle." He held that where
all shareholders who have a right to attend and vote at a general meeting
of the company assent to a matter which a general meeting of the company
could carry into effect, that assent is as binding as a resolution in
general meeting would be. The law looks to the substance of shareholder
consent, not the strict procedural form. If 100% of the voting power
agrees, the corporate mind has been made up, and demanding a formal
meeting is a waste of time.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Duomatic Principle (Unanimous Consent): Strict procedural formalities
for shareholder meetings can be bypassed if there is unanimous, informal
consent among all voting shareholders, provided the act is intra vires
the company.

cases.title: Russell v. Northern Bank Development Corp Ltd
cases.facts:
Five executives formed a company. They entered into a private
Shareholders' Agreement (SHA) which included a specific clause: no new
share capital would be created or issued without the unanimous written
consent of all five executives. The company itself was also made a party
to this SHA. Years later, the Board of Directors proposed a resolution to
increase the share capital, supported by a statutory majority but opposed
by Russell. Russell sued for an injunction to enforce the unanimity
clause in the SHA.
cases.issues:
Can a Shareholders' Agreement legally restrict a company's statutory
right to alter its share capital?

Does an SHA bind the company differently than it binds the individual
shareholders?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Russell)
Russell argued that a contract is a contract. All parties, including the
corporate entity, signed the SHA agreeing to the unanimity rule. The
company must be held to its contractual obligations.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Northern Bank / Company)
The company argued that under the Companies Act, a company has an
unfettered statutory power to increase its share capital via an ordinary
resolution. A company cannot contractually fetter its own statutory
powers. Therefore, the clause in the SHA binding the company was void.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled that the agreement was void as against the
company, but valid and enforceable as an agreement between the
shareholders. Russell was granted an injunction against the other
shareholders.
cases.reasoning:
The Court drew a razor-sharp distinction. A company cannot contract away
its statutory powers. Therefore, the clause in the SHA attempting to
prevent the company from increasing its capital was ultra vires and void.
However, shareholders are free to contract with each other regarding how
they will vote. The SHA was a valid voting agreement among the
executives. By proposing to vote for the capital increase, the other
executives were breaching their personal contract with Russell. The Court
issued an injunction stopping the shareholders from voting for the
resolution, effectively achieving Russell's goal without violating the
company's statutory freedom.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Non-Fettering of Corporate Powers: A company cannot enter into a contract
that restricts its fundamental statutory powers (like altering share
capital or Articles).

Validity of Voting Agreements: Shareholders' Agreements are valid as
private voting contracts between members and can be enforced via
injunctions to prevent members from voting contrary to the agreement.

cases.title: Daniels v. Daniels
cases.facts:
Mr. and Mrs. Daniels were the majority shareholders and the only
directors of a company. They caused the company to sell a piece of
corporate land to Mrs. Daniels for £4,250. Four years later, Mrs. Daniels
sold the exact same piece of land to an outside buyer for £120,000,
pocketing a massive personal profit. The minority shareholders sued the
directors, alleging they sold the land at a gross undervalue.
cases.issues:
Can minority shareholders bypass the rule in Foss v. Harbottle to sue
directors for negligence if the directors also personally benefited from
that negligence?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Minority Shareholders)
The minority argued that the directors breached their fiduciary duty by
selling corporate assets at a fraction of their value. Because the
wrongdoers controlled the company, the company would never sue itself,
requiring an exception to the Foss v. Harbottle rule.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Daniels / Directors)
The directors argued that, at worst, they were merely negligent in
assessing the land's value. Under traditional corporate law, mere
negligence is an internal management issue that can be ratified by the
majority (which they were). Therefore, under Foss v. Harbottle, the
minority had no standing to sue.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of the minority shareholders,
allowing the lawsuit to proceed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court expanded the "fraud on the minority" exception to Foss v.
Harbottle. Templeman J noted that while minority shareholders generally
cannot sue directors for simple, honest mistakes or negligence (as that
is a risk of doing business), the situation changes entirely when the
directors profit from their negligence. If majority directors negligently
sell an asset at an undervalue to themselves, it is legally equivalent to
fraud. The courts will not allow directors to use their majority voting
power to ratify a negligent act that puts corporate wealth directly into
their own pockets.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Exception to Foss v. Harbottle (Negligence + Profit): Minority
shareholders have locus standi to sue directors if the directors commit
an act of negligence that simultaneously confers a direct personal
financial benefit upon themselves at the expense of the company.

cases.title: Piercy v. S. Mills & Co Ltd
cases.facts:
The company had two directors who held a minority of the voting shares.
Piercy, the majority shareholder, disagreed with the directors'
management style and intended to use his majority voting power at the
next general meeting to elect himself to the board and remove the
existing directors. Knowing this, the incumbent directors used their
board power to issue new shares to themselves and their friends. This
massive allotment instantly diluted Piercy's holding, reducing him to a
minority and securing the incumbent directors' control over the company.
Piercy sued to invalidate the allotment.
cases.issues:
Can directors legally exercise their power to issue shares for the sole
purpose of retaining control of the board and defeating a majority
shareholder?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Piercy)
Piercy argued that the directors committed a gross breach of fiduciary
duty. The power to issue shares is granted strictly to raise capital for
the company. Using it as a weapon to manipulate shareholder democracy and
steal his majority control was improper and invalid.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (S. Mills & Co / Directors)
The directors argued that they honestly believed Piercy was unfit to
manage the company and that his taking control would destroy the
business. Therefore, they argued, issuing the shares to retain their own
control was a bona fide act done in the best interests of the company.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of Piercy, declaring the share
allotment void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court firmly established that the directors' subjective belief about
what is best for the company does not justify the unconstitutional use of
corporate power. The power to issue shares is a fiduciary power meant for
raising capital. Directors are not entitled to use this power merely to
maintain their own control or to defeat the wishes of the existing
majority of shareholders. Manipulating the voting structure to prevent a
shareholder from exercising their legal rights is an improper purpose,
rendering the allotment void, regardless of the directors' "good
intentions."
cases.legalPrinciples:
Improper Purpose (Share Allotment): Directors are strictly prohibited
from issuing shares to dilute a majority shareholder or to manipulate the
voting control of the company.

cases.title: Re Astec (BSR) plc
cases.facts:
Astec was a public limited company (plc) listed on the stock exchange.
Emerson Electric Co launched a takeover and acquired 51% of Astec's
shares. A group of minority shareholders who retained their shares
complained that Emerson was running Astec entirely for its own benefit,
ignoring minority interests, and refusing to appoint independent
directors. The minority sued for "unfair prejudice," arguing they had a
"legitimate expectation" that a listed company would be run independently
and in accordance with standard corporate governance codes.
cases.issues:
Can the concept of "legitimate expectation" (quasi-partnership) apply to
a large, publicly listed company?

Does a majority shareholder in a public company owe an equitable duty to
manage the company in a specific way beyond the strict rules of the
Articles?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Minority Shareholders)
The minority argued that investing in a public company comes with an
implicit, equitable expectation that the majority will adhere to standard
corporate governance norms and not run the public entity as if it were a
wholly-owned private subsidiary.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Emerson Electric)
Emerson argued that Astec was a public commercial entity, not a quasi-
partnership. Investors buy shares on the open market subject to the
Articles of Association and the Companies Act. There are no secret,
unwritten equitable agreements in public companies. As the 51% owner,
they had the statutory right to appoint the board and run the company.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Emerson Electric, dismissing the unfair
prejudice claim.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the equitable concept of "legitimate expectation"
(from Ebrahimi v. Westbourne Galleries) has absolutely no place in a
publicly listed company. Public companies are governed strictly by their
Articles of Association and statutory law. Investors buying shares on the
open market do not enter into personal relationships of mutual trust and
confidence with other shareholders. Therefore, a minority shareholder in
a public company cannot claim unfair prejudice based on vague
expectations of "good governance" if the majority is strictly exercising
its legal rights under the Articles.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Rejection of Legitimate Expectation in Public Companies: The equitable
doctrines that protect minorities in closely held private companies
(quasi-partnerships) do not apply to public listed companies, where
rights are strictly defined by the corporate constitution.

cases.title: Re Halt Garage (1964) Ltd
cases.facts:
Mr. and Mrs. Charles were the sole directors and shareholders of Halt
Garage Ltd. They worked hard and the company was profitable, drawing
reasonable directors' remuneration. Later, Mrs. Charles fell seriously
ill and was entirely unable to work or contribute to the business for
several years. Despite her complete absence, the company continued to pay
her a full director's remuneration. When the company eventually went into
liquidation, the liquidator sued to recover the money paid to Mrs.
Charles, arguing it was an illegal return of capital disguised as
remuneration.
cases.issues:
Can a court inquire into the "reasonableness" of a director's
remuneration?

When does excessive remuneration legally transform into an unlawful
disguised dividend or return of capital?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Liquidator)
The liquidator argued that remuneration implies payment for services
rendered. Since Mrs. Charles provided zero services for years, the
payments were gratuitous. Paying out corporate funds for nothing is a
disguised dividend, and since the company was sliding into insolvency, it
was an illegal reduction of capital.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Mr. & Mrs. Charles)
The directors argued that under the company's Articles, the amount of
remuneration is to be determined by the shareholders in a general
meeting. Since they were the only shareholders, they unanimously
authorized the pay. They argued the court has no jurisdiction to dictate
what a company chooses to pay its officers.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled partially in favor of the liquidator,
ordering Mrs. Charles to repay the portion of the money that exceeded a
reasonable director's fee.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a vital distinction. Generally, courts will not
assess the commercial reasonableness of a director's pay if it is a
genuine reward for services. However, if the payment is so grossly
excessive that it clearly has no relation to the services provided (or in
this case, where absolutely zero services were provided), the law will
reclassify the payment. The Court held that paying a full salary to a
director who does no work is not "remuneration" at all; it is a disguised
dividend. Because it was a dividend paid when the company lacked
distributable profits, it was an illegal misapplication of corporate
assets.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Disguised Dividends: While courts hesitate to police executive pay,
payments labeled "remuneration" that are completely divorced from any
actual services rendered will be legally reclassified as gratuitous
distributions or disguised dividends, making directors liable for
repayment if the company is insolvent.

cases.title: Cumbrian Newspapers Group Ltd v. Cumberland & Westmorland Herald
cases.facts:
Cumbrian Newspapers acquired a 10.6% stake in a rival newspaper company
(the Herald). To prevent Cumbrian from taking over, the Herald's
shareholders agreed to alter the Articles of Association. They granted
Cumbrian special rights: the right to appoint one director, and pre-
emption rights over any other shares being sold. Years later, the Herald
proposed to alter its Articles again to remove these special rights given
to Cumbrian. Cumbrian sued, arguing that these were "class rights" that
could not be altered without their explicit consent under the Companies
Act.
cases.issues:
What constitutes a "class right" in corporate law?

Can rights granted to a specific person by name in the Articles be
considered rights attached to a "class of shares"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Cumbrian Newspapers)
Cumbrian argued that although all the shares were ordinary shares, the
special rights granted to them in the Articles essentially created a
separate "class" of shares. Therefore, under statutory law, those rights
could not be varied or canceled without the consent of the class holder.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (The Herald)
The Herald argued that class rights must be attached to the shares
themselves (like preference shares vs. ordinary shares). The rights given
to Cumbrian were attached to Cumbrian as a person, not to the shares. If
Cumbrian sold the shares, the new buyer would not get the right to
appoint a director. Therefore, they were not class rights and could be
altered by a special resolution.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of Cumbrian Newspapers, declaring
the rights to be class rights.
cases.reasoning:
Scott J provided the definitive categorization of rights in a company's
Articles:

Rights attached to particular shares (e.g., dividend rights).

Rights conferred on individuals not in their capacity as members (e.g.,
an outsider's right to be the company solicitor).

Rights conferred on an individual in their capacity as a shareholder, but
not attached to specific shares.
The Court ruled that the third category does constitute a class right.
Because Cumbrian was granted these rights specifically because they were
a shareholder, those rights effectively created a unique class of
membership. Therefore, the company could not strip them of these rights
without following the strict statutory procedure for varying class
rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Definition of Class Rights: Special rights conferred upon a specific
shareholder by name in the Articles of Association are legally treated as
"class rights" and cannot be unilaterally removed by the majority without
the consent of the individual holding those rights.

cases.title: Re Hydrodam (Corby) Ltd
cases.facts:
Hydrodam was a wholly-owned subsidiary of Eagle Trust plc. Hydrodam went
into insolvent liquidation. The liquidator sought to impose personal
liability for "wrongful trading" on the directors of the parent company
(Eagle Trust). The liquidator argued that because Eagle Trust completely
controlled Hydrodam, the directors of Eagle Trust were acting as "shadow
directors" of Hydrodam.
cases.issues:
What is the precise legal test to establish that an individual or a
parent company is a "shadow director" of a subsidiary?

Does the mere fact that a parent company exercises control over a
subsidiary automatically make the parent's directors shadow directors of
the subsidiary?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Liquidator)
The liquidator argued that the de jure directors of Hydrodam were merely
puppets who followed every order given by the Eagle Trust board. Because
the Eagle Trust directors were pulling the strings and directing the
financial decisions that led to Hydrodam's insolvency, they should be
held liable as shadow directors.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Eagle Trust Directors)
The directors argued they were acting as the board of the parent company,
managing its investment. They never gave direct instructions to the
Hydrodam board; they simply passed corporate resolutions at the parent
level. They argued they were not shadows, but standard corporate owners.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Eagle Trust directors, holding they
were not shadow directors.
cases.reasoning:
Millet J delivered a highly precise legal definition, distinguishing
between de jure (legally appointed), de facto (acting as a director
without appointment), and shadow directors. To prove someone is a shadow
director, four elements must be met:

The identity of the formally appointed (de jure) directors.

That the alleged shadow director directed those appointed directors on
how to act.

That those appointed directors acted in accordance with those directions.

That they were accustomed to doing so (a pattern of obedience).
Crucially, the Court held that a shadow director must lurk in the
shadows, not step into the light. If a person acts openly as a director,
they are a de facto director. Furthermore, the Court held that just
because a parent company controls a subsidiary does not make the parent's
directors shadow directors. The liquidator failed to prove that the Eagle
Trust directors gave specific instructions to the Hydrodam board which
the board blindly followed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Definition of a Shadow Director: A person is only a shadow director if
they operate behind the scenes, issuing instructions that the legally
appointed board is accustomed to following blindly. Mere ownership or
corporate control by a parent company does not automatically trigger
shadow director liability.

cases.title: Gramophone and Typewriter Ltd v. Stanley
cases.facts:
An English company, Gramophone and Typewriter Ltd, held all the shares in
a German subsidiary company. The English company was assessed for UK
income tax on the total profits made by the German subsidiary. The UK tax
authorities (represented by Stanley) argued that because the English
company owned 100% of the shares, the German company was merely its agent
or branch, and therefore the business of the German company was
effectively the business of the English company.
cases.issues:
Does the fact that a parent company owns 100% of the shares in a
subsidiary automatically make the subsidiary an "agent" of the parent for
tax purposes?

Does complete share ownership equate to carrying on the business of the
subsidiary?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Gramophone and Typewriter Ltd)
The company relied on the bedrock principle of Salomon v. Salomon. They
argued that holding all the shares does not extinguish the separate legal
personality of the German subsidiary. The German company was managed by
its own directors under German law. The English company only had the
rights of a shareholder (to vote and receive dividends), not the right to
directly manage the German business.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Stanley / Revenue)
The tax authorities argued that the corporate veil should be ignored to
reflect economic reality. Since the English company had the absolute
power to hire and fire the German directors, it exercised ultimate
control, making the German company its de facto agent.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Gramophone and Typewriter Ltd,
holding that the profits of the German subsidiary could not be directly
taxed as the profits of the English parent.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a robust defense of the corporate veil in
multinational structures. Lord Cozens-Hardy MR held that the fact that an
individual or a company owns all the shares in another company does not
make the business of the latter the business of the former. Share
ownership gives the power to vote, not the power to dictate day-to-day
management. The directors of the German company were not the agents of
the English company; they were the agents of the German company. Unless
there was an explicit agency agreement, the distinct legal personalities
must be respected, protecting parent companies from the direct tax
liabilities of their foreign subsidiaries.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Parent-Subsidiary Independence: Complete share ownership by a parent
company does not automatically create an agency relationship. The
subsidiary remains a distinct legal entity responsible for its own
business and tax liabilities.

cases.title: VTB Capital plc v. Nutritek International Corp
cases.facts:
VTB Capital (a UK bank) lent $225 million to a Russian company to buy
assets from Nutritek. The Russian company defaulted. VTB alleged the loan
was obtained through a massive fraud orchestrated by Mr. Malofeev, who
secretly controlled both the borrowing company and Nutritek. VTB sued
Malofeev. Because VTB only had a contract with the borrowing company (not
Malofeev personally), VTB asked the court to pierce the corporate veil
and treat Malofeev as if he were a direct party to the loan contract,
making him personally liable for the breach of contract.
cases.issues:
Can the corporate veil be pierced to make the controller of a company a
direct party to a contract signed only by the company?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (VTB Capital)
VTB argued that Malofeev used the borrowing company as a puppet to
orchestrate a fraud. Under the "evasion principle," the court should
pierce the veil. If the veil is pierced, the legal fiction of the company
falls away, leaving Malofeev as the true contracting party responsible
for the debt.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Nutritek / Malofeev)
Malofeev argued that piercing the veil cannot rewrite history or
contracts. VTB chose to contract with a corporate entity, not with him.
To suddenly make him a party to a contract he never signed would destroy
the foundation of privity of contract.
cases.judgment:
The UK Supreme Court ruled against VTB Capital on the contract claim,
refusing to pierce the veil to make Malofeev a party to the contract.
(VTB was allowed to pursue him in tort for deceit, however).
cases.reasoning:
Lord Neuberger delivered a crucial limitation on the doctrine of piercing
the corporate veil. He held that even in cases of blatant fraud where the
veil might be pierced, the court cannot use this equitable doctrine to
create a new contract. Piercing the veil strips away the corporate
protection; it does not magically forge a signature on a document. It is
a fundamental principle of contract law that a person cannot be bound by
a contract they did not agree to. Therefore, while Malofeev could be sued
for the tort of fraud, he could not be sued for breach of contract via
the piercing of the veil.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Limits of Piercing the Veil: The courts will never pierce the corporate
veil to make the controller of a company liable as a co-contracting party
to a contract entered into exclusively by the company.

cases.title: Greenhalgh v. Arderne Cinemas Ltd
cases.facts:
The company had a provision in its Articles of Association stating that
if any member wished to sell their shares, they must first offer them to
existing members (a right of pre-emption). Mallard, the majority
shareholder, wanted to sell his controlling block of shares to an
outsider. Knowing the minority (Greenhalgh) would block this under the
pre-emption clause, Mallard used his majority voting power to pass a
special resolution altering the Articles. The alteration allowed any
member to sell shares to an outsider if the sale was approved by an
ordinary resolution (which Mallard controlled). Greenhalgh sued, claiming
the alteration was a fraud on the minority.
cases.issues:
What does the phrase "bona fide for the benefit of the company as a
whole" mean when testing the validity of an alteration to the Articles?

Does altering the Articles to remove a minority shareholder's pre-emption
rights constitute a fraud on the minority?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Greenhalgh)
Greenhalgh argued that the alteration was targeted, malicious, and purely
for Mallard's personal financial gain. By stripping away the pre-emption
rights, the alteration was designed to prejudice the minority, not to
benefit the corporate entity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Arderne Cinemas / Mallard)
The defendants argued that the statutory right to alter the Articles is
absolute if the requisite 75% majority is met. They argued it is
beneficial for the company to have shares that are freely transferable,
attracting outside investment, rather than being locked into a hostile
minority.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the defendants, upholding the
validity of the alteration to the Articles.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Evershed MR provided the definitive interpretation of the Allen v.
Gold Reefs test ("bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole").
He held that "the company as a whole" does not mean the corporate entity
as a distinct legal fiction. Instead, it means "the corporators as a
general body." The test is whether a hypothetical, reasonable shareholder
would consider the alteration to be for the benefit of all shareholders
generally. Since making shares more freely transferable is generally
beneficial to shareholders as a class (it increases liquidity), the
alteration was valid. The fact that it practically prejudiced Greenhalgh
in this specific instance did not make it a fraud on the minority.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The "Company as a Whole" Test: When assessing if an alteration of
Articles is valid, courts look at whether it benefits the shareholders as
a general collective, not whether it harms one specific dissenting
member.

cases.title: Pavlides v. Jensen
cases.facts:
A minority shareholder (Pavlides) brought a derivative action on behalf
of the Tunnel Asbestos Cement Company against its directors. Pavlides
alleged that the directors had been grossly negligent in selling an
asbestos mine owned by the company for £182,000, when its true market
value was allegedly over £1,000,000. Crucially, the directors who
authorized the sale did not hold a majority of the voting shares, and
they did not personally pocket any of the money from the sale (it was not
a sale to themselves).
cases.issues:
Does the "fraud on the minority" exception to the rule in Foss v.
Harbottle apply to cases of gross negligence where the directors do not
personally profit?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Pavlides)
Pavlides argued that the negligence was so severe-selling a primary asset
for a fraction of its value-that it amounted to a dereliction of duty
equivalent to fraud. He argued that the minority must be allowed to sue
to protect the company's assets from such catastrophic incompetence.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Jensen / Directors)
The directors relied strictly on Foss v. Harbottle. They argued that mere
negligence, even gross negligence, is an internal management issue.
Unless there is actual fraud or the directors appropriated the company's
property for themselves, the only body with the legal standing to sue the
directors is the company itself, acting through a majority vote.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of the directors, dismissing the
minority shareholder's lawsuit.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly defined the boundaries of the exceptions to Foss v.
Harbottle. Danckwerts J held that to bypass the majority rule, a minority
shareholder must prove actual "fraud" or that the wrongdoers expropriated
corporate property. Mere negligence, incompetence, or poor commercial
judgment does not amount to fraud in equity. Because the directors did
not personally profit from the undervalued sale, their act could
technically be ratified or forgiven by a majority of the shareholders at
a general meeting. Therefore, the minority had no standing to bring a
derivative suit.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Negligence is not Fraud: Minority shareholders cannot bring a derivative
action against directors for negligence or poor business judgment unless
that negligence is coupled with the directors directly expropriating
corporate wealth for their own benefit.

cases.title: Coleman v. Myers
cases.facts:
The Myers family controlled a private, closely-held company. The Chairman
(the father) and the Managing Director (the son) held the majority of
shares. They orchestrated a scheme to buy out the minority shareholders
(who were other relatives). The son recommended the buyout price to the
minority, assuring them it was fair. However, the son possessed highly
confidential information about the company's true asset value and
intended to use the company's own cash reserves to fund his purchase of
their shares. He did not disclose this to the minority relatives, who
sold their shares at a massive undervalue.
cases.issues:
While directors generally owe duties only to the company (Percival v.
Wright), do they owe direct fiduciary duties to individual shareholders
in a closely-held family company during a takeover?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Coleman / Minority Relatives)
The minority argued that this was a family company built on trust. The
son was the financial expert of the family, and they implicitly relied on
his advice regarding the share price. By exploiting that family trust and
withholding vital financial information to enrich himself, he breached a
direct fiduciary duty.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Myers / Directors)
The directors relied heavily on Percival v. Wright. They argued their
legal duty was exclusively to the corporate entity. When buying shares
from other members, it was a standard commercial transaction, and the
principle of caveat emptor (buyer/seller beware) applied.
cases.judgment:
The New Zealand Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the minority
shareholders, ordering the directors to compensate them for the true
value of the shares.
cases.reasoning:
The Court created a powerful exception to the strict rule in Percival v.
Wright. The Court held that while directors do not automatically owe
fiduciary duties to individual shareholders, such a duty can arise based
on the specific facts of the relationship. In a closely-held private
company, where there is a high degree of family dependence, where the
directors possess exclusive insider information, and where the directors
actively advise the minority on a transaction, a direct fiduciary
relationship is forged. The son placed himself in a position of trust and
reliance. Therefore, he had an absolute equitable duty to make full
disclosure of the company's true value before buying their shares.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Fiduciary Duty to Individual Shareholders: In closely-held companies
(quasi-partnerships), the specific dynamics of trust, family relations,
and informational asymmetry can impose a direct fiduciary duty of
disclosure on directors when dealing with minority shareholders.

cases.title: Re Spectrum Plus Ltd
cases.facts:
Spectrum Plus Ltd opened an overdraft account with National Westminster
Bank. To secure the debt, Spectrum granted the bank a charge over its
"book debts" (uncollected invoices/receivables). The debenture document
explicitly labeled this a "Specific [Fixed] Charge." The contract
required Spectrum to pay all collected book debts into a specific account
at the bank. However, Spectrum was allowed to withdraw money from this
account to run its daily business without the bank's prior permission.
When Spectrum went into liquidation, the nature of the charge became
critical: if it was a fixed charge, the bank gets paid first; if
floating, preferential creditors (like employees) get paid before the
bank.
cases.issues:
Is a charge over book debts a "fixed" charge or a "floating" charge if
the company retains the freedom to use the collected proceeds in its
ordinary course of business?
