Does the label applied to the charge in the contract determine its legal
status?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Crown/Preferential Creditors)
The preferential creditors argued that the essence of a fixed charge is
absolute control by the lender. Because Spectrum could freely spend the
money collected from the book debts to buy inventory and pay staff, the
bank did not have control. Therefore, regardless of the label on the
document, it functioned as a floating charge.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (National Westminster Bank)
The Bank relied on a previous precedent (Re New Bullas), arguing that the
parties explicitly contracted to create a fixed charge. They argued that
requiring the money to be paid into a specific bank account was
sufficient control to constitute a fixed charge over the uncollected
debts.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of the preferential creditors,
declaring the charge to be a floating charge, overturning years of
banking practice.
cases.reasoning:
This is the most important corporate finance case of the modern era. The
House of Lords held that the labels used by the parties ("fixed" or
"floating") are entirely irrelevant. The court looks at the legal rights
created by the contract. The defining characteristic of a fixed charge is
that the asset is entirely removed from the company's control; the
company cannot dispose of it without the lender's consent. Because the
bank allowed Spectrum to freely withdraw and spend the cash generated by
the book debts, the charge essentially "hovered" over a fluctuating pool
of assets. This lack of absolute control over the proceeds meant the
charge was legally floating, subordinating the bank to preferential
creditors.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Substance over Form (Charges): The legal classification of a corporate
charge depends entirely on the degree of control the lender actually
exercises over the asset, not the terminology used in the debenture.

Control of Proceeds: To create a fixed charge over book debts, the lender
must totally restrict the company's ability to use the collected cash
(e.g., placing it in a blocked account).

cases.title: Panorama Developments (Guildford) Ltd v. Fidelis Furnishing Fabrics Ltd
cases.facts:
Mr. Bayne was the Company Secretary of Fidelis Furnishing Fabrics Ltd. He
engaged a luxury car hire company (Panorama Developments) to rent a fleet
of Rolls-Royces and Jaguars. He told the car hire company that he was
hiring the cars for important corporate clients of Fidelis. In reality,
Bayne was a fraudster using the luxury cars entirely for his own personal
use. When Panorama sent the massive rental bill to Fidelis, the company
refused to pay, arguing that a Company Secretary is a mere clerk with no
authority to enter into commercial contracts on behalf of the company.
cases.issues:
Does a Company Secretary have the ostensible (apparent) authority to
enter into administrative contracts on behalf of the company?

Has the legal status of the Company Secretary evolved from a mere
clerical role to an executive officer?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Panorama Developments)
Panorama argued that in the modern commercial world, the Company
Secretary is the chief administrative officer of a corporation. An
outsider dealing with the Secretary on administrative matters (like
hiring cars for clients) is entitled to assume that the Secretary has the
authority of the Board to do so.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Fidelis Furnishing)
Fidelis relied on 19th-century precedents which held that a company
secretary is a mere servant whose only duties are to take minutes and
follow direct orders from the board, possessing zero authority to bind
the company to commercial contracts.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Panorama Developments, ordering
Fidelis to pay the car hire bill.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Denning MR officially modernized the role of the Company Secretary.
He explicitly overruled the old Victorian cases, stating that times had
changed. He held that a modern Company Secretary is much more than a mere
clerk; they are the chief administrative officer of the company.
Therefore, the Company Secretary has ostensible authority to enter into
contracts connected with the administrative side of the company's
affairs, such as employing staff, ordering office supplies, and hiring
cars for corporate use. Because hiring cars fell within the apparent
scope of a Secretary's administrative duties, Panorama was protected in
relying on that authority, binding the company.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Authority of the Company Secretary: Established that the Company
Secretary possesses ostensible authority to bind the company in matters
of general corporate administration, elevating the role to an executive
level.

cases.title: Eley v. Positive Government Security Life Assurance Co
cases.facts:
Eley, an ambitious lawyer, helped draft the Articles of Association for
the Positive Government Security Life Assurance Co. He specifically
inserted a clause (Article 118) into the company's constitution stating:
"Mr. William Eley of London shall be the solicitor of the company, and
shall transact all the legal business of the company." Eley also became a
shareholder in the company. After a few years, the directors stopped
using Eley as their lawyer and hired someone else. Eley sued the company
for breach of contract, claiming the Articles constituted a binding
contract guaranteeing his employment.
cases.issues:
Can an "outsider" (someone claiming rights not as a shareholder, but as
an employee or professional) enforce a clause in the Articles of
Association?

Does the fact that the outsider is also a shareholder change their
ability to enforce outsider rights?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Eley)
Eley argued that Section 16 of the Companies Act states that the Articles
bind the company and the members. Since the clause explicitly named him
as the solicitor, and he was a member of the company, the company was
statutorily bound to employ him.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Positive Government Security)
The company argued that the Articles are a contract strictly relating to
the governance of the company and the rights of shareholders qua (in
their capacity as) shareholders. Eley was suing in his capacity as a
solicitor. The company never signed a separate employment contract with
him.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the company, dismissing Eley's
claim for breach of contract.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly interpreted the statutory contract created by the
Articles of Association. The Court held that the Articles only create a
contract between the company and its members in their capacity as
members. The Articles do not create any contractual rights between the
company and third parties (outsiders). Eley was suing to enforce a right
as a solicitor, which is an outsider right. The fact that he
coincidentally held shares did not allow him to use his status as a
member to enforce a right that belonged to him as a lawyer. Since there
was no independent employment contract, he had no claim.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Insider/Outsider Rule: The Articles of Association do not constitute
a contract with any person (even a shareholder) in any capacity other
than as a member. Rights relating to employment, remuneration, or
professional services cannot be enforced solely by relying on the
Articles.

cases.title: Re Saul D Harrison & Sons plc
cases.facts:
Saul D Harrison was a family-run public limited company that had been
running at a heavy loss for years. A minority shareholder (who held non-
voting preference shares) filed an unfair prejudice petition. She argued
that the directors (who held all the voting shares and drew substantial
salaries) were unfairly prejudicing her by continuing to run a failing
business just to keep paying themselves, rather than liquidating the
company, which would have allowed her to recover the capital value of her
preference shares.
cases.issues:
Under what circumstances can a minority shareholder force the liquidation
or buyout of a company on the grounds of "unfair prejudice" based merely
on poor management or continuous financial loss?

Can directors be found guilty of unfair prejudice if they strictly follow
the powers granted to them by the Articles?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Minority Shareholder)
The petitioner argued that she had a "legitimate expectation" that the
board would act commercially. Running a company into the ground purely to
maintain the directors' salaries, while her equity evaporated, was
commercially unfair and highly prejudicial to her interests as an
investor.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Directors)
The directors argued that the Articles granted them the power to manage
the business. The decision to keep trading through a difficult period in
hopes of a turnaround is a standard commercial judgment. They argued the
court should not use the unfair prejudice remedy to second-guess the
honest business decisions of the board.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the directors, dismissing the
unfair prejudice petition.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Hoffmann provided a masterful analysis of the Unfair Prejudice
remedy (Section 459 in the UK, similar to Section 241 in India). He
emphasized that "unfairness" must be tested against the legal framework
of the company-the Articles of Association. Shareholders buy shares
knowing the board has the power to manage. Unless the directors breach
their fiduciary duties, act unlawfully, or breach a specific equitable
agreement (like in a quasi-partnership), poor commercial judgment or
continuing to trade at a loss does not constitute unfair prejudice. Since
the directors honestly believed they could turn the company around, they
were acting within their constitutional powers, and the court will not
interfere.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Objective Test for Unfair Prejudice: Unfairness is not a judge's
subjective view of morality. It requires a breach of the rules (the
Articles) or a breach of an underlying equitable agreement. Poor
commercial management, in the absence of self-dealing or breach of duty,
does not trigger the oppression remedy.

cases.title: Bratton Seymour Service Co Ltd v. Oxborough
cases.facts:
A company was set up specifically to manage a block of residential flats.
The Articles of Association outlined various rules regarding the
management of the property. However, the Articles were completely silent
on whether the shareholders (who were the flat owners) were required to
contribute financially to the upkeep and maintenance of the communal
areas (like the roof and gardens). The company sued one of the flat
owners (Oxborough) to recover maintenance costs, arguing that a term must
be "implied" into the Articles that members must pay for the upkeep,
otherwise, the company's purpose is absurd.
cases.issues:
Can a court imply terms into a company's Articles of Association using
extrinsic evidence (the surrounding circumstances), in the same way it
can imply terms into a standard commercial contract?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Bratton Seymour / Management
Co)
The company argued that under standard contract law, courts routinely
imply terms to give a contract "business efficacy." Since the entire
purpose of the company was to manage the flats, it was glaringly obvious
that the founders intended for the flat owners to pay for the management.
The court should imply this term to prevent the company from failing.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Oxborough / Flat Owner)
Oxborough argued that the Articles of Association are a unique statutory
contract. They are registered publicly so that anyone buying a share can
read exactly what their liabilities are. If courts start implying
unwritten financial obligations based on the founders' secret intentions,
the public register becomes meaningless and dangerous for investors.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of Oxborough, holding that terms
cannot be implied into the Articles using extrinsic evidence. The company
could not force the owner to pay.
cases.reasoning:
The Court drew a strict line between ordinary contracts and the statutory
contract of the Articles. While courts can look at surrounding
circumstances to imply terms into a private contract, they cannot do so
for a company's constitution. The Articles are a public document
registered at Companies House. Third parties (like new buyers of
flats/shares) rely exclusively on the plain text of this registered
document. To imply a heavy financial burden that is not written in the
text would destroy the certainty required by corporate law. If the
company wanted the power to levy maintenance charges, they should have
explicitly written it into the Articles or formally altered them.
cases.legalPrinciples:
No Implied Terms via Extrinsic Evidence: Courts will not imply terms into
the Articles of Association based on the surrounding circumstances or the
original intentions of the founders. The Articles must be interpreted
strictly based on their written text to protect the reliance of future,
innocent shareholders.

cases.title: Sidebottom v. Kershaw, Leese & Co Ltd
cases.facts:
Kershaw, Leese & Co was a private company. Sidebottom held a minority of
shares in the company but also ran a completely separate, heavily
competing business. The majority shareholders passed a special resolution
to alter the company's Articles of Association. The new Article stated
that the directors had the power to require any shareholder who carried
on a competing business to sell their shares to the company's nominees at
a fair price. Sidebottom sued to have the alteration declared void,
arguing it was an oppressive tool designed specifically to expel him.
cases.issues:
Can a company legally alter its Articles to create an expulsion clause
allowing the majority to forcefully buy out a competing minority
shareholder?

Does targeting a specific shareholder through a general alteration of the
Articles constitute a "fraud on the minority"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Sidebottom)
Sidebottom argued that the alteration was deeply mala fide. He claimed a
share is a piece of absolute property, and the majority cannot simply
rewrite the constitution to forcefully expropriate someone's property
just because they dislike the shareholder's external activities.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Kershaw, Leese & Co)
The company argued that having a direct competitor inside the company,
with access to internal financial reports and trade secrets via
shareholder meetings, was a severe commercial threat. The alteration was
a defensive measure enacted in good faith to protect the corporate
entity.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the company, upholding the validity
of the alteration and the expulsion clause.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the Allen v. Gold Reefs test ("bona fide for the
benefit of the company as a whole"). The Court held that protecting a
company from having its internal information accessed by an active
competitor is obviously and objectively for the benefit of the company as
a whole. While the alteration directly prejudiced Sidebottom, the primary
motive of the majority was corporate defense, not personal malice.
Because the new Article included a mechanism ensuring Sidebottom would
receive a fair, independently valued price for his shares, it was not an
unfair expropriation, but a valid commercial safeguard.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Expulsion Clauses: Altering Articles to introduce a power to expel a
member is legally valid, provided it is done bona fide in the genuine
commercial interests of the company (e.g., removing a competitor) and
provides for fair valuation.

cases.title: Derry v. Peek
cases.facts:
The Plymouth, Devonport and District Tramways Company issued a prospectus
to raise capital. The prospectus proudly stated that the company had the
statutory right to use steam-powered trams instead of horse-drawn trams,
making it highly profitable. Peek bought shares relying on this
statement. In reality, the company needed the final consent of the Board
of Trade to use steam power. The directors honestly believed this consent
was a mere formality that would definitely be granted. However, the Board
of Trade surprisingly refused consent. The company went into liquidation,
and Peek sued the directors personally for the tort of deceit (fraudulent
misrepresentation).
cases.issues:
What is the legal standard required to prove "fraud" or "deceit" against
directors regarding false statements in a corporate prospectus?

Can directors be held liable for fraud if they made a false statement
based on an honest, albeit negligent, belief in its truth?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Peek)
Peek argued that the prospectus stated a definitive fact (they had the
right), which was objectively false. As an investor, he relied on the
directors' absolute statement. Their failure to ensure the absolute truth
of their marketing material should make them liable to compensate him.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Derry / Directors)
The directors argued they had no intent to deceive. They had already
received preliminary approvals and honestly, genuinely believed the final
Board of Trade consent was guaranteed. A mistake or over-optimism is not
a fraud.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of the directors, holding them not
liable for the tort of deceit.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Herschell delivered the foundational common law definition of fraud.
He held that for a false statement to be fraudulent, the plaintiff must
prove that the directors made it (1) knowingly, or (2) without belief in
its truth, or (3) recklessly, careless whether it be true or false.
Because the directors honestly believed the statement was true at the
time they made it, they lacked the mens rea (guilty mind) required for
deceit. Mere negligence, even gross negligence or extreme over-optimism,
does not amount to fraud if the belief was genuinely held.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Test for Deceit: Established the strict common law threshold for
fraud in corporate disclosures, protecting directors from personal
liability for honest mistakes. (Note: This harsh outcome led legislatures
to immediately pass statutes, like modern corporate laws, creating strict
liability and negligence-based remedies for prospectus misstatements).

cases.title: R v. Kylsant
cases.facts:
Lord Kylsant, the Chairman of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company,
authorized a prospectus to issue new debenture stock. The prospectus
stated that the company had consistently paid dividends averaging 7% over
the last ten years, including through a recent depression. This statement
was mathematically true. However, the prospectus omitted a catastrophic
fact: for the last several years, the company had actually been making
massive trading losses. It was only able to pay those dividends by
secretly emptying vast reserves accumulated during World War I. Kylsant
was criminally prosecuted for issuing a false prospectus.
cases.issues:
Can a prospectus be legally "false" if every single sentence printed in
it is technically and mathematically true?

Does the deliberate omission of material context create criminal
liability for corporate officers?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Prosecution (The Crown)
The Crown argued that the prospectus was a sophisticated lie. By stating
the dividends but omitting the trading losses, Kylsant created a
deliberate illusion of a thriving, profitable business. The document was
designed to deceive investors into thinking their money was safe.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Lord Kylsant)
Kylsant's defense was strict literalism. He argued that a criminal charge
of issuing a false document cannot stand if no statement in the document
is actually false. The company did pay 7% dividends. There was no
statutory requirement at the time to explicitly detail the source of
those dividends.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Criminal Appeal upheld Lord Kylsant's conviction, and he was
sentenced to 12 months in prison.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the doctrine of the "false impression." The Court
held that a document can be fundamentally false not because of what it
states, but because of what it hides. If a compilation of technically
true statements is deliberately arranged to convey a false impression (in
this case, that the company was currently profitable), the document as a
whole is false. A half-truth is a whole lie in corporate finance. Lord
Kylsant knew the investors would read the dividend history as proof of
current financial health, making his omission a deliberate criminal
deception.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Half-Truth Doctrine: In prospectus law, suppressing material facts to
create a misleading overall impression constitutes fraud, even if every
individual sentence is technically true. Disclosure must be full, frank,
and contextually honest.

cases.title: Lennard's Carrying Co Ltd v. Asiatic Petroleum Co Ltd
cases.facts:
A ship owned by Lennard's Carrying Co was carrying a cargo of benzine
owned by Asiatic Petroleum. Due to the severely defective condition of
the ship's boilers, the ship caught fire and the cargo was destroyed.
Asiatic Petroleum sued the shipowners. Lennard's Carrying Co sought to
rely on Section 502 of the Merchant Shipping Act, which protected
shipowners from liability for fires that happened "without their actual
fault or privity." Mr. Lennard was the Managing Director of the company
and personally knew the boilers were dangerously defective but did
nothing.
cases.issues:
How does the law determine the "actual fault or privity" of an
artificial, juristic entity like a corporation?

Whose mind within the corporate hierarchy represents the "mind of the
company"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Lennard's Carrying Co)
The company argued that it is an abstract legal entity. The fault was the
fault of Mr. Lennard, an agent of the company. Under the statute, the
company itself (the shareholders/entity) had no "actual fault," and
should therefore be protected by the statutory immunity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Asiatic Petroleum)
Asiatic argued that a company has no physical body or mind; it must act
through humans. Mr. Lennard was the absolute boss of the shipping
operations. His fault is indistinguishable from the company's fault.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Asiatic Petroleum, holding the
company fully liable and denying it statutory protection.
cases.reasoning:
Viscount Haldane delivered a watershed judgment regarding corporate
attribution. He stated that a corporation is an abstraction with no mind
of its own. Therefore, the law must find the "directing mind and will" of
the corporation-the person who is the very ego and center of the
personality of the corporation. Mr. Lennard was not merely an employee or
an agent; he was the managing director and the active spirit of the
company. His action was the very action of the company itself. Because
the "directing mind" (Lennard) had actual knowledge of the defect, the
company itself legally possessed "actual fault and privity."
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Alter Ego Doctrine (Directing Mind and Will): A company can be held
personally (rather than vicariously) liable for the acts and state of
mind of its senior officers if those officers represent the "directing
mind and will" of the corporate entity.

cases.title: Tesco Supermarkets Ltd v. Nattrass
cases.facts:
Tesco advertised a promotional discount on washing powder. A customer
went to a Tesco store and found the powder was only available at the
regular, higher price. The customer complained, and Tesco was charged
under the Trade Descriptions Act for offering goods at a false price.
Tesco's defense was that they had a strict corporate policy for pricing,
and the error was entirely the fault of the local branch manager, who had
failed to check the stock and remove the promotional poster. Tesco argued
this was the fault of "another person" (an employee), giving them a
statutory defense.
cases.issues:
Is a local branch manager the "directing mind and will" of a massive
retail corporation?

Can a corporation claim that the negligence of a mid-level manager is the
fault of "another person" rather than the fault of the company itself?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Tesco Supermarkets)
Tesco argued that the Board of Directors sets corporate policy and cannot
possibly oversee every poster in hundreds of stores. The local manager is
an employee (another person). Since the Board took all reasonable
precautions by establishing policies, the company entity itself was not
guilty.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Nattrass / Prosecutor)
The prosecutor argued that the store manager is the absolute
representative of Tesco to the customer. For the purpose of running that
specific store, the manager is Tesco. Therefore, his failure is the
company's failure.
cases.judgment:
The House of Lords ruled in favor of Tesco, acquitting the corporation of
the criminal charge.
cases.reasoning:
The Court significantly narrowed the "directing mind and will" doctrine
from Lennard's Carrying Co. The Court held that a company is only
personally liable for the acts of those who are in actual control of the
company's operations-the Board of Directors, the Managing Director, and
perhaps senior executives. A mere branch manager of a massive supermarket
chain does not represent the "mind" of Tesco. He is a subordinate
employee carrying out orders. Therefore, the manager was legally "another
person." Because the true directing mind (the Board) had exercised due
diligence by creating strict compliance policies, the company could not
be held criminally liable for the manager's localized oversight.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Limitation of Corporate Criminal Liability: In large corporations, the
"directing mind and will" is restricted to top-level management. Mid-
level managers and branch employees are mere agents, and their criminal
negligence cannot automatically be attributed to the corporate entity
itself.

cases.title: Meridian Global Funds Management Asia Ltd v. Securities Commission
cases.facts:
Koo and Ng, two senior investment managers at Meridian Global, used the
company's funds to secretly purchase a 49% stake in a public company
(ENC). Under New Zealand securities law, anyone who acquires more than a
5% stake in a public company must immediately notify the Securities
Commission. Koo and Ng deliberately failed to file the notice. The
Commission sought to fine Meridian Global (the corporate entity) for the
breach. Meridian argued that the Board of Directors and the MD knew
nothing about the scheme, and therefore, under the Tesco v. Nattrass
rule, the managers were not the "directing mind" and the company could
not be liable.
cases.issues:
Is the Tesco "directing mind and will" test the only way to attribute the
actions of an employee to a corporate entity?

How should courts determine corporate liability when statutory duties are
breached by employees who are not top-tier executives?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Meridian Global)
Meridian relied on strict orthodoxy. They argued that corporate liability
requires the knowledge of the Board. Since the rogue managers actively
hid the transaction from the Board, the "mind" of Meridian never knew
about the 49% stake, so the company couldn't have failed to report it.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Securities Commission)
The Commission argued that if companies can only be liable when the Board
knows about a transaction, large financial institutions could easily
evade regulatory laws by delegating trading power to managers and
pleading ignorance.
cases.judgment:
The Privy Council ruled in favor of the Securities Commission, holding
Meridian Global liable for the breach.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Hoffmann revolutionized the law of corporate attribution. He stated
that the "directing mind and will" is not a magic, one-size-fits-all
formula. Instead, courts must look at the specific statute in question
and ask: Whose act was intended by the legislature to count as the act of
the company? The purpose of the securities law was to mandate fast
disclosure of major trades. The company gave Koo and Ng the actual
authority to make those massive trades. Therefore, for the specific
purpose of this disclosure statute, the knowledge of the person who
actually made the trade (the investment manager) must be attributed to
the company. Waiting for the Board to find out would defeat the entire
purpose of the regulatory law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Special Rules of Attribution: The "directing mind" test is not absolute.
Courts will attribute the knowledge and acts of lower-level employees to
the company if the specific purpose and policy of the relevant statute
require it to prevent regulatory evasion.

cases.title: Cook v. Deeks
cases.facts:
The Toronto Construction Company had four directors who each owned 25% of
the shares: Deeks, his brother, Hinds, and Cook. The company specialized
in railway construction. Deeks, his brother, and Hinds had a falling out
with Cook. When the Canadian Pacific Railway approached the company with
a massive new contract, Deeks and his allies secretly negotiated the
contract in their own names. They then formed a brand new company and
took the contract for themselves. To protect themselves, they used their
combined 75% majority voting power in Toronto Construction to pass a
shareholder resolution declaring that the company had no interest in the
railway contract. Cook sued them on behalf of the company.
cases.issues:
Can majority directors/shareholders appropriate a corporate contract for
themselves?

Can the majority use their voting power in a general meeting to ratify
their own breach of fiduciary duty and expropriation of corporate
property?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Cook)
Cook argued that the contract was a "corporate opportunity" that belonged
to Toronto Construction. The directors used their positions to steal the
company's property. The shareholder ratification was a blatant fraud on
the minority, as the thieves were simply voting to pardon themselves.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Deeks and others)
The defendants argued that under Foss v. Harbottle, the majority rules.
The shareholders voted 75% to 25% that the company did not want the
contract. Since the company "rejected" the contract, there was no breach
in the directors taking it.
cases.judgment:
The Privy Council ruled in favor of Cook, ordering Deeks and his allies
to hold the profits of the contract in trust for the Toronto Construction
Company.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on the limits of majority rule. The
Court held that directors who negotiate a contract on behalf of a company
stand in a fiduciary position and cannot divert that contract to
themselves. This contract "belonged in equity" to the company. Regarding
the shareholder vote, the Court ruled that while a majority can ratify
simple negligence or internal errors, they cannot ratify the outright
theft of corporate assets. Permitting majority shareholders to vote to
give themselves the company's property would render minority rights
meaningless. The ratification was void as a fraud on the minority.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Expropriation of Corporate Property: Directors cannot divert corporate
opportunities to themselves.

Unratifiable Wrongs: The expropriation of corporate property or
opportunities by the majority is an unratifiable breach of duty,
constituting a direct fraud on the minority and triggering an exception
to majority rule.

cases.title: Estmanco (Kilner House) Ltd v. Greater London Council
cases.facts:
The Greater London Council (GLC) owned a block of flats. They decided to
sell them to private owners and formed a company (Estmanco) to manage the
block. The GLC held all the voting shares, while the 60 flat buyers held
non-voting shares. The GLC signed an agreement with Estmanco promising to
sell all the flats. However, following a local election, the political
control of the GLC changed. The new council changed policy and decided to
keep the remaining unsold flats for public housing, breaching the
agreement. Estmanco's directors sued the GLC for breach of contract. In
response, the GLC used its 100% voting power to pass a shareholder
resolution instructing the directors to drop the lawsuit against the GLC.
A flat owner sued.
cases.issues:
Can a majority shareholder use its voting power to direct the company to
abandon a valid legal claim against that very majority shareholder?

Does stifling a corporate lawsuit constitute a "fraud on the minority"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Flat Owner / Minority)
The plaintiff argued that the GLC was using its voting power to pardon
its own breach of contract. By forcing the company to drop the lawsuit,
the GLC was expropriating the company's legal asset (the right to sue)
for its own benefit, leaving the non-voting shareholders trapped in a
half-empty building.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (GLC)
The GLC argued that it was the 100% voting shareholder. Under corporate
democracy, the voting majority has the absolute right to direct the
company's litigation strategy, including the decision not to sue.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of the minority shareholder,
allowing the derivative action to proceed and ignoring the GLC's
resolution to drop the suit.
cases.reasoning:
Megarry V-C expanded the concept of "fraud on the minority." He held that
a corporate cause of action (the right to sue) is an asset of the
company. A majority shareholder cannot use their voting power to strip
the company of this asset specifically to protect themselves from
liability. The GLC's resolution was not an honest commercial decision
regarding litigation risks; it was a blatant abuse of power to commit a
wrong and then prevent the victim (the company) from seeking justice.
This maneuver was a textbook fraud on the minority, allowing the non-
voting shareholders to step in and sue the GLC on the company's behalf.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Deprivation of Corporate Action: It is a fraud on the minority for
majority shareholders to use their voting power to force the company to
abandon a valid legal claim against the majority themselves.

cases.title: Flitcroft's Case
cases.facts:
The Exchange Banking Company had suffered severe financial losses and had
no actual profits. However, the directors wished to keep the appearance
of a thriving bank. They presented deliberately falsified accounts to the
shareholders at the general meeting, categorizing massive bad debts as
solid assets. Based on these fraudulent accounts, the shareholders voted
to declare a dividend. The dividend was paid out, but because there were
no profits, the money actually came directly out of the company's
capital. When the bank went into liquidation, the liquidator sued the
directors to recover the money.
cases.issues:
What is the legal consequence of a company paying dividends out of its
paid-up capital rather than its profits?

Are directors personally liable if the shareholders formally approved the
dividend payment in a general meeting?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Liquidator)
The liquidator argued that paying dividends out of capital is strictly
ultra vires the company. The capital is a trust fund for the creditors.
The directors breached their fiduciary duty by falsifying the accounts to
orchestrate this illegal reduction of capital.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Flitcroft / Directors)
The directors argued that the shareholders-the owners of the company-had
passed a formal resolution authorizing the dividend. Therefore, the
payment was ratified by the company, and the directors were simply
executing the will of the members.
cases.judgment:
The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the liquidator, ordering the
directors to personally replace the capital illegally distributed as
dividends.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly enforced the doctrine of capital maintenance. It held
that it is a fundamental, unalterable rule of corporate law that
dividends can only be paid out of bona fide profits, never out of
capital. Because paying dividends from capital is ultra vires the
company, it is completely void. It cannot be ratified or legalized, not
even if 100% of the shareholders agree to it. The shareholders'
resolution was a nullity because it was based on the directors'
fraudulent accounts. The directors, as trustees of the corporate funds,
misapplied the capital and were held strictly, jointly, and severally
liable to replace every penny.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Dividends Out of Capital: The payment of dividends out of corporate
capital is strictly ultra vires and illegal, functioning as a fraud on
the creditors.

Director Liability for Illegal Distributions: Directors who facilitate
the illegal distribution of capital (even with shareholder approval) are
personally liable to restore the funds to the company.

cases.title: Wood v. Odessa Waterworks Co
cases.facts:
The Odessa Waterworks Company was highly profitable and had generated a
massive surplus of profits. However, instead of keeping the profits in
cash, the company had reinvested all the money into constructing new
water mains. When the time came to declare a dividend, the company had no
liquid cash to pay the shareholders. To solve this, the directors passed
a resolution to declare a dividend, but stated it would be paid by
issuing the shareholders "debenture bonds" (debt certificates) bearing
interest, rather than actual cash. Wood, a shareholder, sued for an
injunction to stop this.
cases.issues:
Under standard corporate law, does the declaration of a "dividend" imply
a mandatory payment in cash?

Can a company force its shareholders to accept debt instruments
(debentures) in lieu of a cash dividend?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Wood)
Wood argued that the Articles of Association stated that the directors
could declare a "dividend to be paid to the members." He argued that the
plain English meaning of paying a dividend is the distribution of money.
Forcing him to accept a bond essentially forces him to lend his dividend
back to the company, which he never agreed to.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Odessa Waterworks)
The company argued that the profits were real; they had simply been
capitalized into infrastructure. Issuing debentures was a practical
commercial solution to distribute value to the shareholders without
bankrupting the company's cash flow.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of Wood, granting an injunction to
stop the issuance of the debenture dividends.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strict interpretation of corporate distributions.
Stirling J held that the word "dividend" inherently means a payment in
cash. While a company's Articles of Association can be drafted to
explicitly allow dividends to be paid in shares (scrip dividends) or
other assets, Odessa Waterworks' Articles only used the word "paid." The
Court held that "paid" prima facie means paid in money. A debenture is
not money; it is merely a promise to pay money in the future. The company
cannot unilaterally alter the contractual nature of a dividend by forcing
shareholders to become creditors against their will.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Cash Dividend Rule: Unless the Articles of Association explicitly
authorize otherwise, the declaration of a corporate dividend creates a
legal debt owed to the shareholder that must be satisfied by a payment in
actual cash, not through the issuance of debt instruments or other
assets.
